lessons.learning_objective: Classify polynomials by degree and number of terms, write them in standard form, and add and subtract them
lessons.key_concepts: Monomial, binomial, trinomial; degree of a term and of a polynomial; standard form in descending degree; combine like terms (same variable and exponent); subtracting a polynomial means adding its opposite, distributing -1 to every term; polynomials are closed under addition and subtraction
lessons.prerequisites: Combining like terms, distributive property, exponents
lessons.key_vocabulary: polynomial, monomial, binomial, trinomial, degree, leading coefficient, standard form, like terms
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute (5x^2 + 3x - 4) - (2x^2 - x + 6) as 3x^2 + 2x + 2, subtracting only the first term and not distributing the negative to -x and 6 (correct: 3x^2 + 4x - 10)
lessons.real_world_hook: Adding the cost polynomials for two parts of a business to get total cost

lessons.learning_objective: Multiply polynomials using the distributive property, and recognize the special products (a + b)^2, (a - b)^2, and (a + b)(a - b)
lessons.key_concepts: Multiply a monomial by a polynomial; multiply binomials by distributing each term (area model or FOIL); multiply a binomial by a trinomial; (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; (a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2; polynomials are closed under multiplication
lessons.prerequisites: Adding polynomials, exponent product rule, distributive property
lessons.key_vocabulary: distributive property, FOIL, area model, square of a binomial, difference of squares, product
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write (x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 9, dropping the middle term 6x
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the area of a square garden after each side is extended by 3 feet: (x + 3)^2

lessons.lesson_title: Factoring Out the Greatest Common Factor
lessons.learning_objective: Factor the greatest common factor from a polynomial and factor four-term polynomials by grouping
lessons.key_concepts: The GCF of the coefficients and of each variable (lowest power that appears in every term); factoring is the reverse of distributing; check by multiplying back; factoring out a negative GCF; grouping: x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + 6 = x^2(x + 2) + 3(x + 2) = (x + 2)(x^2 + 3); a binomial can be a common factor
lessons.prerequisites: Greatest common factor of numbers, multiplying polynomials
lessons.key_vocabulary: factor, greatest common factor, factored form, grouping, common binomial factor
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor 6x^3 + 9x as 3x(2x^2 + 3x) or leave out the 1 when factoring 4x^2 + 4x as 4x(x), forgetting that 4x / 4x = 1 (correct: 4x(x + 1))
lessons.real_world_hook: Rewriting a projectile height expression -16t^2 + 48t as -16t(t - 3) to see when the height is zero

lessons.learning_objective: Factor trinomials of the form x^2 + bx + c by finding two numbers with product c and sum b
lessons.key_concepts: Find integers m and n with mn = c and m + n = b, then x^2 + bx + c = (x + m)(x + n); sign patterns: c positive means both factors have the same sign as b, c negative means opposite signs; factor out a GCF first; some trinomials are prime over the integers
lessons.prerequisites: Multiplying binomials, integer operations, GCF factoring
lessons.key_vocabulary: trinomial, factor pair, product, sum, prime polynomial
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor x^2 - 5x - 14 as (x - 7)(x - 2), choosing numbers that multiply to positive 14 instead of -14 (correct: (x - 7)(x + 2))
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the dimensions of a rectangular patio whose area is x^2 + 7x + 12 square feet

lessons.lesson_title: Factoring Trinomials with a Not Equal to 1
lessons.learning_objective: Factor trinomials of the form ax^2 + bx + c with a not equal to 1 using the AC (grouping) method or guess and check
lessons.key_concepts: Factor out any GCF first; AC method: find m and n with mn = ac and m + n = b, split bx into mx + nx, then factor by grouping; check by multiplying; e.g. 6x^2 + 7x - 3: ac = -18, m = 9, n = -2, giving 6x^2 + 9x - 2x - 3 = (2x + 3)(3x - 1)
lessons.prerequisites: Factoring trinomials with a = 1, factoring by grouping
lessons.key_vocabulary: AC method, grouping, leading coefficient, split the middle term
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor 2x^2 + 7x + 3 by finding numbers that multiply to 3 and add to 7 (ignoring a = 2), or write (x + 3)(x + 1/2) instead of (2x + 1)(x + 3)
lessons.real_world_hook: Factoring the expression for the area of a poster, 6x^2 + 7x - 3, to find possible side lengths

lessons.lesson_title: Difference of Squares and Perfect-Square Trinomials
lessons.learning_objective: Recognize and factor differences of two squares and perfect-square trinomials, and factor polynomials completely
lessons.key_concepts: a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2 and a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2; check that the first and last terms are perfect squares and the middle term is 2ab; a sum of squares x^2 + 9 does not factor over the real numbers; factor completely, e.g. x^4 - 16 = (x^2 + 4)(x + 2)(x - 2); seeing structure such as x^4 - y^4 as (x^2)^2 - (y^2)^2
lessons.key_vocabulary: difference of squares, perfect-square trinomial, sum of squares, factor completely, structure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor x^2 + 25 as (x + 5)(x + 5) or (x + 5)(x - 5); students stop at (x^2 + 4)(x^2 - 4) when factoring x^4 - 16 without factoring x^2 - 4

lessons.learning_objective: Simplify expressions using the product, quotient, power of a power, power of a product, and power of a quotient rules
lessons.key_concepts: x^m * x^n = x^(m+n); x^m / x^n = x^(m-n) for x != 0; (x^m)^n = x^(mn); (xy)^n = x^n y^n; (x/y)^n = x^n / y^n; rules apply only to the same base; coefficients multiply normally
lessons.prerequisites: Exponents as repeated multiplication, order of operations
lessons.key_vocabulary: base, exponent, power, product rule, quotient rule, power of a power, power of a product
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students simplify x^3 * x^4 as x^12, multiplying exponents instead of adding them; students simplify (3x^2)^3 as 3x^6, raising only the variable and not the coefficient (correct: 27x^6)
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing data storage sizes: a terabyte is 2^40 bytes and a kilobyte is 2^10 bytes, so a terabyte holds 2^30 kilobytes

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate and simplify expressions with zero and negative integer exponents, writing results with positive exponents
lessons.key_concepts: x^0 = 1 for x != 0, explained by the quotient rule x^n/x^n; x^(-n) = 1/x^n; a negative exponent in the denominator moves to the numerator: 1/x^(-n) = x^n; negative exponents do not make a number negative; scientific notation with negative powers of 10
lessons.key_vocabulary: zero exponent, negative exponent, reciprocal, scientific notation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students evaluate 4^(-2) as -16 or -8 instead of 1/16; students simplify 5x^0 as 1 instead of 5
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing the width of a human hair, about 0.00008 m, as 8 * 10^(-5) m

lessons.learning_objective: Simplify square roots of numbers and variable expressions by factoring out perfect squares, and connect square roots to rational exponents
lessons.key_concepts: sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a) sqrt(b) for a, b >= 0; factor out the largest perfect square: sqrt(72) = sqrt(36 * 2) = 6 sqrt(2); simplified form has no perfect-square factors under the radical; sqrt(x^2) = |x|; x^(1/2) = sqrt(x) and x^(1/n) = n-th root of x, so (x^(1/2))^2 = x by the power rule
lessons.prerequisites: Perfect squares, prime factorization, exponent rules
lessons.key_vocabulary: radical, radicand, square root, perfect square, simplest radical form, rational exponent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students simplify sqrt(72) as 3 sqrt(8) and stop, missing that 8 still contains the perfect square 4 (correct: 6 sqrt(2)); students write sqrt(9 + 16) = 3 + 4 = 7 instead of 5
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the exact diagonal of a 6 ft by 6 ft square room: sqrt(72) = 6 sqrt(2) ft

lessons.learning_objective: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide radical expressions, and rationalize denominators
lessons.key_concepts: Add or subtract only like radicals (same radicand after simplifying): 3 sqrt(2) + 5 sqrt(2) = 8 sqrt(2), and sqrt(12) + sqrt(27) = 2 sqrt(3) + 3 sqrt(3) = 5 sqrt(3); multiply coefficients and radicands: (2 sqrt(3))(4 sqrt(5)) = 8 sqrt(15); distribute with radicals; rationalize a monomial denominator: 6/sqrt(3) = 6 sqrt(3)/3 = 2 sqrt(3)
lessons.prerequisites: Simplifying square roots, combining like terms, distributive property
lessons.key_vocabulary: like radicals, rationalize the denominator, conjugate, radicand
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students add sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) to get sqrt(5); students write 2 sqrt(3) * 4 sqrt(5) as 8 sqrt(8) by adding the radicands

lessons.learning_objective: Simplify expressions using the product, quotient, power of a power, power of a product, and power of a quotient rules
lessons.key_concepts: x^m * x^n = x^(m+n); x^m / x^n = x^(m-n) for x != 0; (x^m)^n = x^(mn); (xy)^n = x^n y^n; (x/y)^n = x^n / y^n; rules apply only to the same base; coefficients multiply normally
lessons.prerequisites: Exponents as repeated multiplication, order of operations
lessons.key_vocabulary: base, exponent, power, product rule, quotient rule, power of a power, power of a product
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students simplify x^3 * x^4 as x^12, multiplying exponents instead of adding them; students simplify (3x^2)^3 as 3x^6, raising only the variable and not the coefficient (correct: 27x^6)
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing data storage sizes: a terabyte is 2^40 bytes and a kilobyte is 2^10 bytes, so a terabyte holds 2^30 kilobytes

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate and simplify expressions with zero and negative integer exponents, writing results with positive exponents
lessons.key_concepts: x^0 = 1 for x != 0, explained by the quotient rule x^n/x^n; x^(-n) = 1/x^n; a negative exponent in the denominator moves to the numerator: 1/x^(-n) = x^n; negative exponents do not make a number negative; scientific notation with negative powers of 10
lessons.key_vocabulary: zero exponent, negative exponent, reciprocal, scientific notation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students evaluate 4^(-2) as -16 or -8 instead of 1/16; students simplify 5x^0 as 1 instead of 5
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing the width of a human hair, about 0.00008 m, as 8 * 10^(-5) m

lessons.learning_objective: Simplify square roots of numbers and variable expressions by factoring out perfect squares, and connect square roots to rational exponents
lessons.key_concepts: sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a) sqrt(b) for a, b >= 0; factor out the largest perfect square: sqrt(72) = sqrt(36 * 2) = 6 sqrt(2); simplified form has no perfect-square factors under the radical; sqrt(x^2) = |x|; x^(1/2) = sqrt(x) and x^(1/n) = n-th root of x, so (x^(1/2))^2 = x by the power rule
lessons.prerequisites: Perfect squares, prime factorization, exponent rules
lessons.key_vocabulary: radical, radicand, square root, perfect square, simplest radical form, rational exponent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students simplify sqrt(72) as 3 sqrt(8) and stop, missing that 8 still contains the perfect square 4 (correct: 6 sqrt(2)); students write sqrt(9 + 16) = 3 + 4 = 7 instead of 5
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the exact diagonal of a 6 ft by 6 ft square room: sqrt(72) = 6 sqrt(2) ft

lessons.learning_objective: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide radical expressions, and rationalize denominators
lessons.key_concepts: Add or subtract only like radicals (same radicand after simplifying): 3 sqrt(2) + 5 sqrt(2) = 8 sqrt(2), and sqrt(12) + sqrt(27) = 2 sqrt(3) + 3 sqrt(3) = 5 sqrt(3); multiply coefficients and radicands: (2 sqrt(3))(4 sqrt(5)) = 8 sqrt(15); distribute with radicals; rationalize a monomial denominator: 6/sqrt(3) = 6 sqrt(3)/3 = 2 sqrt(3)
lessons.prerequisites: Simplifying square roots, combining like terms, distributive property
lessons.key_vocabulary: like radicals, rationalize the denominator, conjugate, radicand
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students add sqrt(2) + sqrt(3) to get sqrt(5); students write 2 sqrt(3) * 4 sqrt(5) as 8 sqrt(8) by adding the radicands
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the exact perimeter of a triangle with sides sqrt(8), sqrt(18), and sqrt(50) feet: 2 sqrt(2) + 3 sqrt(2) + 5 sqrt(2) = 10 sqrt(2) ft

lessons.lesson_title: Rational and Irrational Sums and Products
lessons.learning_objective: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational, the sum of a rational and an irrational number is irrational, and the product of a nonzero rational and an irrational number is irrational
lessons.key_concepts: Rational numbers can be written as a/b with integers a, b and b != 0; irrationals cannot (sqrt(2), pi); rational + rational = (ad + bc)/(bd) is rational; proof by contradiction that rational + irrational is irrational: if r + x = q then x = q - r would be rational; nonzero rational times irrational is irrational; irrational + irrational and irrational times irrational can be either (sqrt(2) * sqrt(2) = 2)
lessons.key_vocabulary: rational number, irrational number, closure, proof by contradiction, counterexample
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students claim the product of two irrational numbers is always irrational, missing the counterexample sqrt(2) * sqrt(2) = 2; students claim 0 * sqrt(2) is irrational, forgetting the nonzero condition
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why a square tile with area 2 square inches can never have a side length measured exactly by a ruler marked in fractions

lessons.learning_objective: Classify polynomials by degree and number of terms, write them in standard form, and add and subtract them
lessons.key_concepts: Monomial, binomial, trinomial; degree of a term and of a polynomial; standard form in descending degree; combine like terms (same variable and exponent); subtracting a polynomial means adding its opposite, distributing -1 to every term; polynomials are closed under addition and subtraction
lessons.prerequisites: Combining like terms, distributive property, exponents
lessons.key_vocabulary: polynomial, monomial, binomial, trinomial, degree, leading coefficient, standard form, like terms
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute (5x^2 + 3x - 4) - (2x^2 - x + 6) as 3x^2 + 2x + 2, subtracting only the first term and not distributing the negative to -x and 6 (correct: 3x^2 + 4x - 10)
lessons.real_world_hook: Adding the cost polynomials for two parts of a business to get total cost

lessons.learning_objective: Multiply polynomials using the distributive property, and recognize the special products (a + b)^2, (a - b)^2, and (a + b)(a - b)
lessons.key_concepts: Multiply a monomial by a polynomial; multiply binomials by distributing each term (area model or FOIL); multiply a binomial by a trinomial; (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2; (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; (a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2; polynomials are closed under multiplication
lessons.prerequisites: Adding polynomials, exponent product rule, distributive property
lessons.key_vocabulary: distributive property, FOIL, area model, square of a binomial, difference of squares, product
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write (x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 9, dropping the middle term 6x
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the area of a square garden after each side is extended by 3 feet: (x + 3)^2

lessons.lesson_title: Factoring Out the Greatest Common Factor
lessons.learning_objective: Factor the greatest common factor from a polynomial and factor four-term polynomials by grouping
lessons.key_concepts: The GCF of the coefficients and of each variable (lowest power that appears in every term); factoring is the reverse of distributing; check by multiplying back; factoring out a negative GCF; grouping: x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + 6 = x^2(x + 2) + 3(x + 2) = (x + 2)(x^2 + 3); a binomial can be a common factor
lessons.prerequisites: Greatest common factor of numbers, multiplying polynomials
lessons.key_vocabulary: factor, greatest common factor, factored form, grouping, common binomial factor
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor 6x^3 + 9x as 3x(2x^2 + 3x) or leave out the 1 when factoring 4x^2 + 4x as 4x(x), forgetting that 4x / 4x = 1 (correct: 4x(x + 1))
lessons.real_world_hook: Rewriting a projectile height expression -16t^2 + 48t as -16t(t - 3) to see when the height is zero

lessons.learning_objective: Factor trinomials of the form x^2 + bx + c by finding two numbers with product c and sum b
lessons.key_concepts: Find integers m and n with mn = c and m + n = b, then x^2 + bx + c = (x + m)(x + n); sign patterns: c positive means both factors have the same sign as b, c negative means opposite signs; factor out a GCF first; some trinomials are prime over the integers
lessons.prerequisites: Multiplying binomials, integer operations, GCF factoring
lessons.key_vocabulary: trinomial, factor pair, product, sum, prime polynomial
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor x^2 - 5x - 14 as (x - 7)(x - 2), choosing numbers that multiply to positive 14 instead of -14 (correct: (x - 7)(x + 2))
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the dimensions of a rectangular patio whose area is x^2 + 7x + 12 square feet

lessons.lesson_title: Factoring Trinomials with a Not Equal to 1
lessons.learning_objective: Factor trinomials of the form ax^2 + bx + c with a not equal to 1 using the AC (grouping) method or guess and check
lessons.key_concepts: Factor out any GCF first; AC method: find m and n with mn = ac and m + n = b, split bx into mx + nx, then factor by grouping; check by multiplying; e.g. 6x^2 + 7x - 3: ac = -18, m = 9, n = -2, giving 6x^2 + 9x - 2x - 3 = (2x + 3)(3x - 1)
lessons.prerequisites: Factoring trinomials with a = 1, factoring by grouping
lessons.key_vocabulary: AC method, grouping, leading coefficient, split the middle term
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor 2x^2 + 7x + 3 by finding numbers that multiply to 3 and add to 7 (ignoring a = 2), or write (x + 3)(x + 1/2) instead of (2x + 1)(x + 3)
lessons.real_world_hook: Factoring the expression for the area of a poster, 6x^2 + 7x - 3, to find possible side lengths

lessons.lesson_title: Difference of Squares and Perfect-Square Trinomials
lessons.learning_objective: Recognize and factor differences of two squares and perfect-square trinomials, and factor polynomials completely
lessons.key_concepts: a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2 and a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2; check that the first and last terms are perfect squares and the middle term is 2ab; a sum of squares x^2 + 9 does not factor over the real numbers; factor completely, e.g. x^4 - 16 = (x^2 + 4)(x + 2)(x - 2); seeing structure such as x^4 - y^4 as (x^2)^2 - (y^2)^2
lessons.key_vocabulary: difference of squares, perfect-square trinomial, sum of squares, factor completely, structure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students factor x^2 + 25 as (x + 5)(x + 5) or (x + 5)(x - 5); students stop at (x^2 + 4)(x^2 - 4) when factoring x^4 - 16 without factoring x^2 - 4

lessons.lesson_title: Change in Tandem and Average Rates of Change
lessons.learning_objective: Describe how input and output values change together, identify where a function is increasing, decreasing, concave up or concave down, and compute average rates of change
lessons.key_concepts: A function pairs each input with exactly one output; increasing means outputs grow as inputs grow; concave up means rates of change are increasing, concave down means they are decreasing; average rate of change on [a, b] is (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a), the slope of the secant line; the rate of change at a point can be approximated with average rates on very small intervals
lessons.prerequisites: Slope, function notation, reading graphs and tables
lessons.key_vocabulary: function, domain, range, increasing, decreasing, concave up, concave down, average rate of change, secant line
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute average rate of change as (b - a)/(f(b) - f(a)), inverting the ratio; students think a graph that is increasing must be concave up, e.g. calling the graph of y = sqrt(x) concave up because it rises
lessons.real_world_hook: A runner's distance-time data shows she is still speeding up after mile 2 even though her pace chart looks flat

lessons.lesson_title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
lessons.learning_objective: Show that linear functions have a constant rate of change and quadratic functions have average rates of change that change at a constant rate
lessons.key_concepts: Over equal-length input intervals, a linear function has equal output differences; a quadratic has first differences that form an arithmetic sequence and constant second differences; the sign of the second difference tells concavity; for f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c the second differences over step h are 2ah^2
lessons.prerequisites: Linear functions, quadratic functions, average rate of change
lessons.key_vocabulary: constant rate of change, first difference, second difference, linear, quadratic, concavity
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students check for a quadratic by looking at first differences in a table with unequal input spacing (x = 0, 1, 3, 6) and conclude the data is not quadratic
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracking the height of a dropped phone every 0.1 second and noticing the drop distances grow by the same amount each step

lessons.lesson_title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
lessons.learning_objective: Identify degree, leading coefficient, relative and absolute extrema, and points of inflection of polynomial functions from graphs and equations
lessons.key_concepts: A polynomial of degree n has at most n - 1 turning points; relative maxima and minima occur where the function changes from increasing to decreasing or vice versa; points of inflection occur where the rate of change changes from increasing to decreasing (concavity changes); global versus local extrema on a domain
lessons.key_vocabulary: polynomial, degree, leading coefficient, relative maximum, relative minimum, absolute extremum, point of inflection, turning point
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say a degree-4 polynomial must have exactly 3 turning points (y = x^4 has only 1); students identify a point of inflection as any point where the graph crosses the x-axis
lessons.real_world_hook: A roller-coaster designer locating the steepest point of a drop modeled by a cubic

lessons.learning_objective: Find real and complex zeros of polynomials, connect zeros to factors and x-intercepts, and use multiplicity to describe graph behavior
lessons.key_concepts: If f(a) = 0 then (x - a) is a factor; a degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex zeros counting multiplicity; non-real zeros of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs a + bi and a - bi; odd multiplicity means the graph crosses the x-axis, even multiplicity means it touches and turns; even functions f(-x) = f(x) and odd functions f(-x) = -f(x)
lessons.prerequisites: Factoring, quadratic formula, imaginary unit i
lessons.key_vocabulary: zero, root, x-intercept, multiplicity, complex conjugate, even function, odd function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write the factor for zero x = -3 as (x - 3) instead of (x + 3); students assume a cubic with zeros 2 and 1 + i is complete without the conjugate zero 1 - i; students think a zero of multiplicity 2 makes the graph cross the axis
lessons.real_world_hook: Engineers check whether a polynomial transfer function has non-real zeros to predict oscillation in a bridge model

lessons.learning_objective: Determine the end behavior of polynomial functions using the degree and leading coefficient, written with limit notation
lessons.key_concepts: As x -> +/- infinity the leading term dominates; even degree means both ends go the same direction, odd degree means opposite directions; the sign of the leading coefficient determines up or down; limit notation lim x->infinity f(x) = -infinity
lessons.prerequisites: Polynomial degree, exponents, multiplying out factored polynomials
lessons.key_vocabulary: end behavior, leading term, limit notation, unbounded, dominant term
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students read the leading coefficient of f(x) = (2 - x)(x + 1)^2 as positive because the first number written is 2, when the leading term is actually -x^3
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why a cubic profit model cannot be trusted for very large production levels

lessons.learning_objective: Determine horizontal asymptotes and end behavior of rational functions by comparing the degrees of the numerator and denominator
lessons.key_concepts: End behavior is governed by the ratio of leading terms; degree of numerator < degree of denominator gives y = 0; equal degrees give y = ratio of leading coefficients; numerator degree exactly one more gives a slant asymptote; larger numerator degree means the ratio of leading terms is unbounded; limit notation for horizontal asymptotes
lessons.key_vocabulary: rational function, horizontal asymptote, slant (oblique) asymptote, end behavior, leading term ratio
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say f(x) = (3x^2 + 1)/(x^2 - 4) has horizontal asymptote y = 0 because they compare constant terms or ignore equal degrees; students believe a graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote
lessons.real_world_hook: The concentration of a medicine in the bloodstream, C(t) = 5t/(t^2 + 1), leveling off toward 0 over time

lessons.lesson_title: Rational Functions: Zeros, Vertical Asymptotes, and Holes
lessons.learning_objective: Find zeros, vertical asymptotes, and holes of rational functions and describe behavior near vertical asymptotes using limits
lessons.key_concepts: Real zeros of a rational function are zeros of the numerator that are in the domain; a zero of the denominator that is not canceled by the numerator gives a vertical asymptote with one-sided limits approaching +/- infinity; a common factor that cancels completely gives a hole at that x-value, whose y-coordinate comes from the simplified function; sign analysis near the asymptote
lessons.prerequisites: Factoring, rational function end behavior, domain
lessons.key_vocabulary: vertical asymptote, hole (removable discontinuity), one-sided limit, zero, domain restriction, sign chart
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say f(x) = (x - 2)(x + 1)/(x - 2) has a vertical asymptote at x = 2 instead of a hole at (2, 3); students list x = 2 as a zero of that function
lessons.real_world_hook: Cost per item C(n) = (500 + 2n)/n blowing up as the number of items n approaches 0

lessons.lesson_title: Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
lessons.learning_objective: Rewrite polynomial and rational expressions in equivalent forms, including polynomial long division and the binomial theorem, to reveal key features
lessons.key_concepts: Standard form reveals end behavior, factored form reveals zeros; long division writes a rational function as quotient + remainder/divisor, revealing slant asymptotes; the binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle expand (a + b)^n
lessons.key_vocabulary: standard form, factored form, polynomial long division, quotient, remainder, binomial theorem, Pascal's triangle
lessons.common_misconceptions: In long division students forget a placeholder 0x term when dividing x^3 - 8 by x - 2 and get a wrong quotient; students expand (x + 2)^3 as x^3 + 8
lessons.real_world_hook: Expanding (1 + r)^n to estimate the first few terms of compound interest growth

lessons.learning_objective: Apply and interpret additive and multiplicative transformations of functions, including g(x) = a f(b(x + h)) + k
lessons.key_concepts: f(x) + k is a vertical translation; f(x + h) is a horizontal translation by -h; a f(x) is a vertical dilation by |a| with reflection over the x-axis if a < 0; f(bx) is a horizontal dilation by factor 1/|b| with reflection over the y-axis if b < 0; transformations change domain and range
lessons.key_vocabulary: translation, vertical dilation, horizontal dilation, reflection, parent function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students shift f(x + 3) three units right instead of left; students stretch f(2x) horizontally by a factor of 2 instead of compressing it by a factor of 1/2
lessons.real_world_hook: Adjusting a sound wave's graph when an audio app doubles the playback speed

lessons.learning_objective: Choose an appropriate linear, quadratic, polynomial, piecewise, or rational model for data or a context, state its assumptions and restrictions, and use it to make predictions
lessons.key_concepts: Select models based on rate-of-change patterns, number of extrema, and contextual meaning; use regression on a calculator; restrict the domain to values that make sense; piecewise models for contexts that change rules; interpret parameters with units; models are estimates with limitations
lessons.prerequisites: Linear, quadratic, polynomial, and rational functions; rates of change
lessons.key_vocabulary: model, regression, assumption, domain restriction, piecewise function, extrapolation, interpolation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students pick a quadratic regression that fits data well and then use it to predict a negative number of sales for next year without questioning the domain
lessons.real_world_hook: Modeling the volume of an open box cut from a 20 cm by 30 cm sheet as V(x) = x(20 - 2x)(30 - 2x) on 0 < x < 10

lessons.lesson_title: Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences; Linear versus Exponential Change
lessons.learning_objective: Compare arithmetic and geometric sequences and connect them to linear and exponential functions
lessons.key_concepts: Arithmetic sequences add a common difference d: a_n = a_0 + dn; geometric sequences multiply by a common ratio r: g_n = g_0 r^n; linear functions have equal output differences over equal input intervals, exponential functions have equal output ratios over equal input intervals; both can be written from an initial value and one other point
lessons.key_vocabulary: arithmetic sequence, geometric sequence, common difference, common ratio, proportional growth
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write the geometric sequence 3, 6, 12, 24 as g_n = 3 + 2n, treating the common ratio as a common difference
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a job that adds $2,000 to salary each year with one that raises it 5% each year

lessons.learning_objective: Identify features of exponential functions f(x) = a b^x including growth versus decay, end behavior, concavity, and asymptotes
lessons.key_concepts: a is the initial value, b > 0 and b != 1 is the base; b > 1 is growth, 0 < b < 1 is decay; the graph is always concave up when a > 0; horizontal asymptote y = 0 for the parent; domain all reals, range y > 0 when a > 0; exponential functions are always increasing or always decreasing
lessons.key_vocabulary: exponential function, base, initial value, growth factor, decay factor, horizontal asymptote
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think f(x) = 2(0.8)^x is exponential growth because the coefficient 2 is greater than 1; students say the graph of y = 3^x eventually touches the x-axis
lessons.real_world_hook: A cup of coffee cooling toward room temperature, or a car's value dropping 15% per year

lessons.learning_objective: Use exponent properties to rewrite exponential expressions and functions in equivalent forms that reveal different information
lessons.key_concepts: Product property b^m b^n = b^(m+n), power property (b^m)^n = b^(mn), negative exponents b^(-n) = 1/b^n; rewriting a b^(x + k) as (a b^k) b^x shows a horizontal translation is a vertical dilation; b^(x/k) rewrites a growth rate per k units as (b^(1/k))^x; rational exponents b^(1/k) as k-th roots
lessons.key_vocabulary: product property, power property, negative exponent, rational exponent, equivalent form
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rewrite 2^(x + 3) as 2^x + 2^3 instead of 8 * 2^x; students rewrite (1.06)^(t/12) as 1.06^t / 12
lessons.real_world_hook: Converting a 12% annual growth rate into an equivalent monthly growth factor 1.12^(1/12)

lessons.lesson_title: Exponential Models and Competing Model Validation
lessons.learning_objective: Build exponential models from data or context, including base e, and use residuals to decide whether a linear, quadratic, or exponential model is most appropriate
lessons.key_concepts: Exponential models from two points or from a percent change: f(t) = a(1 + r)^t; continuous growth with base e, f(t) = a e^(kt); exponential regression; a residual is actual minus predicted; a good model has residuals with no clear pattern; choose the model whose rate-of-change pattern matches the context
lessons.prerequisites: Exponential functions, linear and quadratic regression
lessons.key_vocabulary: exponential model, growth rate, natural base e, regression, residual, residual plot
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write a model for 4% decay as f(t) = 500(0.04)^t instead of 500(0.96)^t; students compute a residual as predicted minus actual and reverse the sign
lessons.real_world_hook: Modeling the number of bacteria in a lab culture that doubles every 3 hours

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate and construct compositions of functions from equations, tables, and graphs, and decompose a function into a composition
lessons.key_concepts: (f o g)(x) = f(g(x)) applies g first then f; composition is generally not commutative; the identity function f(x) = x; decomposing h(x) = sqrt(x^2 + 1) as f(g(x)) with f(x) = sqrt(x), g(x) = x^2 + 1; composing additive and multiplicative transformations
lessons.key_vocabulary: composition, inner function, outer function, identity function, decomposition
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute f(g(x)) as f(x) * g(x), multiplying instead of substituting; students evaluate f(g(2)) by computing g(f(2))
lessons.real_world_hook: A store applying a 20% discount and then a $10 coupon, versus the coupon first, giving different final prices

lessons.learning_objective: Find and verify inverse functions, restrict domains so that inverses exist, and interpret inverses graphically and in context
lessons.key_concepts: An inverse reverses input and output: f^(-1)(f(x)) = x; a function has an inverse on a domain only if it is one-to-one there; the graph of f^(-1) is the reflection of f over y = x; domain of f is the range of f^(-1) and vice versa; restricting f(x) = x^2 to x >= 0
lessons.prerequisites: Composition, solving equations for a variable
lessons.key_vocabulary: inverse function, one-to-one, horizontal line test, domain restriction, reflection over y = x
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat f^(-1)(x) as 1/f(x), writing the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 3 as 1/(2x + 3) instead of (x - 3)/2
lessons.real_world_hook: Converting a Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula into a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit formula

lessons.lesson_title: Logarithmic Expressions and Inverses of Exponential Functions
lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate logarithmic expressions and explain that logarithmic functions are inverses of exponential functions
lessons.key_concepts: log_b(c) = a means b^a = c; the logarithm is the exponent; common log (base 10) and natural log ln (base e); log_b(b^x) = x and b^(log_b x) = x; the graph of y = log_b x is the reflection of y = b^x over y = x; estimating logs between integers
lessons.key_vocabulary: logarithm, base, common logarithm, natural logarithm, exponential form, logarithmic form
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rewrite log_2(8) = 3 as 3^2 = 8 or 8^3 = 2, misplacing the base and exponent; students think log_3(1/9) is undefined because the input is a fraction
lessons.real_world_hook: Measuring earthquakes: a magnitude 6 quake shakes 10 times more strongly than a magnitude 5 quake

lessons.learning_objective: Identify the domain, range, end behavior, concavity, and vertical asymptote of logarithmic functions and their transformations
lessons.key_concepts: f(x) = a log_b x has domain x > 0 and range all reals; vertical asymptote x = 0; for b > 1 and a > 0 it is increasing and concave down; logarithmic functions grow without bound but more slowly than any linear function eventually; output values change by equal amounts when inputs are multiplied by equal factors
lessons.key_vocabulary: logarithmic function, vertical asymptote, domain, concave down, slow growth
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say the domain of f(x) = log(x - 4) is x > 0 instead of x > 4; students think a log graph levels off at a horizontal asymptote
lessons.real_world_hook: Decibel levels: multiplying sound intensity by 10 adds only 10 decibels

lessons.learning_objective: Use the product, quotient, power, and change-of-base properties to rewrite logarithmic expressions
lessons.key_concepts: log_b(mn) = log_b m + log_b n; log_b(m/n) = log_b m - log_b n; log_b(m^p) = p log_b m; change of base log_b x = ln x / ln b; a vertical translation of a log function is equivalent to a horizontal dilation (log(kx) = log k + log x)
lessons.key_vocabulary: product property, quotient property, power property, change of base, expand, condense
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rewrite log(x + 5) as log x + log 5; students rewrite (log x)/(log y) as log x - log y
lessons.real_world_hook: Using change of base on a calculator to find how many doublings it takes a bank balance to reach $1 million

lessons.lesson_title: Exponential and Logarithmic Equations and Inequalities
lessons.learning_objective: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations and inequalities algebraically, and construct inverses of exponential and logarithmic functions
lessons.key_concepts: Isolate the exponential then take a log of both sides; rewrite a log equation in exponential form; use properties to combine logs before solving; check for extraneous solutions outside the domain; solving inequalities using the increasing or decreasing nature of the function
lessons.key_vocabulary: exponential equation, logarithmic equation, extraneous solution, isolate, inequality
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students solve 3(2^x) = 48 by taking log of 3 * 2^x as x log 6, multiplying 3 and 2 before isolating 2^x; students keep x = -1 as a solution of log_2(x) + log_2(x - 3) = 2 (from x(x - 3) = 4) even though log_2(-1) is undefined; the only solution is x = 4
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding how many years until a $5,000 investment at 6% compounded annually reaches $10,000

lessons.learning_objective: Model data with logarithmic functions and use semi-log plots to identify and linearize exponential data
lessons.key_concepts: Logarithmic regression for data that increases quickly then slowly; on a semi-log plot (y-axis logarithmic), exponential data appears linear; if y = a b^x then log y = log a + x log b, a line with slope log b and intercept log a; recovering a and b from a linear model of log y
lessons.prerequisites: Logarithmic functions, linear regression, exponential models
lessons.key_vocabulary: logarithmic regression, semi-log plot, logarithmic scale, linearization, slope
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students read the slope of the line on a semi-log plot as the growth factor b itself rather than log b, giving b = 0.3 instead of b = 10^0.3, about 2
lessons.real_world_hook: Plotting COVID-style early outbreak case counts on a log scale to see whether growth is still exponential

lessons.learning_objective: Describe periodic relationships using period, amplitude, and midline, and use the period to predict future values
lessons.key_concepts: A periodic function repeats its output values over equal input intervals: f(x + p) = f(x); the period is the length of one cycle; within a cycle the graph's increasing, decreasing, and concavity pattern repeats; using known cycles to predict future values
lessons.key_vocabulary: periodic function, period, cycle, amplitude, midline
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students measure the period from a maximum to the next minimum, reporting half the true period
lessons.real_world_hook: A Ferris wheel rider's height above the ground repeating every 8 minutes

lessons.lesson_title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent on the Unit Circle
lessons.learning_objective: Define sine, cosine, and tangent of any angle using the unit circle and find exact values for special angles in radians
lessons.key_concepts: Radian measure: an angle in standard position subtends an arc length of theta on the unit circle; for the terminal point (x, y), cos theta = x, sin theta = y, tan theta = y/x; right-triangle ratios for acute angles; exact values from 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles; reference angles and signs in each quadrant; coterminal angles
lessons.prerequisites: Right-triangle trigonometry, Pythagorean theorem, coordinate plane
lessons.key_vocabulary: unit circle, radian, standard position, terminal ray, reference angle, coterminal angle, sine, cosine, tangent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students give cos(pi/3) = sqrt(3)/2, swapping the x- and y-coordinates of the special point; students forget that cos(2pi/3) is negative in quadrant II
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the x and y position of a point on a spinning bike wheel at a given angle

lessons.learning_objective: Graph y = sin(theta) and y = cos(theta) and describe their period, amplitude, midline, zeros, extrema, and intervals of increase and concavity
lessons.key_concepts: Unwrapping the unit circle: y-coordinate gives sin, x-coordinate gives cos; period 2pi, amplitude 1, midline y = 0; cos is sin shifted left by pi/2; sin is odd, cos is even; locations of zeros, maxima, minima, and inflection points
lessons.key_vocabulary: sine curve, cosine curve, period, amplitude, midline, zero, odd function, even function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think the graph of y = sin x has its maximum at x = 0 (confusing it with cosine); students list the period of sine as pi
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracing the height of a point on a rotating wind-turbine blade over time

lessons.learning_objective: Graph and interpret f(theta) = a sin(b(theta + c)) + d and the cosine equivalent, identifying amplitude, period, phase shift, and midline
lessons.key_concepts: Amplitude |a|; period 2pi/|b|; phase shift -c; midline y = d; maximum d + |a| and minimum d - |a|; sinusoidal means any transformation of sine; cosine is a phase-shifted sine
lessons.prerequisites: Sine and cosine graphs, function transformations
lessons.key_vocabulary: sinusoidal function, amplitude, period, frequency, phase shift, vertical shift, midline
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say the period of y = sin(4x) is 8pi (multiplying 2pi by 4) instead of pi/2; students read the phase shift of sin(2x - pi) as pi instead of pi/2 because they do not factor out the 2
lessons.real_world_hook: Modeling a tide that rises and falls between 2 ft and 10 ft every 12.4 hours

lessons.lesson_title: Sinusoidal Function Context and Data Modeling
lessons.learning_objective: Construct sinusoidal models from a context or data by determining the parameters, and use the model to answer questions with units
lessons.key_concepts: Find the midline as the average of max and min, amplitude as half the difference, period from the cycle length, then the phase shift from a known max, min, or midline crossing; sinusoidal regression on a calculator; interpret the model and its rate of change in context
lessons.key_vocabulary: sinusoidal model, sinusoidal regression, maximum, minimum, cycle length
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students take the amplitude to be the maximum value (10) rather than half the difference between max and min ((10 - 2)/2 = 4)
lessons.real_world_hook: Modeling daily hours of daylight in Chicago across a year (about 9 hours in December to 15 hours in June)

lessons.learning_objective: Graph y = tan(theta) and its transformations, explaining its period, vertical asymptotes, and relationship to slope
lessons.key_concepts: tan theta = sin theta / cos theta is the slope of the terminal ray; period pi; vertical asymptotes where cos theta = 0 (theta = pi/2 + k pi); increasing between consecutive asymptotes; transformations of f(theta) = a tan(b(theta + c)) + d have period pi/|b|
lessons.prerequisites: Unit circle, sine and cosine graphs, rational functions and asymptotes
lessons.key_vocabulary: tangent function, vertical asymptote, period, slope of terminal ray
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say the period of y = tan(2x) is pi (using the sine rule 2pi/b) instead of pi/2; students place tangent's asymptotes at x = 0 and pi, where sine is zero
lessons.real_world_hook: A searchlight's beam location on a wall, d = 50 tan(theta), shooting off to infinity as the beam approaches parallel to the wall

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate inverse sine, cosine, and tangent using their restricted domains and ranges
lessons.key_concepts: To have inverses, sine is restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2], cosine to [0, pi], tangent to (-pi/2, pi/2); arcsin and arccos have domain [-1, 1]; inverse trig outputs are angles; graphs as reflections over y = x
lessons.key_vocabulary: inverse sine (arcsin), inverse cosine (arccos), inverse tangent (arctan), restricted domain, principal value
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students give arccos(-1/2) = -pi/3 or 4pi/3 instead of 2pi/3, ignoring the [0, pi] range; students write sin^(-1)(x) = 1/sin(x)
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the angle of a wheelchair ramp that rises 1 ft over a 12 ft run, using arctan(1/12)

lessons.learning_objective: Solve trigonometric equations and inequalities over a given interval and write general solutions
lessons.key_concepts: Isolate the trig function, find the reference solution with an inverse function, then use symmetry of the unit circle to find all solutions in [0, 2pi); general solutions add multiples of the period; factoring quadratic-type trig equations; using graphs to solve inequalities
lessons.prerequisites: Inverse trig functions, unit circle, factoring
lessons.key_vocabulary: trigonometric equation, general solution, reference solution, solution interval
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students solve sin x = 1/2 on [0, 2pi) and give only x = pi/6, missing 5pi/6; students divide both sides of sin x cos x = sin x by sin x and lose the solutions where sin x = 0
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the times of day when a tide model is above 8 ft so a boat can leave the harbor

lessons.learning_objective: Define and graph the reciprocal trigonometric functions and evaluate them exactly
lessons.key_concepts: sec theta = 1/cos theta, csc theta = 1/sin theta, cot theta = cos theta/sin theta; vertical asymptotes where the reciprocal function is zero; domains and ranges (|sec| >= 1, |csc| >= 1); graphs drawn from the reciprocal function
lessons.prerequisites: Sine, cosine, tangent graphs and values
lessons.key_vocabulary: secant, cosecant, cotangent, reciprocal function, vertical asymptote
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students pair the reciprocals incorrectly, writing sec theta = 1/sin theta; students think csc theta is the same as arcsin theta
lessons.real_world_hook: Surveyors using cosecant to find the length of a guy wire from its height and angle

lessons.learning_objective: Use the Pythagorean identity, sum and difference identities, and double-angle identities to rewrite trigonometric expressions and solve equations
lessons.key_concepts: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1 and its forms 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x, 1 + cot^2 x = csc^2 x; sin(a +/- b) = sin a cos b +/- cos a sin b; cos(a +/- b) = cos a cos b -/+ sin a sin b; double angle sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, cos 2x = cos^2 x - sin^2 x; rewriting to solve equations
lessons.prerequisites: Trig values, reciprocal functions, algebraic simplification
lessons.key_vocabulary: identity, Pythagorean identity, sum identity, difference identity, double-angle identity
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write sin(x + pi/6) = sin x + sin(pi/6); students write sin(2x) = 2 sin x
lessons.real_world_hook: Audio engineers combining two sound waves using sum identities to predict the resulting wave

lessons.learning_objective: Convert between rectangular and polar coordinates and represent complex numbers in polar form
lessons.key_concepts: A point (r, theta) has x = r cos theta, y = r sin theta; r^2 = x^2 + y^2 and tan theta = y/x with quadrant check; the same point has many polar representations, including negative r; a complex number a + bi corresponds to the point (a, b) and can be written r(cos theta + i sin theta)
lessons.prerequisites: Unit circle, Pythagorean theorem, complex numbers
lessons.key_vocabulary: polar coordinates, pole, polar axis, rectangular coordinates, polar form of a complex number
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students convert (-3, 3) to polar using theta = arctan(3/-3) = -pi/4 and do not adjust to 3pi/4, placing the point in the wrong quadrant
lessons.real_world_hook: A radar screen locating an airplane by distance and bearing from the tower

lessons.lesson_title: Polar Function Graphs and Rates of Change
lessons.learning_objective: Graph polar functions r = f(theta), identify circles, roses, and limacons, and describe how the distance from the origin changes as theta changes
lessons.key_concepts: Graph from a table of theta and r values or by unwrapping r versus theta on a rectangular graph; r = a cos theta is a circle, r = a sin(n theta) is a rose, r = a + b cos theta is a limacon or cardioid; when r is positive and increasing, points move away from the origin; when r is negative and decreasing, points also move away; average rate of change of r with respect to theta
lessons.prerequisites: Polar coordinates, sinusoidal graphs, rates of change
lessons.key_vocabulary: polar function, rose curve, limacon, cardioid, distance from the origin, average rate of change of r
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say the graph is getting closer to the origin whenever r is decreasing, even when r is negative and |r| is growing; students think r = 4 sin(3 theta) has 6 petals
lessons.real_world_hook: Designing the cardioid-shaped pickup pattern of a directional microphone

units.unit_title: Functions Involving Parameters, Vectors, and Matrices (not on the AP exam)

lessons.learning_objective: Graph and interpret parametric functions (x(t), y(t)) as the motion of a particle in the plane
lessons.key_concepts: A parametric function gives x and y each as a function of a parameter t; plotting points from a table of t values; the direction of motion as t increases; x(t) and y(t) increasing or decreasing describe horizontal and vertical motion; extrema of x(t) or y(t)
lessons.key_vocabulary: parameter, parametric function, planar motion, orientation, particle
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students plot the points (t, x) and (t, y) instead of (x(t), y(t)); students assume the graph of a parametric function must pass the vertical line test

lessons.lesson_title: Parametric Rates of Change, Circles, and Lines
lessons.learning_objective: Compute average rates of change of parametric functions and parametrize lines, line segments, and circles
lessons.key_concepts: Average rate of change of x(t) and of y(t) on an interval; the slope between two points is (change in y)/(change in x); the line through (x1, y1) and (x2, y2): x(t) = x1 + (x2 - x1)t, y(t) = y1 + (y2 - y1)t, a segment for 0 <= t <= 1; circle of radius r centered at (h, k): x(t) = h + r cos t, y(t) = k + r sin t
lessons.key_vocabulary: average rate of change, parametrization, line segment, circle, orientation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students parametrize the circle centered at (2, -1) with radius 3 as x(t) = 3cos t + 2, y(t) = 3 sin t + 1, using the wrong sign for the center's y-coordinate
lessons.real_world_hook: Programming a video game sprite to move along a straight path between two points in 2 seconds

lessons.lesson_title: Implicitly Defined Functions and Conic Sections
lessons.learning_objective: Graph and analyze implicitly defined relations including parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas, and parametrize them
lessons.key_concepts: Relations like x^2 + y^2 = 25 define curves that are not functions of x; standard forms of parabolas, ellipses (x - h)^2/a^2 + (y - k)^2/b^2 = 1, and hyperbolas (x - h)^2/a^2 - (y - k)^2/b^2 = 1; parametrizing an ellipse as x = h + a cos t, y = k + b sin t; parametrizing y = f(x) as x = t, y = f(t)
lessons.prerequisites: Completing the square, circles, parametric functions
lessons.key_vocabulary: implicitly defined function, conic section, parabola, ellipse, hyperbola, vertex, focus
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students read the ellipse x^2/9 + y^2/4 = 1 as having horizontal semi-axis 9 instead of 3, forgetting to take the square root
lessons.real_world_hook: The elliptical orbit of a planet or the parabolic shape of a satellite dish

lessons.learning_objective: Represent vectors in component and magnitude-direction form, perform vector operations, and interpret vector-valued functions
lessons.key_concepts: A vector <a, b> has magnitude sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and direction angle theta with tan theta = b/a; vector addition, scalar multiplication, and unit vectors; the dot product u . v = u1 v1 + u2 v2 and the angle between vectors; a vector-valued function p(t) = <x(t), y(t)> gives the position of a particle
lessons.key_vocabulary: vector, component, magnitude, direction angle, unit vector, scalar, dot product, vector-valued function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute the magnitude of <3, -4> as 3 + (-4) = -1 or as 7 instead of sqrt(9 + 16) = 5
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding a plane's actual ground velocity by adding its airspeed vector to a crosswind vector

lessons.learning_objective: Multiply matrices and find the determinant and inverse of a 2x2 matrix
lessons.key_concepts: Matrix dimensions rows by columns; matrix multiplication requires inner dimensions to match and is not commutative; for A = [[a, b], [c, d]], det A = ad - bc and A^(-1) = (1/(ad - bc)) [[d, -b], [-c, a]] when det A != 0; the determinant gives the signed area of the parallelogram formed by the column vectors
lessons.prerequisites: Arithmetic of real numbers, systems of equations, vectors
lessons.key_vocabulary: matrix, dimension, entry, matrix multiplication, determinant, inverse matrix, identity matrix
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students multiply matrices entry by entry instead of rows times columns; students compute det [[a, b], [c, d]] as ab - cd
lessons.real_world_hook: Using a 2x2 matrix to encode and decode a secret message

lessons.learning_objective: Use matrices as functions that transform vectors in the plane, compose transformations, and model contexts such as transitions between states
lessons.key_concepts: A 2x2 matrix maps a vector to a new vector; matrices for rotations [[cos t, -sin t], [sin t, cos t]], reflections, and dilations; composing transformations means multiplying matrices (the first transformation applied is on the right); inverse matrices undo transformations; transition matrices predict future states, e.g. A^n times an initial state vector
lessons.key_vocabulary: linear transformation, rotation matrix, composition, transition matrix, state vector, steady state
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compose 'rotate then reflect' as R * F (rotation on the left), applying the transformations in the wrong order
lessons.real_world_hook: Predicting how customers switch between two streaming services month to month with a transition matrix

lessons.learning_objective: Describe the AP Precalculus multiple-choice section and practice both its no-calculator and calculator parts
lessons.key_concepts: Section I is 42 multiple-choice questions in 1 hour 45 minutes, worth 62.5% of the score; Part A is 29 questions in 65 minutes with no calculator permitted (43.75%); Part B is 13 questions in 40 minutes with a graphing calculator required (18.75%), though only some Part B questions actually need it; each question has four answer choices and there is no penalty for wrong answers; only Units 1-3 are tested (Unit 4 is not on the exam); multiple-choice weighting by function type: general functions 15-25%, polynomial and rational 20-25%, exponential and logarithmic 20-30%, trigonometric and polar 30-35%; questions use algebraic, graphical, numerical, and verbal representations; the exam is hybrid digital, so multiple-choice answers are entered in the Bluebook app; for calculator questions, set radian mode and know how to graph, find intersections and zeros, and run regressions
lessons.key_vocabulary: multiple choice, no-calculator, graphing calculator, representation, distractor
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use the calculator to graph every Part B question even when a quick algebraic step is faster; students leave questions blank even though there is no guessing penalty
lessons.real_world_hook: Treating a timed practice set like a dress rehearsal before a performance

lessons.learning_objective: Recognize and practice the four free-response question types: function concepts, modeling a non-periodic context, modeling a periodic context, and symbolic manipulations
lessons.key_concepts: Section II has four free-response questions, each worth 6 points, in 1 hour 10 minutes, worth 37.5% of the score; Part A (2 questions, 35 minutes, graphing calculator required): (1) Function Concepts, working with graphs, tables, compositions, inverses, zeros, and end behavior, and (2) Modeling a Non-Periodic Context, building a model from a real-world context (polynomial, piecewise-defined, exponential, or logarithmic), using average rates of change with units, and judging the model's assumptions or limitations; Part B (2 questions, 35 minutes, no calculator permitted): (3) Modeling a Periodic Context, building a sinusoidal model from a context or graph, and (4) Symbolic Manipulations, solving and rewriting exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric expressions and equations; Questions 2 and 3 use real-world contexts; FRQs are viewed in Bluebook but answered by hand in a paper booklet; show work, use correct notation, and include units
lessons.key_vocabulary: free response, justification, model, units, notation, partial credit
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write a final number with no supporting work or units, e.g. answering a periodic modeling part with '6.2' instead of 'about 6.2 feet at t = 3 hours'; students give a correct model but never answer the interpretation part of the question
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing up a short report that convinces a skeptical reader your answer is right

lessons.learning_objective: Plan pacing for each section of the AP Precalculus exam and build a review plan from practice results
lessons.key_concepts: The exam is 2 hours 55 minutes: Part A multiple choice gives 65 minutes for 29 questions (about 2 minutes 15 seconds each) with no calculator; Part B multiple choice gives 40 minutes for 13 questions (about 3 minutes each) with a graphing calculator; each free-response part gives 35 minutes for 2 questions (about 17 minutes each), calculator required in Part A and not permitted in Part B; do easier questions first and return to marked ones; answer every multiple-choice question; for free response, attempt every part since parts are scored separately; check calculator mode (radians) before trig questions; keep an error log by unit and skill and target the weakest topics
lessons.key_vocabulary: pacing, error log, radian mode, partial credit, review plan
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students leave the calculator in degree mode and get wrong values for sin(2), or spend ten minutes on one multiple-choice question and run out of time for the last several
lessons.real_world_hook: Reviewing game film to find the plays you keep missing before the championship

lessons.lesson_title: Limits from Graphs, Tables, and Algebra
lessons.learning_objective: Estimate limits (including one-sided limits) from graphs and tables, and evaluate limits algebraically by factoring, rationalizing, and simplifying when direct substitution gives 0/0
lessons.key_concepts: A limit describes the value f(x) approaches, not f(c) itself; a two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal; limit properties (sum, product, quotient); direct substitution first; 0/0 is an indeterminate form that signals algebraic manipulation, not an answer
lessons.prerequisites: Function notation and graphs, factoring polynomials, rationalizing with conjugates, piecewise functions
lessons.key_vocabulary: limit, one-sided limit, left-hand limit, right-hand limit, indeterminate form, direct substitution, conjugate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume the limit equals f(c) even when there is a hole or the point is defined elsewhere; students write 0/0 = 0 or 0/0 = undefined and stop instead of simplifying; students say a two-sided limit exists when the left and right limits differ
lessons.real_world_hook: Estimating a sprinter's speed at an exact instant from timing data taken a fraction of a second apart

lessons.lesson_title: Squeeze Theorem, Infinite Limits, and Asymptotes
lessons.learning_objective: Apply the squeeze theorem, including the special trig limits, and use limits involving infinity to identify vertical and horizontal asymptotes
lessons.key_concepts: If g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) near c and g and h share limit L, then f has limit L; lim sin(x)/x = 1 and lim (1 - cos x)/x = 0 as x -> 0; infinite limits indicate vertical asymptotes; limits at infinity use dominant terms (compare degrees of numerator and denominator) to find horizontal asymptotes
lessons.prerequisites: Limits from graphs and algebra, trig values, end behavior of rational and exponential functions
lessons.key_vocabulary: squeeze theorem, bounded, infinite limit, limit at infinity, vertical asymptote, horizontal asymptote, dominant term
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students substitute x = 0 into sin(x)/x and conclude the limit does not exist; students believe a graph can never cross a horizontal asymptote; students treat infinity as a number and write infinity - infinity = 0
lessons.real_world_hook: Long-run concentration of a drug in the bloodstream leveling off toward a horizontal asymptote

lessons.lesson_title: Continuity, Discontinuities, and the Intermediate Value Theorem
lessons.learning_objective: Determine continuity at a point and on an interval using the three-part definition, classify discontinuities, find constants that make a piecewise function continuous, and justify conclusions with the IVT
lessons.key_concepts: f is continuous at c if f(c) is defined, the limit exists, and the limit equals f(c); removable, jump, and infinite discontinuities; polynomial, rational, trig, exponential, and log functions are continuous on their domains; IVT requires continuity on a closed interval [a, b] and guarantees a value between f(a) and f(b)
lessons.prerequisites: Limits, piecewise functions, solving equations for unknown constants
lessons.key_vocabulary: continuous, removable discontinuity, jump discontinuity, infinite discontinuity, closed interval, Intermediate Value Theorem
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students apply the IVT without first stating that f is continuous on [a, b]; students conflate continuity with differentiability; students think the IVT tells where the value occurs or that it rules out other values outside f(a) to f(b)
lessons.real_world_hook: Proving a hiker's temperature reading must have hit exactly 50 degrees at some moment while climbing from 40 to 60 degrees

lessons.lesson_title: The Derivative as a Limit and Differentiability
lessons.learning_objective: Define the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient, estimate derivatives from tables and graphs, and explain why differentiability implies continuity but not the converse
lessons.key_concepts: Average rate of change is a secant slope; f'(a) = lim h->0 [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h and the alternate form lim x->a [f(x) - f(a)]/(x - a); recognizing a limit expression as a derivative; estimating f'(a) from a table with a difference quotient; corners, cusps, vertical tangents, and discontinuities make f non-differentiable
lessons.prerequisites: Limits, slope of a line, average rate of change
lessons.key_vocabulary: derivative, difference quotient, secant line, tangent line, instantaneous rate of change, differentiable, corner, cusp
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students think a continuous function must be differentiable (e.g., |x| at 0); students cannot recognize lim h->0 [(2+h)^3 - 8]/h as f'(2) for f(x) = x^3; students confuse the average rate of change on an interval with the instantaneous rate at a point
lessons.real_world_hook: A car's speedometer reading versus its average speed over a whole trip

lessons.lesson_title: Power Rule and Derivatives of sin, cos, e^x, and ln x
lessons.learning_objective: Differentiate polynomial, root, and negative-power functions with the power, constant multiple, and sum rules, and differentiate sin x, cos x, e^x, and ln x
lessons.key_concepts: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1) for any real n after rewriting roots and reciprocals as powers; derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives; d/dx sin x = cos x, d/dx cos x = -sin x, d/dx e^x = e^x, d/dx ln x = 1/x; writing tangent-line equations
lessons.prerequisites: Exponent rules, rewriting radicals as rational exponents, derivative definition
lessons.key_vocabulary: power rule, constant multiple rule, sum rule, tangent line, rational exponent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students differentiate 1/x^2 as 1/(2x) instead of rewriting as x^(-2) to get -2x^(-3); students write d/dx cos x = sin x (dropping the negative); students apply the power rule to e^x or to 2^x
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the exact slope of a skateboard ramp profile at the lip

lessons.lesson_title: Product Rule, Quotient Rule, and Other Trig Derivatives
lessons.learning_objective: Apply the product and quotient rules and derive and use the derivatives of tan x, cot x, sec x, and csc x
lessons.key_concepts: (fg)' = f'g + fg'; (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g^2; d/dx tan x = sec^2 x, d/dx sec x = sec x tan x, d/dx cot x = -csc^2 x, d/dx csc x = -csc x cot x; choosing to simplify before differentiating
lessons.prerequisites: Power rule, sin and cos derivatives, trig identities
lessons.key_vocabulary: product rule, quotient rule, secant, cosecant, cotangent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write (fg)' = f'g'; students reverse the order in the quotient rule numerator (fg' - f'g) and get the wrong sign; students forget to square the denominator
lessons.real_world_hook: Revenue as price times quantity, both changing over time

units.unit_title: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

lessons.learning_objective: Differentiate composite functions with the chain rule, including nested compositions and compositions given by tables or graphs
lessons.key_concepts: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) * g'(x); identifying inner and outer functions; chaining three or more layers; combining the chain rule with product and quotient rules; evaluating with tabular values of f, g, f', g'
lessons.prerequisites: Function composition, product and quotient rules, basic derivatives
lessons.key_vocabulary: chain rule, composite function, inner function, outer function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget to multiply by the derivative of the inner function (d/dx sin(3x) = cos(3x)); students evaluate f'(g'(x)) instead of f'(g(x)) from a table; students differentiate e^(x^2) as x^2 e^(x^2 - 1)
lessons.real_world_hook: How fast a balloon's volume changes when its radius depends on time

lessons.learning_objective: Find dy/dx for implicitly defined relations, find second derivatives implicitly, and interpret higher-order derivatives
lessons.key_concepts: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x so d/dx y^n = n y^(n-1) dy/dx; collect dy/dx terms and solve; second derivative by differentiating dy/dx and substituting dy/dx back in; notation f'', d^2y/dx^2
lessons.prerequisites: Chain rule, product rule, solving literal equations
lessons.key_vocabulary: implicit differentiation, explicit function, second derivative, higher-order derivative
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students differentiate y^2 as 2y without the dy/dx factor; students treat xy as having derivative 1 * dy/dx instead of using the product rule; students forget to substitute dy/dx when finding d^2y/dx^2
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the slope of a tangent to an elliptical race track at a given point

lessons.lesson_title: Derivatives of Inverse Functions and Inverse Trig Functions
lessons.learning_objective: Find derivatives of inverse functions at a point using (f^-1)'(b) = 1/f'(a) where f(a) = b, and differentiate arcsin, arccos, and arctan
lessons.key_concepts: Inverse function slopes are reciprocals at corresponding points (a, b) and (b, a); d/dx arcsin x = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2), d/dx arccos x = -1/sqrt(1 - x^2), d/dx arctan x = 1/(1 + x^2); selecting the right combination of rules
lessons.prerequisites: Inverse functions, inverse trig values and domains, chain rule
lessons.key_vocabulary: inverse function, reciprocal slope, arcsine, arctangent, corresponding point
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute (f^-1)'(b) as 1/f'(b) instead of 1/f'(a) where f(a) = b; students confuse f^-1(x) with 1/f(x); students forget the chain rule factor in arctan(2x)
lessons.real_world_hook: Converting a thermometer's voltage reading back into temperature and how sensitive that conversion is

lessons.lesson_title: Derivatives in Context and Straight-Line Motion
lessons.learning_objective: Interpret the meaning and units of a derivative in context and analyze particle motion using position, velocity, and acceleration
lessons.key_concepts: Units of f'(t) are units of f per unit of t; v(t) = x'(t), a(t) = v'(t); particle moves right when v > 0; speed is |v(t)|; speed increases when v and a have the same sign; particle changes direction when v changes sign
lessons.key_vocabulary: rate of change, position, velocity, acceleration, speed, displacement, at rest
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say a particle is speeding up whenever a(t) > 0 even if v(t) < 0; students give units of f'(t) as just the units of f; students say the particle changes direction whenever v(t) = 0 without checking for a sign change
lessons.real_world_hook: Interpreting an elevator's velocity and acceleration as it starts and stops between floors

lessons.learning_objective: Set up and solve related-rates problems by writing an equation relating quantities, differentiating implicitly with respect to time, and substituting values only after differentiating
lessons.key_concepts: Identify given and unknown rates; draw and label a diagram; relate quantities with geometry (Pythagorean theorem, similar triangles, volume formulas); differentiate with respect to t; substitute instantaneous values last; sign of a rate shows increasing or decreasing
lessons.prerequisites: Implicit differentiation, chain rule, geometry formulas, similar triangles
lessons.key_vocabulary: related rates, rate with respect to time, implicit differentiation, constant, instantaneous value
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students substitute numerical values for changing quantities before differentiating, turning variables into constants; students give a decreasing quantity a positive rate; students use the full cone volume formula without eliminating r with similar triangles
lessons.real_world_hook: How fast the top of a sliding ladder drops as its base is pulled away from a wall

lessons.learning_objective: Use the tangent line to approximate function values and decide whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate, and evaluate indeterminate limits with L'Hospital's rule
lessons.key_concepts: Linearization L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a); concave up means the tangent line underestimates, concave down means it overestimates; L'Hospital's rule applies only to 0/0 or infinity/infinity: lim f/g = lim f'/g'; it can be repeated if the form persists
lessons.prerequisites: Tangent lines, derivative rules, concavity basics, limits
lessons.key_vocabulary: linearization, local linearity, tangent line approximation, overestimate, underestimate, L'Hospital's rule, indeterminate form
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students apply L'Hospital's rule using the quotient rule on f/g instead of differentiating numerator and denominator separately; students apply it when the form is not indeterminate; students skip verifying the 0/0 form in written justification
lessons.real_world_hook: Estimating the square root of 4.1 without a calculator, the way engineers linearize models

lessons.lesson_title: Mean Value Theorem, Extreme Value Theorem, and Critical Points
lessons.learning_objective: Apply the Mean Value Theorem and Extreme Value Theorem with correct hypotheses, and find critical points where f'(x) = 0 or f' is undefined
lessons.key_concepts: MVT: if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), some c has f'(c) = [f(b) - f(a)]/(b - a); EVT: continuous on a closed interval guarantees an absolute max and min; local vs absolute extrema; critical points as candidates
lessons.prerequisites: Continuity, differentiability, average rate of change
lessons.key_vocabulary: Mean Value Theorem, Extreme Value Theorem, critical point, local extremum, absolute extremum, hypothesis
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students apply the MVT without checking both continuity on [a, b] and differentiability on (a, b); students believe every critical point is an extremum (x^3 at 0); students forget endpoints when finding absolute extrema
lessons.real_world_hook: Proving a speeding ticket: average speed over a toll road means the car hit that exact speed at some instant

lessons.lesson_title: Increasing, Decreasing, and the First Derivative Test
lessons.learning_objective: Determine intervals of increase and decrease, classify relative extrema with the first derivative test, and find absolute extrema with the candidates test
lessons.key_concepts: f' > 0 means f increasing, f' < 0 decreasing; sign chart of f'; relative max where f' changes from positive to negative; candidates test evaluates f at critical points and endpoints; writing justifications that reference the sign change of f'
lessons.prerequisites: Critical points, derivative rules, solving inequalities
lessons.key_vocabulary: increasing, decreasing, sign chart, first derivative test, relative maximum, relative minimum, candidates test
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students justify an extremum by saying f'(c) = 0 alone; students read where f is positive instead of where f' is positive from a graph of f'; students give the x-value when asked for the maximum value
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding when a company's profit stopped growing and started falling

lessons.lesson_title: Concavity, the Second Derivative Test, and Connecting f, f', f''
lessons.learning_objective: Determine concavity and points of inflection, apply the second derivative test, and connect features of the graphs of f, f', and f''
lessons.key_concepts: f'' > 0 concave up, f'' < 0 concave down; inflection point where f'' changes sign; second derivative test at f'(c) = 0; f' increasing corresponds to f concave up; reading f behavior from a graph of f'; behavior of implicit relations
lessons.key_vocabulary: concave up, concave down, point of inflection, second derivative test, graph of f prime
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students identify an inflection point wherever f''(x) = 0 without checking for a sign change (x^4 at 0); students read the graph of f' as if it were f; students conclude the second derivative test is decisive when f''(c) = 0
lessons.real_world_hook: Spotting the moment a viral video's view growth started to slow down

lessons.learning_objective: Model and solve optimization problems by writing a single-variable objective function, finding its domain, and justifying the absolute extremum
lessons.key_concepts: Identify the quantity to optimize; use a constraint to reduce to one variable; determine the practical domain; find critical points; justify with the candidates test or a sign argument showing the only critical point is an absolute extremum
lessons.prerequisites: Critical points, first and second derivative tests, area and volume formulas
lessons.key_vocabulary: objective function, constraint, optimize, feasible domain, absolute maximum, absolute minimum
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students optimize the constraint equation instead of the objective; students ignore the domain and accept a negative length; students report a critical point without justifying that it is the absolute max or min
lessons.real_world_hook: Designing a soda can that holds 355 mL with the least aluminum

lessons.lesson_title: Riemann Sums, Trapezoidal Sums, and the Definite Integral
lessons.learning_objective: Approximate accumulated change with left, right, midpoint, and trapezoidal sums (including unequal subintervals from tables) and express a definite integral as the limit of a Riemann sum
lessons.key_concepts: Area under a rate curve represents accumulated change; left/right/midpoint/trapezoid sums; over- and underestimates from monotonicity (left/right) and concavity (trapezoid); sigma notation; definite integral as lim n->infinity of a Riemann sum with delta x = (b - a)/n
lessons.prerequisites: Area formulas, summation notation, function values from tables
lessons.key_vocabulary: Riemann sum, left sum, right sum, midpoint sum, trapezoidal sum, subinterval, definite integral, sigma notation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use equal widths when table intervals are unequal; students say a left sum always underestimates regardless of whether f is increasing; students cannot translate a limit of a sum into the correct integral bounds and integrand
lessons.real_world_hook: Estimating total rainfall from hourly rain-rate readings

lessons.lesson_title: The Fundamental Theorem and Accumulation Functions
lessons.learning_objective: Use both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate definite integrals and to differentiate and analyze accumulation functions
lessons.key_concepts: d/dx integral from a to x of f(t) dt = f(x), and with a variable upper limit g(x) the result is f(g(x)) g'(x); integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a); properties of definite integrals (reversing bounds, additivity); integrals of signed area; analyzing g(x) = integral of f from a graph of f
lessons.key_vocabulary: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, accumulation function, antiderivative, signed area, net change
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget the chain rule factor when the upper limit is x^2; students treat area below the axis as positive when computing a net integral; students confuse the graph of f with the graph of the accumulation function g
lessons.real_world_hook: Net change in water in a tank given inflow and outflow rates

lessons.learning_objective: Find indefinite integrals using basic antiderivative rules and u-substitution, including changing limits for definite integrals, long division, and completing the square
lessons.key_concepts: Reverse power rule (n not equal to -1), integral of 1/x is ln|x|, trig and exponential antiderivatives, + C; choose u as an inner function whose derivative appears; change bounds to u-values or back-substitute; long division for improper rational functions; completing the square to reach arctan forms
lessons.prerequisites: Derivative rules, chain rule, polynomial division, completing the square
lessons.key_vocabulary: antiderivative, indefinite integral, constant of integration, u-substitution, change of variables
