lessons.common_misconceptions: Students omit + C on indefinite integrals; students keep the original x-bounds after substituting u; students integrate 1/x as x^0/0 using the power rule
lessons.real_world_hook: Reversing a known velocity formula to recover a drone's position

lessons.lesson_title: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions (BC)
lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate integrals using integration by parts, including repeated and tabular application, and using partial fraction decomposition with nonrepeating linear factors
lessons.key_concepts: Integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du; choosing u with LIATE (logarithmic, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential); tabular method for polynomial times exponential or trig; decompose (px + q)/((x - a)(x - b)) into A/(x - a) + B/(x - b) and integrate to logs
lessons.prerequisites: u-substitution, product rule, factoring, solving systems for constants
lessons.key_vocabulary: integration by parts, LIATE, tabular integration, partial fractions, linear factor, decomposition
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose u = e^x and dv = x dx, producing a harder integral; students drop the minus sign in uv - integral of v du; students try partial fractions before dividing when the numerator degree is not less than the denominator degree
lessons.real_world_hook: Computing total drug absorbed when concentration follows t e^(-t)

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate improper integrals with infinite bounds or infinite discontinuities using limits, determine convergence or divergence, and select an appropriate integration technique
lessons.key_concepts: Integral from a to infinity of f = lim b->infinity of integral from a to b; improper at a vertical asymptote inside or at an endpoint of the interval; p-integral: integral from 1 to infinity of 1/x^p converges iff p > 1; strategy for choosing substitution, parts, partial fractions, or algebra
lessons.prerequisites: FTC, limits at infinity, all prior integration techniques
lessons.key_vocabulary: improper integral, converge, diverge, infinite discontinuity, p-integral
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students evaluate integral from -1 to 1 of 1/x^2 directly and get -2 without noticing the asymptote at 0; students think an integral converges because the integrand approaches 0; students write infinity as a bound and plug it in instead of using a limit
lessons.real_world_hook: Total energy emitted by a cooling object over an unlimited amount of time

lessons.lesson_title: Modeling, Verifying Solutions, and Slope Fields
lessons.learning_objective: Write differential equations from verbal descriptions, verify solutions, sketch and interpret slope fields, and match slope fields to equations
lessons.key_concepts: "Rate proportional to amount" means dy/dt = ky; verifying by substituting y and y' into the equation; slope field segments with slope dy/dx at each point; dependence on x only, y only, or both; sketching a solution curve through an initial condition
lessons.key_vocabulary: differential equation, general solution, particular solution, slope field, initial condition, proportional
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students draw a solution curve that crosses slope segments instead of following them; students assume slopes depend only on x; students verify a solution by checking only the initial condition
lessons.real_world_hook: Modeling how a rumor spreads in a school

lessons.learning_objective: Approximate solutions to differential equations numerically with Euler's method and determine whether the approximation is an over- or underestimate
lessons.key_concepts: Step: y_new = y_old + (dy/dx at (x_old, y_old)) * delta x; organize steps in a table; error grows with step size and number of steps; concavity of the solution determines over- or underestimate
lessons.prerequisites: Slope fields, linearization, evaluating expressions in x and y
lessons.key_vocabulary: Euler's method, step size, approximation, iteration, tangent line step
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute the slope at the new point instead of the old point; students forget to update both x and y each step; students use the wrong number of steps to reach the target x
lessons.real_world_hook: How video game physics engines approximate motion one frame at a time

lessons.lesson_title: Separation of Variables and Exponential Models
lessons.learning_objective: Solve separable differential equations to find general and particular solutions, including exponential growth and decay models dy/dt = ky
lessons.key_concepts: Separate to g(y) dy = f(x) dx, integrate both sides, include + C immediately, solve for C using the initial condition, solve for y; domain restrictions of the particular solution; dy/dt = ky gives y = y0 e^(kt)
lessons.prerequisites: Antiderivatives, logarithm and exponent rules, u-substitution
lessons.key_vocabulary: separable, separation of variables, particular solution, exponential growth, exponential decay, half-life
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students add + C only at the very end after exponentiating, getting y = e^x + C instead of y = Ce^x; students do not separate (multiply instead of divide) the y terms; students forget absolute values in ln|y|
lessons.real_world_hook: Carbon-14 dating of ancient artifacts

lessons.learning_objective: Interpret logistic differential equations dP/dt = kP(1 - P/L), identify carrying capacity and the point of fastest growth, and find limits of solutions
lessons.key_concepts: Growth rate is proportional to both P and (L - P); carrying capacity L; lim t->infinity P(t) = L for P0 > 0; P grows fastest when P = L/2 (where d^2P/dt^2 = 0); populations above L decrease toward L
lessons.key_vocabulary: logistic model, carrying capacity, limiting value, inflection point, fastest growth
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students say growth is fastest at the carrying capacity; students think a population starting above L grows; students misread the constant in a rewritten form such as dP/dt = 0.02P(500 - P) as a carrying capacity of 0.02 instead of 500
lessons.real_world_hook: Fish population in a lake with limited food

lessons.lesson_title: Average Value, Motion, and Accumulation in Context
lessons.learning_objective: Find average value of a function, compute displacement and total distance from velocity, and use integrals to model accumulation in applied contexts
lessons.key_concepts: Average value = (1/(b - a)) * integral from a to b of f; displacement = integral of v; total distance = integral of |v|; position x(b) = x(a) + integral of v from a to b; amount = initial amount + integral of (rate in - rate out)
lessons.key_vocabulary: average value, displacement, total distance, net change, rate in, rate out
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute total distance as integral of v instead of integral of |v|; students confuse average value of a function with average rate of change; students forget to add the initial amount when finding a final amount
lessons.real_world_hook: How many people are in an amusement park at closing given entry and exit rates

lessons.learning_objective: Compute areas of regions between curves by integrating with respect to x or y, including regions where curves intersect more than twice
lessons.key_concepts: Area = integral of (top - bottom) dx or (right - left) dy; find intersection points for bounds; split the integral where curves switch; choose dy when a region has a single left and right boundary
lessons.prerequisites: Definite integrals, solving equations, graph sketching
lessons.key_vocabulary: area between curves, intersection point, top function, bottom function, integrate with respect to y
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students integrate bottom minus top and get a negative area; students integrate over the full interval without splitting where the curves cross; students use x-bounds when integrating with respect to y
lessons.real_world_hook: Estimating the area of a lake from survey curves of its two shorelines

lessons.lesson_title: Volumes: Cross Sections, Disks, and Washers
lessons.learning_objective: Find volumes of solids with known cross sections and of solids of revolution using the disk and washer methods, including revolution about lines other than the axes
lessons.key_concepts: Volume = integral of A(x) dx; square, rectangle, equilateral triangle, and semicircle cross-section areas; disk: pi * integral of R^2; washer: pi * integral of (R^2 - r^2); radii measured from the axis of rotation, e.g., R = 3 - f(x) about y = 3
lessons.prerequisites: Area between curves, area formulas, transformations of distances
lessons.key_vocabulary: cross section, solid of revolution, disk method, washer method, outer radius, inner radius, axis of rotation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute the washer as pi * integral of (R - r)^2 instead of R^2 - r^2; students use f(x) as the radius when rotating about y = 3 instead of the distance 3 - f(x); students use the full diameter where a semicircle needs the radius
lessons.real_world_hook: Calculating the volume of a vase from its profile curve

lessons.lesson_title: Arc Length of a Smooth Planar Curve (BC)
lessons.learning_objective: Find the length of a smooth curve y = f(x) on an interval using the arc length integral, and set up arc length integrals that require a calculator
lessons.key_concepts: Arc length L = integral from a to b of sqrt(1 + (f'(x))^2) dx; derived from the Pythagorean theorem on tiny segments; for x = g(y), L = integral of sqrt(1 + (g'(y))^2) dy; most integrals need numerical evaluation
lessons.key_vocabulary: arc length, smooth curve, differential segment, numerical integration
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget to square f'(x) inside the radical; students integrate sqrt(1 + f(x)^2) using f instead of f'; students take the square root term by term as 1 + f'(x)
lessons.real_world_hook: Measuring the length of cable needed for a hanging power line

units.unit_title: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates, and Vector-Valued Functions

lessons.learning_objective: Define curves parametrically, find dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), identify horizontal and vertical tangents, and write tangent lines to parametric curves
lessons.key_concepts: x = x(t), y = y(t) with parameter t and direction of motion; dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) when dx/dt is not 0; horizontal tangent where dy/dt = 0 and dx/dt is not 0; vertical tangent where dx/dt = 0 and dy/dt is not 0; eliminating the parameter
lessons.prerequisites: Chain rule, tangent lines, trig identities
lessons.key_vocabulary: parametric equation, parameter, orientation, horizontal tangent, vertical tangent, eliminate the parameter
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute dy/dx as (dx/dt)/(dy/dt); students set dy/dx = 0 by setting dx/dt = 0; students lose the direction of motion when they eliminate the parameter
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracing a drone's flight path where x and y each depend on time

lessons.learning_objective: Compute d^2y/dx^2 for parametric curves and use it to determine concavity
lessons.key_concepts: d^2y/dx^2 = [d/dt (dy/dx)] / (dx/dt); differentiate the expression for dy/dx with respect to t, then divide by dx/dt; sign gives concavity at a value of t
lessons.prerequisites: Parametric first derivatives, quotient rule, concavity
lessons.key_vocabulary: second derivative, concavity, parametric derivative
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute d^2y/dx^2 as (d^2y/dt^2)/(d^2x/dt^2); students differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and forget to divide by dx/dt; students differentiate dy/dx with respect to x while it is written in t
lessons.real_world_hook: Determining whether a roller coaster track bends upward or downward at a given moment

lessons.learning_objective: Find the length of a parametric curve over an interval of t and distinguish arc length from displacement
lessons.key_concepts: L = integral from t = a to t = b of sqrt((dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2) dt; this equals total distance traveled only if the curve is traced once; integrand is speed
lessons.prerequisites: Arc length for y = f(x), parametric derivatives, definite integrals
lessons.key_vocabulary: parametric arc length, speed, distance traveled, traced once
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use x-values instead of t-values as the bounds; students compute straight-line distance between endpoints instead of path length; students forget to square each derivative
lessons.real_world_hook: Measuring the distance a point on a bicycle wheel travels (a cycloid)

lessons.learning_objective: Differentiate and integrate vector-valued functions component by component and use initial conditions to find particular position vectors
lessons.key_concepts: r(t) = <x(t), y(t)>; r'(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)> is the velocity vector tangent to the path; integrate each component and add a vector constant; use initial position to solve for constants
lessons.key_vocabulary: vector-valued function, component, position vector, velocity vector, tangent vector
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students add one scalar + C instead of a constant for each component; students treat <x, y> as a single number; students confuse the position vector with the direction of motion
lessons.real_world_hook: GPS tracking of a delivery truck as a moving position vector

lessons.learning_objective: Solve planar motion problems using parametric and vector-valued functions to find velocity, speed, acceleration, displacement, and total distance
lessons.key_concepts: v(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)>; a(t) = <x''(t), y''(t)>; speed = |v(t)| = sqrt(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2); total distance = integral of speed; position at time b = position at a + integral of v from a to b; slope of path = y'(t)/x'(t)
lessons.prerequisites: Vector-valued derivatives and integrals, parametric arc length
lessons.key_vocabulary: velocity vector, acceleration vector, speed, magnitude, displacement vector, total distance
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students report speed as x'(t) + y'(t) instead of the magnitude; students give speed as a vector; students compute total distance as the magnitude of displacement
lessons.real_world_hook: Analyzing the path of a soccer ball kicked across a field

lessons.learning_objective: Convert between polar and rectangular coordinates, graph polar curves, find dy/dx for polar curves, and interpret dr/dtheta
lessons.key_concepts: x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), r^2 = x^2 + y^2; polar curves as parametric in theta; dy/dx = (dy/dtheta)/(dx/dtheta) with dy/dtheta = r' sin(theta) + r cos(theta) and dx/dtheta = r' cos(theta) - r sin(theta); dr/dtheta > 0 with r > 0 means the curve moves away from the origin
lessons.prerequisites: Unit circle, parametric derivatives, product rule
lessons.key_vocabulary: polar coordinates, pole, polar curve, rose curve, limacon, cardioid, dr/dtheta
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat dr/dtheta as the slope of the tangent line; students forget the product rule when differentiating r sin(theta); students misinterpret dr/dtheta < 0 with r < 0 (the point is actually moving away from the origin)
lessons.real_world_hook: Radar screens that locate aircraft by distance and angle

lessons.learning_objective: Find the area of a region bounded by one polar curve and the area between two polar curves, determining correct theta bounds
lessons.key_concepts: Area = (1/2) integral from alpha to beta of r^2 dtheta, built from sectors; bounds from where r = 0 or curves intersect; area between curves = (1/2) integral of (R^2 - r^2) dtheta; using symmetry; avoiding double-tracing
lessons.prerequisites: Polar graphing, sector area, solving trig equations
lessons.key_vocabulary: polar area, sector, inner loop, intersection, theta bounds, symmetry
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students integrate r instead of (1/2) r^2; students compute (1/2) integral of (R - r)^2 for the region between curves; students use bounds that trace a rose petal twice
lessons.real_world_hook: Calculating the coverage area of a lawn sprinkler with a non-circular spray pattern

lessons.lesson_title: Convergent and Divergent Series and Geometric Series
lessons.learning_objective: Define convergence of an infinite series through partial sums and determine convergence and sums of geometric series
lessons.key_concepts: Sequence vs series; partial sums S_n; series converges if lim S_n exists; geometric series sum a r^n converges iff |r| < 1 with sum = first term/(1 - r); telescoping as an illustration of partial sums
lessons.prerequisites: Limits at infinity, sequences, exponent rules
lessons.key_vocabulary: sequence, series, partial sum, converge, diverge, geometric series, common ratio
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students confuse a sequence converging with the series converging; students use a/(1 - r) with the wrong first term when the index starts at n = 1; students apply the geometric sum formula when |r| >= 1
lessons.real_world_hook: Total distance a bouncing ball travels if each bounce is 80% of the last

lessons.lesson_title: nth Term Test, Integral Test, and p-Series
lessons.learning_objective: Use the nth term test for divergence, the integral test, and the p-series test, including the harmonic series, to determine convergence
lessons.key_concepts: If lim a_n is not 0 the series diverges; lim a_n = 0 is inconclusive; integral test requires f positive, continuous, and decreasing; p-series sum 1/n^p converges iff p > 1; harmonic series diverges
lessons.key_vocabulary: nth term test, divergence test, integral test, p-series, harmonic series, inconclusive
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students conclude a series converges because its terms approach 0 (harmonic series); students think the integral test gives the sum of the series; students mix up p-series and geometric series (1/n^2 vs 1/2^n)
lessons.real_world_hook: Why stacking blocks can overhang an arbitrarily long distance (harmonic series)

lessons.learning_objective: Determine convergence of positive-term series by comparing them to known geometric or p-series with the direct and limit comparison tests
lessons.key_concepts: Direct comparison: 0 <= a_n <= b_n and sum b_n converges implies sum a_n converges, and the reverse for divergence; limit comparison: if lim a_n/b_n is finite and positive both series behave the same; choosing b_n from dominant terms
lessons.prerequisites: p-series, geometric series, limits of rational functions
lessons.key_vocabulary: direct comparison test, limit comparison test, dominant term, bounded above, bounded below
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue a series is smaller than a divergent series and conclude it diverges; students use comparison tests on series with negative terms; students forget to state the comparison series converges or diverges
lessons.real_world_hook: Bounding the cost of an infinite payment plan with a simpler known plan

lessons.learning_objective: Apply the alternating series test to determine convergence of alternating series
lessons.key_concepts: Series sum (-1)^n b_n with b_n > 0 converges if b_n is decreasing and lim b_n = 0; the alternating harmonic series converges; both conditions must be stated in justification
lessons.key_vocabulary: alternating series, alternating series test, decreasing, alternating harmonic series
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use the alternating series test to conclude divergence when its conditions fail; students skip checking that b_n is decreasing; students think all alternating series converge
lessons.real_world_hook: Approximating ln 2 by adding and subtracting smaller and smaller fractions

lessons.learning_objective: Apply the ratio test to determine convergence, especially for series involving factorials and exponentials
lessons.key_concepts: L = lim |a_(n+1)/a_n|; L < 1 converges absolutely, L > 1 diverges, L = 1 inconclusive; simplifying (n+1)!/n! = n + 1; ratio test fails for p-series
lessons.prerequisites: Factorials, exponent rules, limits at infinity
lessons.key_vocabulary: ratio test, factorial, absolute convergence, inconclusive
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students conclude divergence when L = 1; students simplify (n+1)!/n! incorrectly as 1 or n; students compute a_n/a_(n+1) instead of a_(n+1)/a_n
lessons.real_world_hook: Why compound growth factors like 2^n eventually lose to n!

lessons.lesson_title: Absolute and Conditional Convergence and the Alternating Series Error Bound
lessons.learning_objective: Classify series as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent, and bound the error of an alternating series partial sum
lessons.key_concepts: Absolute convergence: sum |a_n| converges; conditional: sum a_n converges but sum |a_n| diverges; absolute convergence implies convergence; alternating series error |S - S_n| <= b_(n+1), the first omitted term; sign of the error
lessons.prerequisites: Alternating series test, p-series, comparison tests
lessons.key_vocabulary: absolute convergence, conditional convergence, error bound, remainder, first omitted term
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use the last included term instead of the first omitted term as the error bound; students think conditionally convergent means it might diverge; students check only the absolute series and wrongly call a series divergent
lessons.real_world_hook: Knowing how many terms a calculator needs to guarantee four correct decimal places

lessons.learning_objective: Construct Taylor and Maclaurin polynomials of a given degree centered at a point and use them to approximate function values
lessons.key_concepts: P_n(x) = sum from k = 0 to n of f^(k)(a)/k! (x - a)^k; coefficients match derivatives at the center; Maclaurin means centered at 0; higher degree generally improves accuracy near the center; reading derivative values from a given polynomial
lessons.key_vocabulary: Taylor polynomial, Maclaurin polynomial, center, degree, coefficient, nth derivative
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget to divide by k!; students write (x)^k instead of (x - a)^k for a non-zero center; students confuse the coefficient of x^3 with f'''(0) instead of f'''(0)/3!
lessons.real_world_hook: How calculators compute sin(0.3) using only multiplication and addition

lessons.learning_objective: Use the Lagrange error bound to find the maximum possible error of a Taylor polynomial approximation and determine the degree needed for a given accuracy
lessons.key_concepts: |R_n(x)| <= M |x - a|^(n+1)/(n+1)! where M bounds |f^(n+1)| between a and x; for sin and cos, M = 1; choosing M from given derivative bounds; comparing with the alternating series error bound
lessons.prerequisites: Taylor polynomials, factorials, bounding functions on an interval
lessons.key_vocabulary: Lagrange error bound, remainder, maximum error, bound M, (n+1)th derivative
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use the nth derivative instead of the (n+1)th to find M; students use n! instead of (n+1)!; students evaluate M at the center only instead of maximizing over the whole interval
lessons.real_world_hook: Guaranteeing a GPS calculation is accurate to within a meter

lessons.learning_objective: Find the radius and interval of convergence of a power series using the ratio test and test endpoints separately
lessons.key_concepts: Power series sum c_n (x - a)^n; ratio test gives |x - a| < R; endpoints must be tested individually (often with p-series or alternating series tests); differentiating or integrating a power series keeps the radius but may change endpoint behavior
lessons.prerequisites: Ratio test, alternating series test, p-series, absolute value inequalities
lessons.key_vocabulary: power series, radius of convergence, interval of convergence, endpoint, center
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students skip testing the endpoints or assume both endpoints behave the same way; students give the interval as centered at 0 when the series is centered at a; students think integrating a series cannot change endpoint convergence
lessons.real_world_hook: Knowing the range of inputs where a computer's series formula can be trusted

lessons.lesson_title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series and Power Series Representations
lessons.learning_objective: Write Maclaurin series for e^x, sin x, cos x, 1/(1 - x), and ln(1 + x), and build new series by substitution, multiplication, differentiation, and integration
lessons.key_concepts: e^x = sum x^n/n!, sin x = sum (-1)^n x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)!, cos x = sum (-1)^n x^(2n)/(2n)!, 1/(1 - x) = sum x^n for |x| < 1; substitute (e.g., x^2 for x) and manipulate term by term; general term notation; using series to evaluate limits and integrals like integral of e^(-x^2)
lessons.prerequisites: Taylor polynomials, geometric series, differentiation and integration rules
lessons.key_vocabulary: Taylor series, Maclaurin series, power series representation, general term, term-by-term differentiation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students substitute 2x into the sin x series but forget to raise the 2 to each power; students mix up the even and odd powers of the sin and cos series; students forget the constant of integration when integrating a series term by term
lessons.real_world_hook: Computing the bell-curve integral of e^(-x^2), which has no elementary antiderivative

units.unit_title: Vectors and the Geometry of Space

lessons.learning_objective: Represent vectors geometrically and in component form, perform vector addition and scalar multiplication, and find magnitudes and unit vectors
lessons.key_concepts: A vector has magnitude and direction but no fixed position; the vector from P(x1, y1) to Q(x2, y2) is <x2 - x1, y2 - y1>, e.g. P(1, 2) to Q(4, 6) gives <3, 4>; magnitude |<a, b>| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), so |<3, 4>| = 5; the unit vector in the direction of v is v/|v| = <3/5, 4/5>; addition is componentwise (tip-to-tail / parallelogram rule); scalar multiplication cv scales length by |c| and reverses direction if c < 0; standard unit vectors i = <1, 0>, j = <0, 1>; triangle inequality |u + v| <= |u| + |v|
lessons.prerequisites: Pythagorean theorem, right-triangle trigonometry, coordinate plane
lessons.key_vocabulary: vector, scalar, component form, magnitude, unit vector, standard unit vectors, initial point, terminal point, parallelogram rule, zero vector
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute the vector from P to Q as P - Q instead of Q - P (terminal minus initial); students assume |u + v| = |u| + |v|, e.g. claiming |<3, 0> + <0, 4>| = 7 when it is 5
lessons.real_world_hook: A pilot heading east at 500 km/h in a 50 km/h north wind computes her true ground velocity <500, 50> and ground speed sqrt(252500), about 502.5 km/h

lessons.learning_objective: Locate points in R^3, compute distances, write equations of spheres, and interpret simple equations as surfaces in space
lessons.key_concepts: Right-handed xyz coordinate system; distance between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) is sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2 + (z2 - z1)^2), e.g. (1, 2, 3) to (4, 6, 15) is sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = 13; sphere of radius r centered at (a, b, c): (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 + (z - c)^2 = r^2, completing the square to find center and radius; vectors in space <a, b, c> = ai + bj + ck with magnitude sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2); in R^3 an equation in one variable such as y = 2 describes a plane
lessons.prerequisites: Vectors in the plane, distance formula, completing the square
lessons.key_vocabulary: octant, right-hand rule, coordinate plane, sphere, standard unit vectors i, j, k, distance formula
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students interpret y = 2 in R^3 as a line, when it is the plane parallel to the xz-plane; students read the sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 4y = 4 as having radius 2, forgetting that completing the square gives (x - 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 + z^2 = 9, radius 3
lessons.real_world_hook: A drone at (10, 20, 30) meters must stay within 50 m of its controller at the origin; the sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 2500 is its flight boundary

lessons.learning_objective: Compute dot products, use them to find angles between vectors, test orthogonality, and compute scalar and vector projections and work
lessons.key_concepts: u . v = u1 v1 + u2 v2 + u3 v3 = |u||v| cos(theta) where theta in [0, pi] is the angle between them; u . u = |u|^2; u and v are orthogonal iff u . v = 0, e.g. <1, 2, 2> . <2, -2, 1> = 2 - 4 + 2 = 0; direction cosines; scalar projection comp_v u = (u . v)/|v|; vector projection proj_v u = ((u . v)/|v|^2) v, e.g. proj of <3, 4> onto <1, 0> is <3, 0>; work done by a constant force along displacement d is W = F . d
lessons.prerequisites: Vectors in space, law of cosines, inverse cosine
lessons.key_vocabulary: dot product, scalar product, orthogonal, angle between vectors, direction cosines, scalar projection, vector projection, work
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students divide by |v| instead of |v|^2 in the vector projection formula, producing a vector of the wrong length; students think the dot product of two vectors is a vector, writing <1, 2> . <3, 4> = <3, 8> instead of 11
lessons.real_world_hook: Pulling a wagon 20 m with a 50 N force at 30 degrees above the ground does W = 50 * 20 * cos(30 deg) = 500 sqrt(3), about 866 J of work

lessons.learning_objective: Compute cross products with the determinant formula, use the right-hand rule, and apply cross products to area, volume, and torque
lessons.key_concepts: u x v = <u2 v3 - u3 v2, u3 v1 - u1 v3, u1 v2 - u2 v1>, computed as a 3x3 determinant with i, j, k in the first row, e.g. <1, 2, 3> x <4, 5, 6> = <-3, 6, -3>; u x v is orthogonal to both u and v with direction given by the right-hand rule; i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j; anticommutative: v x u = -(u x v); |u x v| = |u||v| sin(theta) = area of the parallelogram spanned by u and v; scalar triple product u . (v x w) gives the signed volume of the parallelepiped; torque tau = r x F
lessons.key_vocabulary: cross product, vector product, determinant, right-hand rule, anticommutative, parallelogram area, scalar triple product, parallelepiped, torque
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget the minus sign on the j-component in the cofactor expansion, getting <-3, -6, -3> for <1, 2, 3> x <4, 5, 6>; students assume u x v = v x u, when actually v x u = -(u x v)
lessons.real_world_hook: A mechanic pushing 40 N perpendicular to the end of a 0.25 m wrench produces 10 N-m of torque, while pushing along the handle produces none

lessons.lesson_title: Equations of Lines and Planes in Space
lessons.learning_objective: Write vector, parametric, and symmetric equations of lines and scalar equations of planes, and compute distances and angles between them
lessons.key_concepts: Line through P0 with direction v: r(t) = r0 + tv, e.g. through (1, 2, 3) with direction <2, -1, 4>: x = 1 + 2t, y = 2 - t, z = 3 + 4t, symmetric form (x - 1)/2 = (y - 2)/(-1) = (z - 3)/4; lines in space can be parallel, intersecting, or skew; plane through P0 with normal n = <a, b, c>: a(x - x0) + b(y - y0) + c(z - z0) = 0, e.g. normal <3, -1, 2> through (1, 0, 2) gives 3x - y + 2z = 7; a plane through three points uses n = PQ x PR; distance from (x0, y0, z0) to ax + by + cz = d is |a x0 + b y0 + c z0 - d|/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2), so the origin is 7/sqrt(14) from 3x - y + 2z = 7; angle between planes is the angle between normals
lessons.prerequisites: Dot product, cross product, parametric equations
lessons.key_vocabulary: parametric equations, symmetric equations, direction vector, normal vector, skew lines, scalar equation of a plane, distance from a point to a plane
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students conclude two non-parallel lines in space must intersect, forgetting skew lines; students use the coefficients <3, -1, 2> of the plane 3x - y + 2z = 7 as a direction vector lying in the plane, when it is the normal, perpendicular to the plane
lessons.real_world_hook: A flight-path planner checks whether two aircraft routes, modeled as lines in 3D, intersect or are skew and safely separated

lessons.learning_objective: Sketch and identify cylinders and the six quadric surfaces using traces and the signs and powers in their equations
lessons.key_concepts: A cylinder is generated by lines parallel to an axis whose variable is missing, e.g. x^2 + y^2 = 1 in R^3 is a circular cylinder along the z-axis; traces are intersections with planes x = k, y = k, z = k; standard quadrics: ellipsoid x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1, hyperboloid of one sheet x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 - z^2/c^2 = 1 (one minus sign), hyperboloid of two sheets -x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2 = 1 (two minus signs), elliptic cone z^2 = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2, elliptic paraboloid z = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2, hyperbolic paraboloid (saddle) z = y^2/b^2 - x^2/a^2; the variable that is linear (or has the different sign) identifies the axis
lessons.prerequisites: Conic sections, 3D coordinates, completing the square
lessons.key_vocabulary: cylinder, rulings, trace, quadric surface, ellipsoid, hyperboloid of one sheet, hyperboloid of two sheets, elliptic cone, elliptic paraboloid, hyperbolic paraboloid
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students read x^2 + y^2 = 1 in R^3 as a circle rather than an infinite cylinder; students mix up the hyperboloids, calling x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1 (one negative term, connected) a hyperboloid of two sheets
lessons.real_world_hook: Cooling towers at power plants are hyperboloids of one sheet, and a Pringles chip is a piece of a hyperbolic paraboloid

lessons.learning_objective: Convert points and equations among rectangular, cylindrical, and spherical coordinates and choose the system that best fits a surface
lessons.key_concepts: Cylindrical (r, theta, z): x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), z = z, r^2 = x^2 + y^2; spherical (rho, theta, phi) with rho >= 0, 0 <= phi <= pi measured down from the positive z-axis: x = rho sin(phi) cos(theta), y = rho sin(phi) sin(theta), z = rho cos(phi), rho^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2; e.g. (1, 1, sqrt(2)) is cylindrical (sqrt(2), pi/4, sqrt(2)) and spherical (2, pi/4, pi/4); r = c is a cylinder, rho = c a sphere, phi = c a cone, theta = c a half-plane; choose theta in the correct quadrant rather than trusting arctan(y/x)
lessons.key_vocabulary: cylindrical coordinates, spherical coordinates, rho, azimuthal angle theta, polar angle phi, half-plane, cone
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students measure phi from the xy-plane (like latitude) instead of from the positive z-axis, giving z = rho sin(phi); students convert (-1, -1, 0) with theta = arctan(1) = pi/4 instead of 5pi/4, ignoring the quadrant
lessons.real_world_hook: GPS and planetary science use spherical-type coordinates: a point on Earth is described by a radius, a longitude (theta), and a colatitude (phi = 90 degrees minus latitude)

lessons.learning_objective: Describe curves in space with vector-valued functions, find their domains, sketch them, and compute limits componentwise
lessons.key_concepts: A vector-valued function r(t) = <f(t), g(t), h(t)> traces a space curve as t varies; its domain is the intersection of the component domains; limits and continuity are computed componentwise; the helix r(t) = <cos t, sin t, t> winds around the cylinder x^2 + y^2 = 1; parametrizing the intersection of two surfaces, e.g. the cylinder x^2 + y^2 = 1 and the plane z = y gives r(t) = <cos t, sin t, sin t>
lessons.prerequisites: Parametric equations, lines in space, limits
lessons.key_vocabulary: vector-valued function, space curve, parameter, helix, componentwise limit, orientation of a curve
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat r(t) = <cos t, sin t, t> as a surface rather than a one-dimensional curve; students state the domain of r(t) = <sqrt(t), ln(3 - t), 1/t> as t >= 0, missing the restrictions t < 3 and t != 0, so the domain is (0, 3)
lessons.real_world_hook: Roller-coaster track designers and DNA models both describe helices with r(t) = <a cos t, a sin t, bt>

lessons.learning_objective: Differentiate and integrate vector-valued functions, find unit tangent vectors and tangent lines, and apply derivative rules for dot and cross products
lessons.key_concepts: r'(t) = <f'(t), g'(t), h'(t)> is tangent to the curve; unit tangent T(t) = r'(t)/|r'(t)|; for the helix <cos t, sin t, t>, r'(t) = <-sin t, cos t, 1> with |r'(t)| = sqrt(2); product rules d/dt[u . v] = u' . v + u . v' and d/dt[u x v] = u' x v + u x v' (order must be kept); if |r(t)| is constant then r(t) . r'(t) = 0; integrals are componentwise with a constant vector C, found from an initial condition
lessons.prerequisites: Vector-valued functions, single-variable derivatives and integrals, cross product
lessons.key_vocabulary: derivative of a vector function, tangent vector, unit tangent vector, smooth curve, indefinite integral of a vector function, constant vector
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write the cross-product rule as u' x v + v' x u, swapping the order in the second term and flipping its sign; students add a scalar + C instead of a constant vector <C1, C2, C3> when integrating
lessons.real_world_hook: A spacecraft's velocity is the derivative of its position vector, and integrating measured acceleration twice reconstructs its trajectory

lessons.learning_objective: Compute arc length of space curves, reparametrize by arc length, and compute curvature, the unit normal, and the binormal
lessons.key_concepts: Arc length L = integral from a to b of |r'(t)| dt; the helix <cos t, sin t, t> for 0 <= t <= 2pi has L = 2pi sqrt(2); arc-length function s(t) = integral from a to t of |r'(u)| du; curvature kappa = |dT/ds| = |T'(t)|/|r'(t)| = |r'(t) x r''(t)|/|r'(t)|^3; a circle of radius a has kappa = 1/a; for the helix, r' x r'' = <sin t, -cos t, 1> with magnitude sqrt(2), so kappa = sqrt(2)/(sqrt(2))^3 = 1/2; for y = f(x), kappa = |f''(x)|/(1 + f'(x)^2)^(3/2); principal unit normal N = T'/|T'|, binormal B = T x N
lessons.prerequisites: Calculus of vector functions, cross product, arc length in single-variable calculus
lessons.key_vocabulary: arc length, arc-length parametrization, curvature, radius of curvature, principal unit normal, binormal, osculating circle, TNB frame
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute curvature as |T'(t)| without dividing by |r'(t)|, which is only correct for unit-speed curves (for the helix |T'(t)| = 1/sqrt(2), but kappa = 1/2); students think a curve's curvature depends on how fast it is traversed
lessons.real_world_hook: Highway engineers limit the curvature of exit ramps because the sideways force on a car is proportional to kappa times speed squared

lessons.learning_objective: Model position, velocity, and acceleration of objects in space and decompose acceleration into tangential and normal components
lessons.key_concepts: v(t) = r'(t), speed = |v(t)|, a(t) = r''(t); a = a_T T + a_N N with a_T = (v . a)/|v| = d|v|/dt and a_N = |v x a|/|v| = kappa |v|^2; for r(t) = <t, t^2> at t = 1: v = <1, 2>, a = <0, 2>, a_T = 4/sqrt(5), a_N = 2/sqrt(5), and a_T^2 + a_N^2 = 4 = |a|^2; projectile motion r(t) = <v0 cos(alpha) t, v0 sin(alpha) t - (1/2) g t^2>; uniform circular motion has acceleration of magnitude v^2/R pointing toward the center
lessons.prerequisites: Calculus of vector functions, curvature, dot and cross product
lessons.key_vocabulary: position vector, velocity, speed, acceleration, tangential component, normal component, projectile motion, centripetal acceleration
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students claim an object moving at constant speed has zero acceleration, ignoring the normal component a_N = kappa |v|^2 (e.g. uniform circular motion); students assume acceleration always points in the direction of velocity
lessons.real_world_hook: A baseball hit at 45 m/s at 30 degrees: solving the y-component for landing time t = 2 v0 sin(alpha)/g and plugging into x gives range v0^2 sin(2 alpha)/g, about 179 m without air resistance

units.unit_title: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables

lessons.learning_objective: Find domains and ranges of functions of two and three variables and interpret graphs, level curves, contour maps, and level surfaces
lessons.key_concepts: z = f(x, y) assigns one output to each point of a domain in R^2; e.g. f(x, y) = sqrt(9 - x^2 - y^2) has domain the closed disk x^2 + y^2 <= 9 and range [0, 3], and its graph is the upper hemisphere; level curve f(x, y) = k; a contour map shows level curves at equally spaced k, with closely spaced curves meaning steep terrain; level surfaces f(x, y, z) = k for functions of three variables, e.g. x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = k are spheres
lessons.prerequisites: Function notation, quadric surfaces, inequalities in two variables
lessons.key_vocabulary: function of two variables, domain, range, graph, level curve, contour map, level surface
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students confuse a level curve with a trace of the graph in a vertical plane; students assume level curves for equally spaced k are equally spaced in the plane, e.g. for f = x^2 + y^2 the circles for k = 1, 2, 3, 4 have radii 1, 1.41, 1.73, 2, getting closer together
lessons.real_world_hook: Hikers read topographic maps whose contour lines are level curves of elevation; tight contour spacing warns of a steep slope

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate limits of functions of two variables, prove limits do not exist using different paths, and determine continuity
lessons.key_concepts: lim (x, y) -> (a, b) f(x, y) = L requires f to approach L along every path; if two paths give different values the limit does not exist, e.g. xy/(x^2 + y^2) along y = mx gives m/(1 + m^2), which depends on m; checking all lines is not enough: x^2 y/(x^4 + y^2) -> 0 along every line through the origin but -> 1/2 along y = x^2; polar substitution or squeeze proves existence, e.g. x^2 y/(x^2 + y^2) = r cos^2(theta) sin(theta) -> 0; polynomials and rational functions are continuous on their domains; compositions of continuous functions are continuous
lessons.prerequisites: Single-variable limits, squeeze theorem, polar coordinates
lessons.key_vocabulary: limit of a function of two variables, path, neighborhood, open disk, continuity, squeeze theorem, interior point, boundary point
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students conclude a limit exists because it agrees along the x-axis, the y-axis, and all lines y = mx, missing curved paths such as y = x^2; students treat a polar result r g(theta) as going to 0 even when g(theta) is unbounded
lessons.real_world_hook: Engineers check that a temperature model on a metal plate has no jump at a seam: approaching the seam from different directions must give the same temperature

lessons.learning_objective: Compute first and higher-order partial derivatives, interpret them as slopes and rates, and apply Clairaut's theorem
lessons.key_concepts: f_x is the derivative with respect to x holding y constant: the slope of the trace in the plane y = b; for f = x^2 y^3 + sin(xy), f_x = 2x y^3 + y cos(xy) and f_y = 3x^2 y^2 + x cos(xy); second partials f_xx, f_yy, f_xy, f_yx; Clairaut's theorem: if f_xy and f_yx are continuous near a point they are equal, and here both are 6x y^2 + cos(xy) - xy sin(xy); partial derivatives of functions of three variables; partial differential equations such as the heat equation u_t = k u_xx
lessons.prerequisites: Single-variable differentiation rules, functions of several variables
lessons.key_vocabulary: partial derivative, f_x, df/dx (partial), trace, second-order partial derivative, mixed partial, Clairaut's theorem, partial differential equation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students differentiate the held-constant variable, e.g. writing d/dx (x^2 y^3) = 2x y^3 + 3x^2 y^2; students believe that existence of f_x and f_y at a point implies continuity there, though f = xy/(x^2 + y^2) with f(0, 0) = 0 has f_x(0, 0) = f_y(0, 0) = 0 and is discontinuous
lessons.real_world_hook: An economist uses the partial derivative of a production function with respect to labor to measure the marginal output of one more worker while capital is held fixed

lessons.learning_objective: Find tangent planes to surfaces, use linearization and differentials to approximate values and errors, and state the meaning of differentiability
lessons.key_concepts: Tangent plane to z = f(x, y) at (a, b): z = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x - a) + f_y(a, b)(y - b); for f = x^2 + y^2 at (1, 2): z = 5 + 2(x - 1) + 4(y - 2), so f(1.1, 1.9) is about 4.8 (actual 4.82); linearization L(x, y) is the tangent plane function; total differential dz = f_x dx + f_y dy estimates change and propagated error; f is differentiable at (a, b) if the error of L goes to 0 faster than the distance to (a, b); if f_x and f_y are continuous near (a, b), f is differentiable there
lessons.prerequisites: Partial derivatives, equations of planes, single-variable linearization
lessons.key_vocabulary: tangent plane, linear approximation, linearization, differentiable, total differential, error estimation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students leave f_x(x, y) unevaluated in the tangent plane formula, producing a curved surface instead of a plane; students use dz = f_x + f_y without multiplying by dx and dy
lessons.real_world_hook: A machinist measures a cylinder as r = 3 cm and h = 10 cm, each with 0.1 cm error; dV = 2 pi r h dr + pi r^2 dh = 6 pi + 0.9 pi = 6.9 pi, about 21.7 cubic cm of possible error

lessons.learning_objective: Apply the multivariable chain rule using tree diagrams and use it for implicit differentiation
lessons.key_concepts: If z = f(x, y) with x = x(t), y = y(t), then dz/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt; e.g. z = x^2 y, x = cos t, y = sin t gives dz/dt = -2 cos t sin^2 t + cos^3 t, matching direct differentiation of cos^2 t sin t; with x = x(s, t), y = y(s, t): dz/ds = z_x x_s + z_y y_s; tree diagrams track every path from z to the final variable; implicit differentiation: if F(x, y) = 0 then dy/dx = -F_x/F_y, e.g. x^2 + y^2 = 25 gives dy/dx = -x/y; if F(x, y, z) = 0 then dz/dx = -F_x/F_z
lessons.prerequisites: Partial derivatives, single-variable chain rule, implicit differentiation
lessons.key_vocabulary: chain rule, tree diagram, intermediate variable, independent variable, implicit differentiation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students drop a branch of the tree diagram, writing dz/dt = f_x dx/dt only; students forget the negative sign in dy/dx = -F_x/F_y, giving x/y for the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25
lessons.real_world_hook: The rate a gas's pressure changes as a balloon rises depends on how both its temperature and its volume change with time, combined through the chain rule applied to P = nRT/V

lessons.learning_objective: Compute directional derivatives and gradients, interpret the gradient as the direction of steepest ascent, and use it to find normal lines and tangent planes to level surfaces
lessons.key_concepts: Gradient grad f = <f_x, f_y> (or <f_x, f_y, f_z>); directional derivative D_u f = grad f . u for a unit vector u; for f = x^2 + 3xy at (1, 2), grad f = <8, 3>, and in the direction of <3, 4>, u = <3/5, 4/5> and D_u f = 36/5; maximum rate of increase is |grad f| = sqrt(73) in the direction of grad f, minimum is -|grad f|; grad f is perpendicular to level curves; tangent plane to the level surface F(x, y, z) = k at P is grad F(P) . <x - x0, y - y0, z - z0> = 0
lessons.prerequisites: Partial derivatives, dot product, unit vectors, chain rule
lessons.key_vocabulary: directional derivative, gradient, steepest ascent, level curve, level surface, normal line, tangent plane to a level surface
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use a non-unit direction vector, e.g. computing <8, 3> . <3, 4> = 36 instead of 36/5; students think the gradient of f(x, y) is a vector in R^3 tangent to the graph, rather than a vector in the xy-plane perpendicular to the level curve
lessons.real_world_hook: A heat-seeking robot moves in the direction of the temperature gradient to reach the hottest point fastest

lessons.learning_objective: Find critical points, classify them with the second derivative test, and find absolute extrema on closed, bounded regions
lessons.key_concepts: Critical points occur where grad f = 0 or a partial does not exist; second derivative test with D = f_xx f_yy - (f_xy)^2: D > 0 and f_xx > 0 local min, D > 0 and f_xx < 0 local max, D < 0 saddle point, D = 0 inconclusive; e.g. f = x^3 - 3x + y^2 has critical points (1, 0) with D = 12 > 0, f_xx = 6 > 0, a local min with f = -2, and (-1, 0) with D = -12, a saddle; extreme value theorem: a continuous f on a closed bounded region attains an absolute max and min, found by comparing interior critical values with the extremes on the boundary
lessons.key_vocabulary: critical point, local maximum, local minimum, saddle point, discriminant, second derivative test, absolute extremum, closed and bounded region, extreme value theorem
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students conclude D > 0 always means a minimum, forgetting to check the sign of f_xx; students treat D = 0 as meaning a saddle, though f = x^4 + y^4 has D = 0 at the origin and a minimum there
lessons.real_world_hook: A company chooses the prices of two competing products to maximize total profit P(x, y), checking with the second derivative test that the critical point is really a maximum

lessons.learning_objective: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to optimize a function subject to one or two constraints
lessons.key_concepts: At a constrained extremum of f subject to g(x, y) = k, the level curve of f is tangent to the constraint curve, so grad f = lambda grad g; solve f_x = lambda g_x, f_y = lambda g_y, g = k together; e.g. maximize f = xy on x + y = 10: y = lambda, x = lambda, so x = y = 5 and f = 25; f = x + y on x^2 + y^2 = 1 gives (1/sqrt(2), 1/sqrt(2)) with max sqrt(2) and (-1/sqrt(2), -1/sqrt(2)) with min -sqrt(2); two constraints: grad f = lambda grad g + mu grad h; evaluate f at every candidate to decide max vs min
lessons.key_vocabulary: constraint, Lagrange multiplier, constrained optimization, objective function, tangency condition
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students solve f_x = lambda g_x and f_y = lambda g_y but forget to use the constraint equation g = k, leaving infinitely many solutions; students report the value of lambda as the maximum instead of evaluating f at the candidate points
lessons.real_world_hook: Designing a closed box of volume 1000 cubic cm with the least material: minimizing surface area subject to xyz = 1000 gives a 10 cm cube

lessons.learning_objective: Define double integrals with Riemann sums and evaluate them over rectangles as iterated integrals using Fubini's theorem
lessons.key_concepts: The double integral of f over R is the limit of Riemann sums sum f(x_ij*, y_ij*) dA; when f >= 0 it equals the volume under the surface; Fubini's theorem: over R = [a, b] x [c, d] with f continuous, the integral equals either iterated integral; e.g. integral over [0, 2] x [0, 1] of (x + 2y) dA = integral from 0 to 2 of (x + 1) dx = 4; if f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) the integral splits into a product; average value = (1/Area(R)) times the double integral, here 4/2 = 2
lessons.prerequisites: Definite integrals, Riemann sums, functions of two variables
lessons.key_vocabulary: double integral, Riemann sum, iterated integral, Fubini's theorem, volume under a surface, average value
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students attach the limits to the wrong variable, integrating dy with the x-limits 0 to 2; students multiply integrals of non-separable functions, e.g. writing the integral of (x + 2y) as (integral of x dx)(integral of 2y dy)
lessons.real_world_hook: Estimating total rainfall over a rectangular county from a rainfall-depth map is a Riemann sum for a double integral

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate double integrals over Type I and Type II regions, reverse the order of integration, and compute areas and volumes
lessons.key_concepts: Type I region a <= x <= b, g1(x) <= y <= g2(x): integrate dy first; Type II region c <= y <= d, h1(y) <= x <= h2(y): integrate dx first; area of D is the double integral of 1 dA, e.g. between y = x^2 and y = x the area is the integral from 0 to 1 of (x - x^2) dx = 1/6; reversing the order requires redrawing the region: integral from 0 to 1, integral from x to 1 of e^(y^2) dy dx becomes integral from 0 to 1, integral from 0 to y of e^(y^2) dx dy = integral from 0 to 1 of y e^(y^2) dy = (e - 1)/2; outer limits must be constants
lessons.prerequisites: Double integrals over rectangles, area between curves
lessons.key_vocabulary: Type I region, Type II region, reversing the order of integration, iterated integral, region of integration
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students reverse the order of integration by swapping dx and dy but keeping the old limits, e.g. writing integral from 0 to 1, integral from x to 1 dx dy; students leave a variable in the outer limits, producing an answer that depends on x
lessons.real_world_hook: Computing the volume of concrete in an irregularly shaped foundation slab whose thickness varies across the slab

lessons.learning_objective: Convert double integrals to polar coordinates with dA = r dr d(theta) and evaluate them over disks, sectors, and polar regions
lessons.key_concepts: x = r cos(theta), y = r sin(theta), x^2 + y^2 = r^2, dA = r dr d(theta); polar rectangles and regions r between h1(theta) and h2(theta); e.g. the volume under z = 4 - x^2 - y^2 above the xy-plane is integral from 0 to 2pi, integral from 0 to 2 of (4 - r^2) r dr d(theta) = 8 pi; integral over the disk of radius a of e^(-(x^2 + y^2)) dA = pi(1 - e^(-a^2)), and letting a -> infinity shows the integral of e^(-x^2) over the real line is sqrt(pi); area enclosed by a polar curve r = f(theta) is (1/2) times the integral of f(theta)^2 d(theta)
lessons.prerequisites: Polar coordinates, double integrals over general regions
lessons.key_vocabulary: polar coordinates, polar rectangle, area element r dr d(theta), polar region, Gaussian integral
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget the r in dA = r dr d(theta) when converting to polar, getting 32 pi/3 instead of 8 pi for the paraboloid volume; students integrate theta from 0 to pi for a full disk
lessons.real_world_hook: The Gaussian integral computed with polar coordinates is the reason the normal distribution's bell curve has the constant 1/sqrt(2 pi)

lessons.lesson_title: Mass, Center of Mass, and Moments of Inertia in the Plane
lessons.learning_objective: Use double integrals to compute mass, moments, centers of mass, and moments of inertia of thin plates (laminas) with variable density
lessons.key_concepts: Mass m = double integral of rho(x, y) dA; moment about the x-axis M_x = double integral of y rho dA, about the y-axis M_y = double integral of x rho dA; center of mass (x-bar, y-bar) = (M_y/m, M_x/m); for the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1) and rho = 1: m = 1/2, M_y = 1/6, so (x-bar, y-bar) = (1/3, 1/3), the average of the vertices; moments of inertia I_x = double integral of y^2 rho dA, I_y = double integral of x^2 rho dA, I_0 = I_x + I_y; with constant density the center of mass is the centroid
lessons.prerequisites: Double integrals over general and polar regions
lessons.key_vocabulary: lamina, density, mass, first moment, center of mass, centroid, moment of inertia, polar moment of inertia
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students swap the moments, using x-bar = M_x/m when M_x = double integral of y rho dA so x-bar = M_y/m; students forget to divide by mass and report the moment as the center of mass
lessons.real_world_hook: Engineers find the balance point of an aircraft wing panel whose density increases toward the fuselage to place mounting points correctly

lessons.lesson_title: Change of Variables and the Jacobian
lessons.learning_objective: Use transformations and the Jacobian determinant to change variables in double integrals and simplify regions or integrands
lessons.key_concepts: A transformation T(u, v) = (x(u, v), y(u, v)) has Jacobian J = d(x, y)/d(u, v) = x_u y_v - x_v y_u; dA = |J| du dv; polar coordinates have J = r; x = u + v, y = u - v gives J = -2 and |J| = 2; x = au, y = bv maps the unit disk to the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 <= 1 with J = ab, so its area is pi ab; choose u and v from the boundary equations, e.g. u = x + y, v = x - y for a region bounded by lines x + y = c and x - y = c; d(x, y)/d(u, v) = 1/(d(u, v)/d(x, y)); in 3D spherical coordinates the Jacobian is rho^2 sin(phi)
lessons.prerequisites: Double integrals, polar coordinates, determinants, partial derivatives
lessons.key_vocabulary: transformation, change of variables, Jacobian, determinant, image of a region, one-to-one
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use d(u, v)/d(x, y) directly instead of its reciprocal when u and v are given in terms of x and y; students forget the absolute value, using J = -2 and getting a negative area
lessons.real_world_hook: Mapmakers and computer graphics programs stretch and warp regions; the Jacobian tells how much each tiny area is magnified

lessons.learning_objective: Set up and evaluate triple integrals over boxes and general solid regions in any of the six orders of integration
lessons.key_concepts: Triple integral = limit of Riemann sums f dV; Fubini over a box B: integral over [0, 1] x [0, 2] x [0, 3] of xyz dV = (1/2)(2)(9/2) = 9/2; general regions z between u1(x, y) and u2(x, y) over a projection D in the xy-plane; volume = triple integral of 1 dV, e.g. the tetrahedron x + y + z <= 1 in the first octant has volume integral from 0 to 1, integral from 0 to 1 - x, integral from 0 to 1 - x - y dz dy dx = 1/6; six possible orders, chosen by the shape of the region; average value over E is (1/V) times the triple integral
lessons.prerequisites: Double integrals over general regions, equations of planes, quadric surfaces
lessons.key_vocabulary: triple integral, iterated integral, solid region, projection onto a coordinate plane, order of integration, volume
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use limits for z that involve x and y, then put z into the limits of an outer integral; students project the solid onto the wrong plane, e.g. using the triangle in the xz-plane while writing dy dx as the outer differentials
lessons.real_world_hook: Calculating the total mass of a gold ingot from a 3D density scan uses a triple integral of density

lessons.learning_objective: Convert and evaluate triple integrals in cylindrical coordinates using dV = r dz dr d(theta)
lessons.key_concepts: dV = r dz dr d(theta); best for solids with circular symmetry about an axis: cylinders, paraboloids, cones; e.g. the solid inside r = 1 between z = 0 and z = 4 - r^2 has volume integral from 0 to 2pi, integral from 0 to 1 of (4 - r^2) r dr d(theta) = 2 pi (2 - 1/4) = 7 pi/2; the solid between the cone z = r and the plane z = 2 has volume integral from 0 to 2pi, integral from 0 to 2 of (2 - r) r dr d(theta) = 8 pi/3; describe z first, then project onto the xy-plane in polar coordinates
lessons.prerequisites: Cylindrical coordinates, double integrals in polar coordinates, triple integrals
lessons.key_vocabulary: cylindrical coordinates, cylindrical box, volume element, axis of symmetry
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget the factor r in dV = r dz dr d(theta); students use cylindrical coordinates with z-limits but integrate r out to the wrong boundary, e.g. using r = 2 for the solid inside the cylinder x^2 + y^2 = 2, whose radius is sqrt(2)
lessons.real_world_hook: Computing the volume of fluid in a parabolic satellite-dish-shaped tank

lessons.learning_objective: Convert and evaluate triple integrals in spherical coordinates using dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta)
lessons.key_concepts: dV = rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta), with 0 <= phi <= pi; the volume of a ball of radius a is integral from 0 to 2pi, from 0 to pi, from 0 to a of rho^2 sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta) = (2pi)(2)(a^3/3) = 4 pi a^3/3; the ice-cream-cone region inside rho = a above the cone phi = pi/4 has volume (2 pi a^3/3)(1 - sqrt(2)/2); best for spheres, cones phi = c, and integrands involving x^2 + y^2 + z^2; the Jacobian rho^2 sin(phi) is the determinant of the spherical change of variables
lessons.prerequisites: Spherical coordinates, change of variables, triple integrals
lessons.key_vocabulary: spherical coordinates, spherical wedge, volume element, Jacobian, cone phi = c
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write dV = rho sin(phi) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta) or rho^2 sin(theta) d(rho) d(phi) d(theta) instead of rho^2 sin(phi); students let phi range from 0 to 2pi, doubling the volume of a sphere
lessons.real_world_hook: Astronomers estimating the mass of a star whose density depends only on distance from its center integrate in spherical coordinates

lessons.lesson_title: Mass, Centers of Mass, and Moments in Three Dimensions
lessons.learning_objective: Use triple integrals to compute mass, centers of mass, centroids, and moments of inertia of solids, choosing an efficient coordinate system
lessons.key_concepts: m = triple integral of rho dV; first moments M_yz = triple integral of x rho dV, M_xz = of y rho dV, M_xy = of z rho dV; center of mass (M_yz/m, M_xz/m, M_xy/m); symmetry often makes coordinates zero; the solid hemisphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 <= a^2, z >= 0 with constant density has M_xy = pi a^4/4 and volume 2 pi a^3/3, so z-bar = 3a/8; moment of inertia about the z-axis I_z = triple integral of (x^2 + y^2) rho dV
lessons.prerequisites: Triple integrals in all three coordinate systems, center of mass of laminas
lessons.key_vocabulary: center of mass, centroid, first moment, moment of inertia, symmetry, density function
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students guess that the centroid of a solid hemisphere is at height a/2, when it is 3a/8; students compute M_xy with x instead of z, mixing up which coordinate the moment about the xy-plane uses
lessons.real_world_hook: Naval architects compute a ship hull's center of mass and center of buoyancy to make sure it rights itself after rolling

lessons.learning_objective: Sketch and interpret vector fields in two and three dimensions, including gradient, radial, and rotational fields
lessons.key_concepts: A vector field F assigns a vector to each point: F(x, y) = <P(x, y), Q(x, y)>; the rotational field <-y, x> circles the origin counterclockwise; the radial field <x, y> points away from the origin; gradient fields F = grad f are perpendicular to level curves of the potential f; inverse-square fields such as gravity F = -GMm r/|r|^3; flow lines (integral curves) are curves whose tangent at each point is F
lessons.prerequisites: Vectors, gradient, functions of several variables
lessons.key_vocabulary: vector field, gradient field, potential function, radial field, rotational field, flow line, inverse-square field
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students draw every vector of the field starting at the origin instead of at its base point (x, y); students assume every vector field is a gradient field, though <-y, x> has no potential function
lessons.real_world_hook: Weather maps of wind velocity and maps of ocean currents are vector fields

lessons.learning_objective: Parametrize curves and evaluate scalar line integrals with respect to arc length, and apply them to mass and length of wires
lessons.key_concepts: Integral over C of f ds = integral from a to b of f(r(t)) |r'(t)| dt; it does not depend on orientation or on the choice of smooth parametrization; e.g. integral of (x^2 + y^2) ds over the circle of radius 2 is 4 times the circumference 4 pi = 16 pi; for piecewise smooth curves add the pieces; mass of a wire with linear density rho is integral of rho ds; line integrals with respect to x or y, integral of f dx = integral of f(r(t)) x'(t) dt
lessons.prerequisites: Parametric curves, arc length, vector-valued functions
lessons.key_vocabulary: line integral, arc length element ds, parametrization, piecewise smooth curve, linear density
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget the factor |r'(t)| and integrate f(r(t)) dt, which gives 8 pi instead of 16 pi for the circle example; students think reversing the direction of C changes the sign of a scalar line integral with respect to arc length
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the total mass of a curved metal railing whose thickness, and hence density, varies along its length

lessons.lesson_title: Line Integrals of Vector Fields and Work
lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate line integrals of vector fields, interpret them as work, circulation, and flux across plane curves, and account for orientation
lessons.key_concepts: Integral over C of F . dr = integral from a to b of F(r(t)) . r'(t) dt = integral of P dx + Q dy + R dz; it equals the integral of F . T ds, the work done by F along C; reversing orientation changes the sign: integral over -C = -integral over C; for F = <-y, x> around the unit circle counterclockwise, F(r(t)) . r'(t) = sin^2 t + cos^2 t = 1, so the circulation is 2 pi; flux of F = <P, Q> across a plane curve with outward normal is integral of F . n ds = integral of P dy - Q dx
lessons.prerequisites: Scalar line integrals, dot product, vector fields
lessons.key_vocabulary: line integral of a vector field, work, circulation, flux across a curve, orientation, closed curve
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students ignore orientation and report +2 pi for the clockwise circle, which gives -2 pi; students multiply by |r'(t)| as well as dotting with r'(t), double-counting the speed
lessons.real_world_hook: Computing the work a river current does on a barge towed along a curved channel

lessons.lesson_title: Conservative Vector Fields and the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
lessons.learning_objective: Test whether a vector field is conservative, find potential functions, and evaluate line integrals with the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
lessons.key_concepts: Fundamental Theorem: integral over C of grad f . dr = f(r(b)) - f(r(a)), so the integral is path independent and is 0 around every closed curve; on an open simply connected region, F = <P, Q> is conservative iff P_y = Q_x (in 3D iff curl F = 0); e.g. F = <2xy, x^2 + 3y^2> has P_y = Q_x = 2x and potential f = x^2 y + y^3, so the integral from (0, 0) to (1, 2) is f(1, 2) - f(0, 0) = 10; find f by integrating P in x and determining the function of y from Q; the field <-y/(x^2 + y^2), x/(x^2 + y^2)> has P_y = Q_x but circulation 2 pi around the unit circle because its domain is not simply connected; conservation of energy
lessons.prerequisites: Line integrals of vector fields, gradient, partial derivatives
lessons.key_vocabulary: conservative vector field, potential function, path independence, simply connected region, closed curve, cross-partial test, conservation of energy
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students conclude a field is conservative from P_y = Q_x on a domain with a hole, such as the plane minus the origin; students find the potential by integrating P dx and Q dy separately and adding them, counting the shared term twice (getting 2x^2 y + y^3 instead of x^2 y + y^3)
lessons.real_world_hook: Gravity is conservative, so the work it does on a hiker depends only on the change in elevation, not on the trail chosen

lessons.learning_objective: Apply Green's theorem in circulation and flux form to convert line integrals around closed curves into double integrals and to compute areas
lessons.key_concepts: For a positively oriented (counterclockwise, region on the left) simple closed piecewise smooth curve C bounding D: integral around C of P dx + Q dy = double integral over D of (Q_x - P_y) dA; e.g. for P = xy, Q = x^2 around the boundary of the unit square, Q_x - P_y = 2x - x = x and the integral is 1/2; for F = <-y, x>, Q_x - P_y = 2 so the circulation around the unit circle is 2 times pi = 2 pi; area of D = (1/2) integral around C of x dy - y dx; flux form: integral of F . n ds = double integral of (P_x + Q_y) dA; extends to regions with holes by orienting inner boundaries clockwise
lessons.prerequisites: Line integrals of vector fields, double integrals, partial derivatives
lessons.key_vocabulary: Green's theorem, positive orientation, simple closed curve, circulation form, flux form, region with holes
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute P_x - Q_y or reverse the order to P_y - Q_x, getting the wrong sign; students apply Green's theorem to a clockwise curve without negating, or to a curve that is not closed
lessons.real_world_hook: A planimeter, a mechanical device that measures the area of a region on a map by tracing its boundary, works because of Green's theorem

units.unit_title: Surface Integrals and the Fundamental Theorems

lessons.learning_objective: Compute the divergence and curl of vector fields, interpret them physically, and use identities and the curl test for conservative fields
lessons.key_concepts: With del = <d/dx, d/dy, d/dz>: div F = del . F = P_x + Q_y + R_z, a scalar measuring outflow per unit volume; curl F = del x F = <R_y - Q_z, P_z - R_x, Q_x - P_y>, a vector measuring rotation; e.g. F = <xy, yz, zx> has div F = x + y + z and curl F = <-y, -z, -x>; identities curl(grad f) = 0 and div(curl F) = 0; if F is defined on all of R^3 with continuous partials and curl F = 0, then F is conservative; the k-component of curl in 2D is Q_x - P_y, the integrand of Green's theorem
lessons.prerequisites: Partial derivatives, cross product, conservative fields
lessons.key_vocabulary: divergence, curl, del operator, irrotational, incompressible, source, sink, Laplacian
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students report divergence as a vector <P_x, Q_y, R_z> and curl as a scalar, reversing which is which; students get the sign of the middle component of curl wrong, writing R_x - P_z instead of P_z - R_x
lessons.real_world_hook: Meteorologists use the curl of wind velocity (vorticity) to spot rotating storms and its divergence to find regions of rising or sinking air

lessons.learning_objective: Parametrize surfaces, find tangent planes and normal vectors with r_u x r_v, and compute surface area
lessons.key_concepts: A parametric surface r(u, v) = <x(u, v), y(u, v), z(u, v)> over a parameter domain D; r_u x r_v is normal to the surface; surface area = double integral over D of |r_u x r_v| dA; the sphere of radius a, r(phi, theta) = <a sin(phi) cos(theta), a sin(phi) sin(theta), a cos(phi)>, has |r_phi x r_theta| = a^2 sin(phi), so its area is 4 pi a^2; the cylinder r(theta, z) = <a cos(theta), a sin(theta), z>; for a graph z = g(x, y), dS = sqrt(1 + g_x^2 + g_y^2) dA, e.g. the part of the plane z = 2x + 2y over a region D has area 3 times area(D)
lessons.prerequisites: Cross product, double integrals, spherical and cylindrical coordinates
lessons.key_vocabulary: parametric surface, parameter domain, grid curves, normal vector, smooth surface, surface area, surface element dS
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat dS as dA, so they compute the projected area instead of the surface area; students forget the absolute value (magnitude) of r_u x r_v and integrate the vector itself
lessons.real_world_hook: Estimating how much paint is needed to coat a domed roof means computing a surface area integral

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate surface integrals of scalar functions and flux integrals of vector fields across oriented surfaces
lessons.key_concepts: Scalar surface integral: double integral over S of f dS = double integral over D of f(r(u, v)) |r_u x r_v| dA; an orientation is a continuous choice of unit normal n; closed surfaces are oriented outward by convention; flux = double integral of F . n dS = double integral over D of F(r(u, v)) . (r_u x r_v) dA when r_u x r_v points in the chosen direction; for the sphere, r_phi x r_theta = a sin(phi) r points outward; e.g. the flux of F = <x, y, z> outward through the sphere of radius a is a times 4 pi a^2 = 4 pi a^3; for z = g(x, y) oriented upward, F . n dS = (-P g_x - Q g_y + R) dA; a Mobius strip is not orientable
lessons.prerequisites: Parametric surfaces, line integrals, dot product
lessons.key_vocabulary: surface integral, oriented surface, unit normal vector, flux, outward orientation, orientable surface, Mobius strip
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use r_v x r_u when the problem asks for outward or upward orientation and get the flux with the wrong sign, without checking the direction of the normal; students divide F . (r_u x r_v) by |r_u x r_v| and then forget to multiply back, computing the integral of F . n dA instead of F . n dS
lessons.real_world_hook: Engineers compute the flux of water through a fishing net or of air through a filter to rate how much flow passes per second

lessons.learning_objective: Use Stokes' theorem to relate the circulation of a vector field around a closed curve to the flux of its curl through a surface the curve bounds
lessons.key_concepts: Integral around C of F . dr = double integral over S of curl F . n dS, where S is an oriented piecewise smooth surface with boundary C and C is oriented by the right-hand rule (walking along C with your head pointing in the direction of n, S is on your left); e.g. F = <-y, x, 0> with S the upper unit hemisphere oriented upward: curl F = <0, 0, 2>, and both sides equal 2 pi; the flux of curl F is the same for any surface with the same boundary, so a hemisphere can be replaced by the flat disk; Green's theorem is the special case of a flat region in the xy-plane
lessons.prerequisites: Curl, surface integrals, line integrals, Green's theorem
lessons.key_vocabulary: Stokes' theorem, boundary curve, right-hand rule, positive orientation, surface independence, circulation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students orient the boundary curve clockwise while using an upward normal, getting -2 pi instead of 2 pi; students think the flux of curl F depends on which surface with boundary C is chosen, and evaluate a hard hemisphere integral instead of the flat disk
lessons.real_world_hook: Faraday's law of induction, which explains how generators and wireless chargers produce current, is Stokes' theorem applied to the electric field

lessons.learning_objective: Use the divergence theorem to relate the outward flux through a closed surface to the triple integral of divergence over the enclosed solid
lessons.key_concepts: For a solid E with closed boundary S oriented outward: double integral over S of F . n dS = triple integral over E of div F dV; e.g. F = <x, y, z> has div F = 3, so the flux out of the sphere of radius a is 3(4 pi a^3/3) = 4 pi a^3, matching the direct computation; F = <x^3, y^3, z^3> through the unit sphere: div F = 3 rho^2, triple integral of 3 rho^2 rho^2 sin(phi) = 3(1/5)(4 pi) = 12 pi/5; to use it for an open surface, close the surface and subtract the flux through the added piece; divergence as flux density; Gauss's law: flux of the electric field through a closed surface is the enclosed charge over epsilon_0
lessons.prerequisites: Divergence, surface integrals, triple integrals in spherical coordinates
lessons.key_vocabulary: divergence theorem, Gauss's theorem, closed surface, outward normal, flux density, Gauss's law, source and sink
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students apply the divergence theorem to an open surface such as a hemisphere without the base disk, then report the triple integral as the hemisphere's flux; students use the spherical volume element without the rho^2 sin(phi) factor when evaluating the triple integral
lessons.real_world_hook: Gauss's law lets physicists find the electric field of a charged sphere in one line instead of a hard surface integral

units.unit_title: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data

lessons.learning_objective: Write a statistical investigative question and classify the variables needed to answer it as categorical or quantitative
lessons.key_concepts: Statistics answers questions using data that vary; an investigative question names a population and a variable and can be answered with data; individuals and variables; categorical versus quantitative variables; a question about one variable versus a question comparing groups
lessons.key_vocabulary: investigative question, individual, variable, categorical, quantitative, population
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students call zip codes or jersey numbers quantitative because they are written as numbers, even though averaging them has no meaning
lessons.real_world_hook: Turning a school cafeteria complaint into a question a survey can actually answer

lessons.learning_objective: Summarize categorical data using frequency tables and bar charts
lessons.key_concepts: Frequency, relative frequency, marginal
lessons.key_vocabulary: categorical, frequency, relative frequency
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use histograms instead of bar charts for categorical data
lessons.real_world_hook: Market research surveys

lessons.learning_objective: Construct and interpret displays for quantitative data
lessons.key_concepts: Dot plots, stem plots, histograms, choice of bins
lessons.key_vocabulary: distribution, skew, mode
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students describe shape using subjective terms
lessons.real_world_hook: Test score analysis

lessons.learning_objective: Compute mean, median, percentiles, and z scores
lessons.key_concepts: Robustness to outliers, position measures
lessons.key_vocabulary: percentile, quartile, z score
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compute percentile using only ranking, not value
lessons.real_world_hook: College admissions and class rank

lessons.learning_objective: Compute range, IQR, standard deviation, and variance
lessons.key_concepts: Interpretation of variability measures, boxplots from the five-number summary, 1.5 times IQR outlier rule
lessons.key_vocabulary: variance, standard deviation, IQR, five-number summary, boxplot
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use sd formula without dividing by n minus one
lessons.real_world_hook: Risk assessment in finance

lessons.lesson_title: Comparing Distributions of a Quantitative Variable
lessons.learning_objective: Compare two or more distributions of a quantitative variable by shape, center, variability, and unusual features, and use z scores to compare relative position
lessons.key_concepts: Back-to-back stemplots, parallel dotplots, and side-by-side boxplots; comparisons must use comparative words (greater than, less than, about the same) for center and variability, in context; z score as number of standard deviations from the mean for comparing values from different distributions

lessons.key_vocabulary: comparative boxplots, back-to-back stemplot, z score, relative position

lessons.lesson_title: The Investigative Question Revisited: Observational Studies and Experiments
lessons.learning_objective: Choose a data collection method that fits an investigative question and explain what kind of conclusion an observational study or an experiment supports

lessons.lesson_title: Type I and Type II Errors
lessons.learning_objective: Identify Type I and Type II errors and their consequences in context, and explain how significance level and sample size affect error probabilities and power
lessons.key_concepts: Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis and has probability alpha; Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis; power is 1 minus the probability of a Type II error; lowering alpha raises the chance of a Type II error; increasing sample size increases power
lessons.key_vocabulary: Type I error, Type II error, significance level, power
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students define a Type I error as 'the null hypothesis is wrong' instead of 'we reject the null hypothesis when it is actually true', and leave out the context of the problem
lessons.real_world_hook: A smoke detector that goes off for burnt toast versus one that stays silent during a real fire

lessons.learning_objective: Perform two sample t procedures
lessons.key_concepts: Two sample standard error, degrees of freedom approximation
lessons.key_vocabulary: two sample t, independent samples
