lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why a square tile with area 2 square feet has a side length you can never measure exactly with a ruler

lessons.learning_objective: Add, subtract, and multiply polynomials and write results in standard form
lessons.key_concepts: Like terms have the same variable and exponent; subtracting a polynomial means distributing the negative to every term; multiplying with the distributive property or an area model; special products (a + b)^2 and (a + b)(a - b); degree and leading coefficient; interpreting parts of an expression in context
lessons.key_vocabulary: polynomial, monomial, binomial, trinomial, degree, leading coefficient, like terms, standard form
lessons.common_misconceptions: Computes (5x^2 + 3x) - (2x^2 - 4x) as 3x^2 - x by subtracting only the first term; squares (x + 4)^2 as x^2 + 16
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing an expression for the area of a garden whose length is 3 feet more than twice its width

lessons.learning_objective: Factor quadratic and polynomial expressions using GCF, trinomial factoring, difference of squares, and perfect square trinomials
lessons.key_concepts: Always factor out the GCF first; x^2 + bx + c: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b; ax^2 + bx + c by grouping (ac method); a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); perfect square trinomials; check factoring by multiplying back
lessons.key_vocabulary: factor, greatest common factor, trinomial, difference of squares, perfect square trinomial, grouping
lessons.common_misconceptions: Factors x^2 - 5x - 14 as (x - 7)(x - 2), picking numbers that multiply to 14 and ignoring the signs; factors x^2 + 9 as (x + 3)(x - 3)
lessons.real_world_hook: Factoring an area expression x^2 + 7x + 12 to find possible dimensions of a rectangular patio

lessons.learning_objective: Solve literal equations and formulas for a specified variable
lessons.key_concepts: Treat other letters as constants and undo operations in reverse order; isolate the target variable; factor it out when it appears in two terms; common formulas: d = rt, A = lw, P = 2l + 2w, C = (5/9)(F - 32), y = mx + b, I = Prt
lessons.key_vocabulary: literal equation, formula, isolate, inverse operation, variable, coefficient
lessons.common_misconceptions: Solving P = 2l + 2w for w, subtracts 2l and then divides only the 2l term by 2, writing w = P - l; solving A = (1/2)bh for h, multiplies by 1/2 instead of by 2
lessons.real_world_hook: Rearranging d = rt to find how fast you must drive to cover 180 miles in 3 hours

lessons.learning_objective: Solve multi-step linear equations and inequalities, including variables on both sides, and graph inequality solutions on a number line
lessons.key_concepts: Distribute, combine like terms, collect variables on one side; no solution vs infinitely many solutions; reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative; open vs closed circles; compound inequalities with and/or; writing equations and inequalities from word problems
lessons.key_vocabulary: equation, inequality, solution, no solution, infinitely many solutions, compound inequality, open circle, closed circle
lessons.common_misconceptions: Writes -2x < 10 as x < -5 without flipping the sign; uses a closed circle for x > 3; distributes -3(x - 4) as -3x - 12
lessons.real_world_hook: A phone costs $240; you have $60 saved and can save $15 a week; how many weeks until you have at least enough?

lessons.lesson_title: Slope, intercepts, and forms of linear equations
lessons.learning_objective: Calculate and interpret slope and intercepts from graphs, tables, equations, and context, and convert among slope-intercept, point-slope, and standard form
lessons.key_concepts: Slope as rate of change from two points or a table; y = mx + b, y - y1 = m(x - x1), Ax + By = C; finding intercepts by setting x or y to 0; parallel and perpendicular slopes; interpreting slope and intercept with units; effect of changing m or b on the graph (F-BF.B.3)
lessons.key_vocabulary: slope, rate of change, y-intercept, x-intercept, slope-intercept form, point-slope form, standard form, parallel, perpendicular
lessons.common_misconceptions: Calculates slope as change in x over change in y; from a table where x goes up by 2 and y goes up by 6, reports the slope as 6 instead of 3; says y = 4 has an undefined slope
lessons.real_world_hook: A car rental costs $35 a day plus a $20 fee; interpret what the slope and y-intercept mean on the cost graph

lessons.lesson_title: Writing linear models from tables, graphs, and context
lessons.learning_objective: Write a linear function from two points, a table, a graph, or a verbal description, and use it to make predictions
lessons.key_concepts: Check for a constant rate of change in a table; find slope then solve for b; arithmetic sequences as linear functions; domain restrictions in context (no negative time or fractional people); using the model to predict and checking whether the prediction is reasonable
lessons.prerequisites: Slope, intercepts, and forms of linear equations
lessons.key_vocabulary: linear model, constant rate of change, arithmetic sequence, domain, prediction, initial value
lessons.common_misconceptions: Uses the first y-value in a table as the y-intercept even though the table starts at x = 1, not x = 0; writes the model as y = bx + m with the roles of rate and starting value switched
lessons.real_world_hook: A candle is 12 inches tall after 1 hour and 9 inches after 3 hours; write its height function and find when it burns out

lessons.lesson_title: Systems of linear equations and inequalities
lessons.learning_objective: Solve systems of linear equations by graphing, substitution, and elimination and graph systems of linear inequalities to find solution regions
lessons.key_concepts: Solution is the intersection point; substitution when a variable is already isolated; elimination by adding multiples of equations; one, none, or infinitely many solutions; graphing inequalities with dashed (< , >) or solid (<=, >=) boundary lines and shading; testing a point like (0, 0); writing systems from context
lessons.key_vocabulary: system, intersection, substitution, elimination, solution region, boundary line, dashed line, solid line, test point
lessons.common_misconceptions: Shades above the line for y < 2x + 1 and uses a solid line; after finding x in a system, stops without solving for y and reports a single number
lessons.real_world_hook: Planning a fundraiser selling cookies at $2 and brownies at $3 with a goal of at least $300 and a limit of 150 items

lessons.learning_objective: Use function notation to evaluate and interpret functions, determine whether a relation is a function, and identify domain and range from graphs, tables, and context
lessons.key_concepts: A function gives exactly one output for each input; vertical line test; f(3) means the output at x = 3; solving f(x) = 7 means finding the input; domain and range from graphs including endpoints and arrows; reasonable domain in context (discrete vs continuous); inequality and interval notation
lessons.key_vocabulary: function, relation, input, output, domain, range, function notation, discrete, continuous, vertical line test
lessons.common_misconceptions: Says {(1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 5)} is not a function because 4 repeats; mixes up domain and range by listing the y-values as the domain; reads f(2) as f times 2
lessons.real_world_hook: A school store sells notebooks for $3 each; explain why a domain of {0, 1, 2, ...} makes more sense than all real numbers

lessons.learning_objective: Identify and interpret the vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts, maximum or minimum, and intervals of increase and decrease of a quadratic function
lessons.key_concepts: Parabola opens up when a > 0 and down when a < 0; vertex as maximum or minimum; axis of symmetry x = -b/(2a); y-intercept is c in standard form; zeros are x-intercepts; increasing and decreasing intervals; average rate of change over an interval; interpreting features in projectile problems
lessons.key_vocabulary: parabola, vertex, axis of symmetry, maximum, minimum, zero, x-intercept, y-intercept, increasing, decreasing
lessons.common_misconceptions: Computes the axis of symmetry of y = 2x^2 - 8x + 1 as x = -2 by dropping the negative in -b/(2a); in a height-over-time graph, reports the maximum height as the time coordinate of the vertex
lessons.real_world_hook: A water fountain's arc modeled by h(x) = -0.5x^2 + 4x; how high and how far does the water go?

lessons.lesson_title: Solving quadratics by factoring and square roots
lessons.learning_objective: Solve quadratic equations by factoring, taking square roots, and graphing, and relate solutions to x-intercepts
lessons.key_concepts: Set the equation equal to zero before factoring; zero product property; x^2 = k gives x = +/- sqrt k; solving (x - h)^2 = k; reading solutions from where the graph crosses the x-axis; a graphing calculator's zero or intersect feature
lessons.key_vocabulary: quadratic equation, zero product property, root, solution, x-intercept, square root property
lessons.common_misconceptions: Solves x^2 = 49 and writes only x = 7; tries to factor x^2 + 3x = 10 without first moving 10 to the left side, setting x = 10 and x + 3 = 10
lessons.real_world_hook: A square photo with an area of 144 square inches gets a frame; find the photo's side length

lessons.lesson_title: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
lessons.learning_objective: Solve any quadratic equation with the quadratic formula and use the discriminant to determine the number of real solutions
lessons.key_concepts: x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a); write in standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 first and identify a, b, c with their signs; discriminant > 0 two real solutions, = 0 one, < 0 none; exact vs decimal answers; choosing a method (factoring, square roots, formula, completing the square)
lessons.prerequisites: Solving quadratics by factoring, simplifying radicals
lessons.key_vocabulary: quadratic formula, discriminant, real solution, standard form, coefficient, exact answer
lessons.common_misconceptions: For x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0 uses b = 6 instead of -6; computes -b^2 as -36 instead of b^2 = 36 under the radical; divides only the radical by 2a and not the -b term
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding when a model rocket with h(t) = -16t^2 + 64t + 5 hits the ground

lessons.lesson_title: Forms and transformations of quadratic functions
lessons.learning_objective: Convert among standard, vertex, and factored forms and describe how a, h, and k transform the graph of y = x^2
lessons.key_concepts: Standard form shows the y-intercept, factored form shows zeros, vertex form y = a(x - h)^2 + k shows the vertex; completing the square to get vertex form; |a| > 1 narrower, 0 < |a| < 1 wider, negative a reflects; h shifts horizontally, k vertically; comparing two quadratics given in different representations
lessons.key_vocabulary: standard form, vertex form, factored form, completing the square, translation, reflection, vertical stretch, compression
lessons.common_misconceptions: Says y = (x - 5)^2 shifts the parabola 5 units left; claims y = 0.5x^2 is narrower than y = x^2 because 0.5 is 'stretching' it
lessons.real_world_hook: Designing a parabolic arch for a stage, choosing vertex form so the highest point is easy to set

lessons.learning_objective: Write, evaluate, and graph exponential functions y = a(b)^x for growth and decay and interpret a, b, and the percent rate in context
lessons.key_concepts: a is the initial value, b is the growth or decay factor; b > 1 growth, 0 < b < 1 decay; b = 1 + r or 1 - r with r as a decimal; percent rate of change from b (b = 0.85 means 15% decay); y-intercept and horizontal asymptote; geometric sequences as exponential functions
lessons.key_vocabulary: exponential function, initial value, growth factor, decay factor, percent rate, asymptote, geometric sequence
lessons.common_misconceptions: Writes a population growing 3% per year as P = 500(3)^t or P = 500(0.03)^t instead of 500(1.03)^t; interprets b = 0.8 as an 80% decrease
lessons.real_world_hook: A used car worth $18,000 loses 12% of its value each year; what is it worth after 5 years?

lessons.learning_objective: Distinguish linear from exponential relationships in tables, graphs, and contexts and explain why exponential growth eventually exceeds linear growth
lessons.key_concepts: Linear: equal differences over equal intervals (add the same amount); exponential: equal ratios over equal intervals (multiply by the same factor); checking first differences and ratios in a table; an exponential growth function eventually exceeds any linear function; choosing a model from context; comparing functions given in different representations
lessons.prerequisites: Linear models, exponential growth and decay
lessons.key_vocabulary: linear function, exponential function, common difference, common ratio, rate of change, growth factor
lessons.common_misconceptions: Classifies a table with y-values 2, 6, 18, 54 as linear because 'it goes up each time'; concludes a linear function with a large slope will always stay above an exponential function
lessons.real_world_hook: Choosing between a job paying $1,000 more each year and one paying 5% more each year over a long career

lessons.learning_objective: Represent data with dot plots, histograms, and box plots and compare data sets using appropriate measures of center and spread
lessons.key_concepts: Mean and median as center; range, IQR, and standard deviation as spread; five-number summary and box plots; outliers by the 1.5 x IQR rule; use median and IQR for skewed data or outliers, mean and standard deviation for symmetric data; effect of an outlier on each measure
lessons.key_vocabulary: mean, median, range, interquartile range, standard deviation, five-number summary, box plot, outlier, skewed, symmetric
lessons.common_misconceptions: Thinks the longer whisker in a box plot contains more data points; says removing an outlier changes the median a lot but the mean very little
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two basketball players' points per game to decide who is more consistent

lessons.lesson_title: Scatterplots, lines of fit, correlation, and residuals
lessons.learning_objective: Fit a linear function to bivariate data, interpret its slope and intercept, assess fit with residuals and the correlation coefficient, and distinguish correlation from causation
lessons.key_concepts: Positive, negative, or no association; linear regression on a graphing calculator; interpreting slope and y-intercept of the regression line with units; correlation coefficient r between -1 and 1 measures strength and direction of a linear relationship; residual = actual - predicted; a random residual plot suggests a good linear fit; correlation does not imply causation
lessons.key_vocabulary: scatterplot, association, line of best fit, regression, correlation coefficient, residual, residual plot, causation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Computes a residual as predicted minus actual; believes r = -0.9 is a weaker relationship than r = 0.5 because it is negative; concludes ice cream sales cause sunburns because they are correlated
lessons.real_world_hook: Using data on daily temperature and lemonade cups sold to predict sales on a 90-degree day

lessons.learning_objective: Summarize categorical data in two-way frequency tables and interpret joint, marginal, and conditional relative frequencies to identify associations
lessons.key_concepts: Joint frequencies in the cells; marginal totals in the margins; relative frequency = count/total; conditional relative frequency uses a row or column total; comparing conditional relative frequencies to decide whether there is an association between variables
lessons.key_vocabulary: two-way table, categorical data, joint frequency, marginal frequency, relative frequency, conditional relative frequency, association
lessons.common_misconceptions: Finds the percent of 9th graders who prefer soccer by dividing by the grand total instead of the 9th-grade total; compares raw counts between groups of different sizes to claim an association
lessons.real_world_hook: A school survey of grade level vs preferred lunch option used to decide what the cafeteria should stock

lessons.learning_objective: Locate and correctly apply formulas from a state Algebra 1 reference sheet and recognize which formulas you must know without it
lessons.key_concepts: Most state Algebra 1 exams provide a reference sheet, but contents differ by state, so check your state's reference sheet and practice with that exact page; typical entries may include slope, forms of linear equations, the quadratic formula, axis of symmetry, exponential and compound interest forms, and geometry formulas; matching each variable on the sheet to the numbers in the problem; formulas not on your state's sheet must be memorized
lessons.prerequisites: Familiarity with linear, quadratic, and exponential formulas
lessons.key_vocabulary: reference sheet, formula, variable, substitute, standard form, vertex
lessons.common_misconceptions: Plugs values into the quadratic formula from the sheet without first rewriting the equation in standard form, using the wrong value of c; assumes a formula is on the sheet on test day without having checked the state's actual sheet
lessons.real_world_hook: Before a practice test, a student highlights the three formulas on their state's reference sheet they used most in class

lessons.learning_objective: Use a graphing calculator (or the on-screen calculator your exam provides) to graph, find intersections and zeros, use tables, and run regressions to check answers
lessons.ccss_code: EOC Test Skills: Calculator use / MP5
lessons.key_concepts: Calculator availability and type vary by state and by test session, so confirm your state's rules; graph both sides of an equation and use intersect to check a solution; zero feature for x-intercepts; table feature to check a function's values; linear and exponential regression from lists; adjusting the window when the graph is not visible; parentheses for negative numbers and fractions
lessons.key_vocabulary: graphing calculator, window, intersect, zero, table, regression, trace
lessons.common_misconceptions: Types -3^2 into the calculator and gets -9 when the problem means (-3)^2 = 9; concludes a quadratic has no zeros because none appear in the standard window
lessons.real_world_hook: Checking a hand-solved system 2x + y = 7, x - y = 2 by graphing both lines and finding the intersection (3, 1)

lessons.learning_objective: Answer gridded/fill-in and constructed-response items with correctly formatted answers and clear written justification
lessons.key_concepts: Many Algebra 1 exams include items where you enter a number instead of choosing an answer, and some include written responses scored with a rubric; follow the exam's instructions for fractions, decimals, negatives, and rounding; show the equation you set up, each key step, and a final answer with units; explain reasoning in complete sentences when asked to 'justify' or 'explain'; partial credit depends on visible work
lessons.key_vocabulary: griddable, constructed response, justify, rubric, units, rounding, exact answer
lessons.common_misconceptions: Rounds an answer to the nearest whole number when the item asks for the nearest tenth; writes only a final number on a constructed-response item that asks for an explanation and loses the reasoning points
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a complete justification for why a phone plan with a lower monthly fee becomes more expensive after 8 months

lessons.lesson_title: Checking answers by substitution and estimation
lessons.learning_objective: Verify solutions by substituting them back, estimating, and testing answer choices, and use answer choices strategically on multiple-choice items
lessons.key_concepts: Substitute a solution into the original equation, not a rewritten step; check both solutions of a quadratic; test answer choices (backsolving) for equations and systems; test a point to check an inequality's shaded region; estimate to rule out unreasonable answers; reread the question to confirm what it asks for; manage time so every item gets an answer
lessons.key_vocabulary: substitution, check, backsolve, estimate, reasonable, original equation, extraneous
lessons.common_misconceptions: Checks a solution by substituting it into a later line of their own work that already contains an error, so the wrong answer 'checks'; on a system question, substitutes an answer choice into only one of the two equations
lessons.real_world_hook: A student solves 3(x - 2) = 2x + 5, gets x = 11, and confirms it by substituting into the original equation: 27 = 27

lessons.learning_objective: Write the converse, inverse, contrapositive, and biconditional of a conditional statement, decide whether each is true, and use the laws of detachment and syllogism to draw valid conclusions
lessons.key_concepts: A conditional 'if p, then q' has a hypothesis p and a conclusion q; converse: if q, then p; inverse: if not p, then not q; contrapositive: if not q, then not p; a conditional and its contrapositive always have the same truth value, and so do the converse and the inverse; one counterexample is enough to show a statement is false; a biconditional 'p if and only if q' is true only when the conditional and its converse are both true, and good definitions are biconditionals; law of detachment: if p implies q and p is true, then q is true; law of syllogism: if p implies q and q implies r, then p implies r; Venn diagrams for 'all', 'some', and 'no' statements; inductive reasoning finds patterns, deductive reasoning proves
lessons.prerequisites: Angle and polygon vocabulary from earlier grades
lessons.key_vocabulary: conditional statement, hypothesis, conclusion, converse, inverse, contrapositive, biconditional, counterexample, law of detachment, law of syllogism, deductive reasoning, inductive reasoning
lessons.common_misconceptions: Given 'If an angle measures 30 degrees, then it is acute,' claims the converse 'If an angle is acute, then it measures 30 degrees' must also be true; given 'If it rains, the game is canceled' and 'The game was canceled,' concludes that it rained, which is not a valid use of the law of detachment
lessons.real_world_hook: A store sign says 'If you have a receipt, then you can return the item'; deciding what that policy does and does not promise to a customer who lost the receipt

lessons.learning_objective: Prove theorems about lines and angles, including vertical angles and angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal, in two-column and paragraph form
lessons.key_concepts: Vertical angles are congruent; a linear pair is supplementary; when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding, alternate interior, and alternate exterior angles are congruent and same-side (consecutive) interior angles are supplementary; the converses of these theorems are used to prove lines parallel; points on the perpendicular bisector of a segment are equidistant from its endpoints; a two-column proof lists statements with a reason for each (given, definition, postulate, property, or theorem) and ends with the statement to be proved; paragraph and flow proofs use the same logic; algebraic properties of equality, reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and substitution properties; segment and angle addition postulates
lessons.prerequisites: Conditional statements and logical reasoning, solving linear equations
lessons.key_vocabulary: transversal, corresponding angles, alternate interior angles, alternate exterior angles, same-side interior angles, vertical angles, linear pair, postulate, theorem, two-column proof, paragraph proof
lessons.common_misconceptions: Uses 'If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then alternate interior angles are congruent' as the reason to prove lines are parallel instead of its converse; with parallel lines, sets same-side interior angles 3x + 10 and 5x - 30 equal to each other (x = 20) instead of supplementary (8x - 20 = 180, so x = 25 and the angles are 85 and 95 degrees)
lessons.real_world_hook: A carpenter checks that two shelves are parallel by measuring the angle each one makes with the same vertical support

lessons.learning_objective: Prove and apply theorems about triangles (angle sum, exterior angle, isosceles, midsegment, medians) and parallelograms (sides, angles, diagonals)
lessons.key_concepts: Interior angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees; an exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles; base angles of an isosceles triangle are congruent, and the converse holds; a midsegment is parallel to the third side and half its length; the medians meet at the centroid, which is 2/3 of the way from each vertex to the opposite midpoint; triangle inequality: any two sides sum to more than the third; parallelograms have congruent opposite sides, congruent opposite angles, supplementary consecutive angles, and diagonals that bisect each other; rectangles also have congruent diagonals; rhombuses also have perpendicular diagonals that bisect the angles; a square has all of these properties
lessons.key_vocabulary: exterior angle, remote interior angles, isosceles triangle, base angles, midsegment, median, centroid, parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square, diagonal
lessons.common_misconceptions: Assumes the diagonals of every parallelogram are congruent, a property only rectangles are guaranteed; thinks the centroid cuts a median in half, so for a median of length 12 says the centroid is 6 units from the vertex instead of 8
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why a scissor lift built from parallelogram linkages keeps its platform level as it rises

lessons.learning_objective: Perform and describe translations, reflections, and rotations on and off the coordinate plane, including sequences of transformations and the symmetries that map a figure onto itself
lessons.key_concepts: Translation (x, y) to (x + a, y + b); reflections over the x-axis (x, -y), the y-axis (-x, y), the line y = x (y, x), and the line y = -x (-y, -x); rotations about the origin: 90 degrees counterclockwise (-y, x), 180 degrees (-x, -y), 270 degrees counterclockwise or 90 degrees clockwise (y, -x); rigid motions preserve distance and angle measure, while dilations do not preserve distance; reflections reverse orientation; the order of a composition can change the final image; a regular n-gon has rotational symmetry by multiples of 360/n degrees and n lines of symmetry; describing a transformation precisely (center and angle, line of reflection, or translation vector)
lessons.prerequisites: Coordinate plane, prior work with transformations
lessons.key_vocabulary: transformation, pre-image, image, rigid motion, translation, reflection, rotation, line of symmetry, rotational symmetry, composition, orientation
lessons.common_misconceptions: Rotates the point (2, 5) 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin and writes (5, -2), which is the clockwise image; the counterclockwise image is (-5, 2); assumes reflecting and then translating a figure always gives the same result as translating and then reflecting
lessons.real_world_hook: A game designer writes the coordinate rules that make a character sprite turn a quarter turn and flip to face the other direction

lessons.learning_objective: Use rigid motions and the SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and HL criteria to prove triangles congruent, then use corresponding parts to prove further relationships
lessons.key_concepts: Two figures are congruent if a sequence of rigid motions maps one onto the other; congruent triangles have all pairs of corresponding sides and angles congruent; criteria: SSS, SAS (included angle), ASA (included side), AAS, and HL for right triangles; SSA and AAA do not prove congruence; the order of letters in a congruence statement shows the correspondence; CPCTC (corresponding parts of congruent triangles are congruent) is used only after the triangles are proved congruent; watch for shared sides (reflexive property) and vertical angles hidden in a diagram
lessons.prerequisites: Rigid transformations and symmetry, Lines, angles, and writing proofs
lessons.key_vocabulary: congruent, corresponding parts, SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL, included angle, included side, CPCTC, reflexive property
lessons.common_misconceptions: Claims two triangles are congruent by SSA when two sides and a non-included angle match; writes 'angle B is congruent to angle E by CPCTC' as a proof step before proving the triangles congruent; writes triangle ABC congruent to triangle FED when A matches D
lessons.real_world_hook: Explaining why the triangular trusses in a bridge hold their shape: three fixed side lengths determine one triangle (SSS)

lessons.learning_objective: Perform formal constructions with compass and straightedge and explain why each construction works
lessons.key_concepts: Copy a segment and copy an angle; construct the perpendicular bisector of a segment; bisect an angle; construct a perpendicular to a line through a point on or off the line; construct a line parallel to a given line through a point not on it by copying a corresponding angle; construct an equilateral triangle, a square, and a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle (step the radius around the circle six times); each construction works because of equal radii and congruent triangles; the same steps can be done with string, reflective devices, paper folding, or geometry software
lessons.key_vocabulary: compass, straightedge, construction, arc, perpendicular bisector, angle bisector, inscribed, regular hexagon
lessons.common_misconceptions: When constructing a perpendicular bisector, changes the compass width between the arc from one endpoint and the arc from the other, so the intersection points do not lie on the bisector; measures with a ruler to find a midpoint instead of constructing it
lessons.real_world_hook: Laying out a regular hexagon garden bed using only a rope and stakes, the outdoor version of a compass

lessons.learning_objective: Perform dilations with a given center and scale factor, verify their properties, and use similarity transformations to decide whether figures are similar
lessons.key_concepts: A dilation centered at the origin maps (x, y) to (kx, ky); about any other center C, the image is C + k(P - C); k > 1 enlarges and 0 < k < 1 reduces; a dilation maps a line not through the center to a parallel line and a line through the center to itself; lengths multiply by k and angle measures stay the same; two figures are similar if a sequence of rigid motions and dilations maps one onto the other; AA similarity follows from this definition; perimeters scale by k, areas by k^2, and volumes by k^3
lessons.key_vocabulary: dilation, center of dilation, scale factor, enlargement, reduction, similar figures, similarity transformation, AA similarity
lessons.common_misconceptions: Dilates (4, 6) by a scale factor of 1/2 about the center (2, 2) by halving both coordinates to get (2, 3), as if the center were the origin; the correct image is (3, 4); doubles every side of a rectangle and says the area doubles when it is multiplied by 4
lessons.real_world_hook: Enlarging a 4 by 6 inch photo to an 8 by 12 inch print doubles each length but uses 4 times as much paper (24 to 96 square inches)

lessons.learning_objective: Prove triangles similar with AA, SAS, and SSS similarity, apply the triangle proportionality theorem, and use the altitude to the hypotenuse to find missing lengths
lessons.key_concepts: Similarity criteria: AA, SAS similarity (two proportional sides and the included angle), SSS similarity; write proportions with corresponding sides in the same order; triangle proportionality (side-splitter) theorem: a line parallel to one side divides the other two sides proportionally, and its converse; the altitude to the hypotenuse of a right triangle forms two triangles similar to the original and to each other; geometric mean relationships: altitude^2 = product of the two hypotenuse segments, and each leg^2 = adjacent hypotenuse segment x whole hypotenuse; similarity gives a proof of the Pythagorean theorem; indirect measurement with shadows and mirrors
lessons.prerequisites: Dilations and similarity, Triangle congruence and CPCTC
lessons.key_vocabulary: similar triangles, SAS similarity, SSS similarity, proportion, triangle proportionality theorem, geometric mean, altitude, indirect measurement
lessons.common_misconceptions: In triangle ABC with segment DE parallel to BC, AD = 4, DB = 6, and DE = 5, sets up 4/6 = 5/BC (getting 7.5) instead of 4/10 = 5/BC (so BC = 12.5), because the ratio AD/DB applies to the divided sides, not to the parallel segments
lessons.real_world_hook: A 6-foot person casts a 4-foot shadow at the same time a flagpole casts an 18-foot shadow, so the flagpole is 27 feet tall

lessons.lesson_title: Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles
lessons.learning_objective: Use the Pythagorean theorem and its converse and the 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 relationships to solve right triangle problems with exact and approximate answers
lessons.key_concepts: a^2 + b^2 = c^2 where c is the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle; converse: if c^2 = a^2 + b^2 the triangle is right, if c^2 < a^2 + b^2 it is acute, and if c^2 > a^2 + b^2 it is obtuse (c is the longest side); common Pythagorean triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and their multiples; 45-45-90: legs x and hypotenuse x sqrt2, so leg = hypotenuse / sqrt2 = (hypotenuse x sqrt2)/2; 30-60-90: short leg x, long leg x sqrt3, hypotenuse 2x; give exact answers in simplest radical form when asked
lessons.prerequisites: Similar triangles and proportional segments, simplifying square roots
lessons.key_vocabulary: hypotenuse, leg, Pythagorean theorem, converse, Pythagorean triple, 45-45-90 triangle, 30-60-90 triangle, simplest radical form
lessons.common_misconceptions: In a 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 10, gives the long leg as 10 sqrt3 instead of 5 sqrt3 (the short leg is 5, so the long leg is 5 sqrt3); finds the missing leg of a right triangle with leg 5 and hypotenuse 13 as sqrt(5^2 + 13^2) instead of sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = 12
lessons.real_world_hook: A 13-foot ladder with its base 5 feet from a wall reaches 12 feet up the wall

lessons.lesson_title: Trigonometric ratios and solving right triangles
lessons.learning_objective: Define sine, cosine, and tangent from similar right triangles, use the complementary-angle relationship, and solve right triangles in applied problems including angles of elevation and depression
lessons.key_concepts: For an acute angle A of a right triangle: sin A = opposite/hypotenuse, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan A = opposite/adjacent (SOH-CAH-TOA); the ratios depend only on the angle because all right triangles with that angle are similar; sin A = cos(90 degrees - A) for complementary angles; solving for a side with the ratio that links the known and unknown sides; inverse trig functions to find an angle; the angle of depression from an observer equals the angle of elevation from the object (alternate interior angles); keep the calculator in degree mode and round only at the end
lessons.prerequisites: Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles
lessons.key_vocabulary: sine, cosine, tangent, opposite side, adjacent side, hypotenuse, inverse trigonometric function, complementary angles, angle of elevation, angle of depression
lessons.common_misconceptions: Leaves the calculator in radian mode, so 20 tan 35 gives about 9.48 instead of the correct 20 tan 35 degrees, about 14.00; labels the side next to the given angle as 'opposite' after the triangle is drawn in a rotated position; thinks sin 40 degrees = cos 40 degrees instead of sin 40 degrees = cos 50 degrees
lessons.real_world_hook: A kite flies on 100 feet of taut string at a 40 degree angle of elevation, so it is about 100 sin 40 degrees, or 64.3 feet, above the hand holding the string

lessons.learning_objective: Find measures of central, inscribed, and tangent-related angles and arcs, and use the properties of inscribed quadrilaterals and angles formed by intersecting chords, secants, and tangents
lessons.key_concepts: All circles are similar; a central angle equals its intercepted arc; an inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc; inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are congruent; an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle; opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle are supplementary; a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency; an angle formed by a tangent and a chord is half the intercepted arc; two chords intersecting inside the circle form an angle equal to half the sum of the intercepted arcs; two secants, two tangents, or a secant and a tangent meeting outside the circle form an angle equal to half the difference of the intercepted arcs; arcs in a circle sum to 360 degrees
lessons.prerequisites: Triangle and parallelogram theorems, angle relationships
lessons.key_vocabulary: central angle, inscribed angle, intercepted arc, minor arc, major arc, semicircle, chord, secant, tangent, point of tangency, inscribed quadrilateral
lessons.common_misconceptions: Two chords intersect inside a circle and intercept arcs of 100 and 40 degrees; answers 30 degrees (half the difference, the rule for angles outside the circle) instead of 70 degrees (half the sum); sets an inscribed angle equal to its intercepted arc instead of half of it
lessons.real_world_hook: Every seat on the same circular arc through the two ends of a stage views the stage at the same angle, because inscribed angles intercepting the same arc are congruent

lessons.learning_objective: Find lengths of chords, secants, and tangents using intersecting-segment theorems and the relationships among radii, chords, and tangents
lessons.key_concepts: Two chords intersecting inside a circle: the products of their segments are equal (a x b = c x d); two secants from an external point: outside segment x whole secant is equal for both; a secant and a tangent from an external point: tangent^2 = outside segment x whole secant; two tangent segments from the same external point are congruent; a radius or diameter perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord; congruent chords are equidistant from the center; the radius, half a chord, and the distance from the center to the chord form a right triangle
lessons.prerequisites: Angles and arcs in circles, Pythagorean theorem and special right triangles
lessons.key_vocabulary: chord, secant segment, external segment, tangent segment, intersecting chords theorem, perpendicular bisector of a chord
lessons.common_misconceptions: A secant from external point P has an outside segment of 4 and passes through the circle along a chord of 5; finds the tangent length t from P using t^2 = 4 x 5 = 20 instead of t^2 = 4 x (4 + 5) = 36, so t = 6
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the radius of a broken plate from a fragment: a chord of 8 inches with a 2-inch rise at its middle gives 4 x 4 = 2 x (2r - 2), so the radius is 5 inches

lessons.learning_objective: Calculate arc lengths and sector areas in degrees and radians and explain radian measure as a ratio of arc length to radius
lessons.key_concepts: Arc length = (central angle / 360) x 2 pi r; sector area = (central angle / 360) x pi r^2; arc length is proportional to the radius because all circles are similar; radian measure = arc length / radius, so 360 degrees = 2 pi radians and 180 degrees = pi radians; to convert degrees to radians multiply by pi/180; in radians, arc length s = r theta and sector area = (1/2) r^2 theta; area of a circular segment = sector area minus triangle area; give answers in terms of pi or rounded as the item directs
lessons.prerequisites: Angles and arcs in circles, circumference and area of a circle
lessons.key_vocabulary: arc length, sector, central angle, radian, circumference, segment of a circle, in terms of pi
lessons.common_misconceptions: For a 60 degree sector of a circle with radius 6, computes (60/360) x 2 pi (6) = 2 pi and reports it as the sector's area; that is the arc length, and the area is (60/360) x pi (6^2) = 6 pi
lessons.real_world_hook: A 16-inch pizza cut into 8 equal slices: each slice has 2 pi, about 6.28 inches, of crust and 8 pi, about 25.1 square inches, of area

lessons.learning_objective: Derive the equation of a circle from the Pythagorean theorem, write it from given information, and complete the square to find the center and radius
lessons.key_concepts: Standard form (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2 has center (h, k) and radius r, derived from the distance formula; the signs inside the parentheses are opposite the center's coordinates; writing an equation from a center and a point on the circle, or from the endpoints of a diameter (midpoint is the center); completing the square for x and for y, adding the same amounts to both sides: x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0 becomes (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 25, center (3, -2) and radius 5; a point is on, inside, or outside the circle when its distance from the center equals, is less than, or is greater than r
lessons.prerequisites: Pythagorean theorem, completing the square from Algebra 1
lessons.key_vocabulary: standard form of a circle, center, radius, diameter, completing the square, distance formula
lessons.common_misconceptions: For (x + 2)^2 + (y - 5)^2 = 49, gives the center as (2, -5) and the radius as 49; the center is (-2, 5) and the radius is 7; when completing the square, adds 9 and 4 to the left side only
lessons.real_world_hook: A cell tower at (3, -2) covers a 5-mile radius on a map grid in miles; a house at (6, 3) is sqrt34, about 5.83 miles, away, so it is outside the coverage area

lessons.learning_objective: Use the distance and midpoint formulas and find the point that partitions a directed segment in a given ratio
lessons.key_concepts: Distance formula d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2) comes from the Pythagorean theorem; (1, 2) to (7, 10) is sqrt(36 + 64) = 10; midpoint is the average of the coordinates; finding a missing endpoint from a midpoint; partitioning a directed segment from A to B in the ratio a:b: the point is a/(a + b) of the way from A, found by adding that fraction of the change in x and change in y to A; for A(-2, 1), B(10, 9) and the ratio 1:3 the point is 1/4 of the way, (1, 3); the order 'from A to B' matters
lessons.key_vocabulary: distance formula, midpoint formula, directed line segment, partition, ratio, endpoint
lessons.common_misconceptions: Partitions the directed segment from A(-2, 1) to B(10, 9) in the ratio 1:3 by moving 1/3 of the way and getting (2, 11/3), instead of 1/(1 + 3) = 1/4 of the way to (1, 3); computes distance by subtracting the coordinates and adding them without squaring
lessons.real_world_hook: A trail map places a water station on a straight trail so the distances from the trailhead and to the summit are in the ratio 1:3

lessons.lesson_title: Slope criteria, coordinate proofs, and polygon perimeter and area
lessons.learning_objective: Use slope and distance to prove geometric properties of figures on the coordinate plane and compute perimeters and areas of polygons
lessons.key_concepts: Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have opposite reciprocal slopes (product -1, except vertical and horizontal); writing the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line through a point; proving a quadrilateral is a parallelogram (both pairs of opposite sides parallel, or diagonals with the same midpoint), a rectangle (a parallelogram with a right angle or congruent diagonals), a rhombus (four congruent sides or a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals), or a square (both); proving a right triangle with perpendicular slopes or the Pythagorean converse; perimeter with the distance formula; area by base and height, decomposition, or enclosing rectangle; ending a coordinate proof with a concluding sentence that names the property shown
lessons.prerequisites: Distance, midpoint, and partitioning segments, Proving triangle and parallelogram theorems, slope
lessons.key_vocabulary: slope, parallel, perpendicular, opposite reciprocal, coordinate proof, parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square, perimeter
lessons.common_misconceptions: Concludes that ABCD with A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(5, 5), D(1, 4) is a square because all four sides measure sqrt17, without checking for a right angle; slopes 1/4 and 4 are reciprocals but not opposite reciprocals, so ABCD is a rhombus but not a square; thinks slopes 2 and -2 are perpendicular
lessons.real_world_hook: A landscaper checks with coordinates that four stakes marking a garden bed form a true rectangle before ordering edging

lessons.learning_objective: Use area and volume formulas for polygons, circles, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres, and give informal arguments for them, including Cavalieri's principle
lessons.key_concepts: Areas of triangles, parallelograms, trapezoids, circles, and regular polygons (1/2 x apothem x perimeter); prism and cylinder V = Bh where B is the area of the base; pyramid and cone V = (1/3)Bh; sphere V = (4/3) pi r^3; informal arguments: dissecting a circle into wedges to justify its area, and a cone holding 1/3 of a cylinder with the same base and height; Cavalieri's principle: solids with equal heights and equal cross-sectional areas at every level have equal volumes, so an oblique cylinder has the same volume as a right cylinder with the same base and height; height is perpendicular to the base and is different from slant height; composite solids by adding or subtracting volumes; lateral and total surface area where your state includes them
lessons.prerequisites: Area of basic figures, Pythagorean theorem
lessons.key_vocabulary: area, volume, base area, height, slant height, prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone, sphere, Cavalieri's principle, oblique, composite solid
lessons.common_misconceptions: Finds the volume of a cone with radius 3 and slant height 5 by using 5 as the height, getting 15 pi; the height is 4 (a 3-4-5 right triangle), so the volume is (1/3) pi (9)(4) = 12 pi
lessons.real_world_hook: A straight stack of coins and the same stack pushed into a slant have the same volume, which is Cavalieri's principle in action

lessons.lesson_title: Cross sections and solids of revolution
lessons.learning_objective: Identify the shapes of two-dimensional cross sections of three-dimensional solids and the solids produced by rotating two-dimensional figures about a line
lessons.key_concepts: A plane parallel to the base of a prism or cylinder gives a cross section congruent to the base; parallel to the base of a pyramid or cone gives a similar, smaller shape; perpendicular slices through a prism or cylinder give rectangles; a cube can have square, rectangular, triangular, pentagonal, and hexagonal cross sections; every plane section of a sphere is a circle; rotations: a rectangle about one side makes a cylinder, a right triangle about a leg makes a cone, a semicircle about its diameter makes a sphere; the side on the axis becomes the height and the perpendicular distance from the axis becomes the radius
lessons.key_vocabulary: cross section, plane, solid of revolution, axis of rotation, cylinder, cone, sphere, prism, pyramid
lessons.common_misconceptions: Rotates a 3 by 5 rectangle about its 5-unit side and uses 5 as the radius; the radius is 3 and the height is 5, so the volume is pi (3^2)(5) = 45 pi; claims a cube can never have a hexagonal cross section
lessons.real_world_hook: A medical CT scan builds a 3-D picture from many parallel cross sections, and a potter shapes a vase by rotating a profile around an axis

lessons.lesson_title: Modeling with geometry: density and design
lessons.learning_objective: Model real objects with geometric shapes and solve problems involving density, unit conversion, and design constraints
lessons.key_concepts: Modeling objects with shapes (a tree trunk as a cylinder, a silo as a cylinder with a hemisphere on top); density = mass / volume and population density = people / area, keeping units; an aluminum cube 2 cm on a side with density 2.7 g per cubic cm has mass 8 x 2.7 = 21.6 g; converting area and volume units with the square or cube of the length factor: 1 square foot = 144 square inches, 1 cubic foot = 1,728 cubic inches, 1 cubic yard = 27 cubic feet; design problems that meet constraints or minimize cost; rounding up when buying materials; stating assumptions in a model
lessons.prerequisites: Area, volume, and Cavalieri's principle, unit rates
lessons.key_vocabulary: model, density, mass, population density, unit conversion, constraint, cubic yard, assumption
lessons.common_misconceptions: Converts 2 cubic yards to cubic feet by multiplying by 3 and gets 6 cubic feet instead of multiplying by 27 to get 54 cubic feet; finds population density by dividing area by population
lessons.real_world_hook: A 10 by 12 foot patio poured 4 inches thick needs 10 x 12 x (1/3) = 40 cubic feet, about 1.48 cubic yards, of concrete, so the order must be rounded up

lessons.learning_objective: Locate and correctly apply formulas from a state Geometry reference sheet and recognize which relationships you must know without it
lessons.key_concepts: Most state Geometry exams provide a reference sheet, but contents differ by state, so check your state's reference sheet and practice with that exact page; typical entries may include volume formulas, sometimes area, surface area, or trigonometry and special right triangle information, and unit conversions; matching each variable to the problem, especially B (area of the base, not a base length), h (perpendicular height), and l (slant height); relationships often not on the sheet, such as circle angle and segment theorems, the equation of a circle, and slope criteria, must be memorized
lessons.prerequisites: Familiarity with area, volume, circle, and right triangle formulas
lessons.key_vocabulary: reference sheet, formula, base area, height, slant height, substitute, exact answer
lessons.common_misconceptions: Treats B in V = (1/3)Bh as a base edge length: for a square pyramid with base edge 6 and height 10 computes (1/3)(6)(10) = 20 instead of (1/3)(36)(10) = 120; assumes the circle angle theorems will be on the sheet without having checked the state's actual sheet
lessons.real_world_hook: Before a practice test, a student marks which formulas on their state's reference sheet they used most and lists the theorems they must memorize because the sheet leaves them out

lessons.learning_objective: Use a scientific or graphing calculator (or the on-screen calculator your exam provides) accurately for trigonometry, radicals, and pi, and use it to check answers
lessons.ccss_code: EOC Test Skills: Calculator use / MP5
lessons.key_concepts: Calculator availability and type vary by state and by test session, so confirm your state's rules; set degree mode before any trig problem; use inverse trig keys to find angles and wrap fractions in parentheses; use the pi key rather than 3.14 unless told otherwise; store or chain intermediate values instead of rounding mid-problem; check a side found with trig by using the Pythagorean theorem or another ratio; convert exact radical or pi answers to decimals to compare with answer choices
lessons.prerequisites: Trigonometric ratios and solving right triangles, Arc length and sector area
lessons.key_vocabulary: degree mode, radian mode, inverse tangent, pi key, rounding, exact answer, approximate answer
lessons.common_misconceptions: Finds the angle whose tangent is 7/4 by typing tan^-1(7)/4, getting about 20.5 degrees, instead of tan^-1(7/4), about 60.3 degrees; rounds sin 35 degrees to 0.57 partway through, so 50 sin 35 degrees becomes 28.5 instead of about 28.7
lessons.real_world_hook: Checking a hand-solved triangle with legs 8 and 15 by confirming that the calculator gives a hypotenuse of 17 and that tan^-1(8/15) plus tan^-1(15/8) is 90 degrees

lessons.learning_objective: Write complete, well-justified answers to constructed-response items, including short proofs and explanations, that earn full rubric credit
lessons.ccss_code: EOC Test Skills: Response formats / MP3
lessons.key_concepts: Some Geometry exams, such as the New York Regents, include written-response items and proofs scored for partial credit, while others use mostly selected-response and technology-enhanced items, so check your state's format; show the equation or theorem used, each key step, and a final answer with units; when asked to justify or explain, name the theorem or property in a complete sentence; every proof step needs a valid reason, and the last statement must be what was to be proved; label diagrams you add; follow directions on rounding and exact form
lessons.key_vocabulary: constructed response, justify, explain, rubric, partial credit, theorem, concluding statement, units
lessons.common_misconceptions: Writes only 'x = 25' on an item that asks to justify the answer and loses the reasoning points; in a proof, gives 'given' or 'it looks like it' as the reason for a fact that was not given and must be proved
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two student answers to the same item, one with a bare number and one with the theorem named, and scoring them with a sample rubric

lessons.learning_objective: Explain a fraction a/b as a copies of the unit fraction 1/b, where the whole is split into b equal parts
lessons.key_concepts: The denominator names how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts how many of those parts; parts must be equal in size; the whole must be identified; 5/4 is five copies of 1/4 and is more than one whole
lessons.prerequisites: Whole-number counting, equal sharing, multiplication facts
lessons.key_vocabulary: fraction, numerator, denominator, unit fraction, equal parts, whole
lessons.common_misconceptions: Treats a fraction as two separate whole numbers instead of one number; calls a shape split into unequal pieces 'fourths'; believes a fraction can never be greater than 1, so 5/4 is 'impossible'
lessons.real_world_hook: Splitting a pizza fairly among friends

lessons.learning_objective: Locate and represent fractions, including fractions greater than 1, as points on a number line by partitioning each unit interval into equal lengths
lessons.key_concepts: A fraction is a single point (a distance from 0) on the number line; partition 0 to 1 into b equal intervals and count a of them; fractions fill the gaps between whole numbers; 3/3 and 1 are the same point
lessons.key_vocabulary: number line, interval, partition, point, distance from zero, improper fraction
lessons.common_misconceptions: Counts tick marks instead of intervals, so places 1/4 at the fourth tick when the space is split into 5 parts; places 3/4 past 1 because 3 and 4 are 'big numbers'; thinks fractions are not real numbers that can go on a number line
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a ruler to the nearest eighth of an inch

lessons.lesson_title: Fractions as Division and Mixed Numbers
lessons.learning_objective: Interpret a/b as a divided by b and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers
lessons.key_concepts: 3/4 means 3 divided by 4, which is the share each of 4 people gets from 3 items; remainders become fractions; 7/3 = 2 1/3 because 7 thirds make 2 wholes with 1 third left over
lessons.key_vocabulary: fraction as division, quotient, mixed number, improper fraction, remainder
lessons.common_misconceptions: Writes 3 divided by 4 as 4/3 (puts the larger number on top); converts 2 1/3 to 3/3 by adding 2 + 1; thinks a remainder is just 'R1' and not a fraction of the divisor
lessons.real_world_hook: Sharing 3 sandwiches equally among 4 people

lessons.learning_objective: Generate and recognize equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number, and explain why the value stays the same
lessons.key_concepts: Equivalent fractions name the same point on the number line; multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1; splitting each part into n smaller parts multiplies both the count and the number of parts; simplest form
lessons.prerequisites: Fraction meaning, multiplication and division facts, factors
lessons.key_vocabulary: equivalent fractions, simplest form, common factor, multiply by one
lessons.common_misconceptions: Adds the same number to top and bottom (2/3 = 4/5 by adding 2); thinks 2/4 is bigger than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger; simplifies by subtracting (6/8 = 4/6)
lessons.real_world_hook: Following a recipe when you only have a 1/4-cup measure and need 1/2 cup

lessons.learning_objective: Compare and order fractions with unlike numerators and denominators using common denominators, common numerators, and benchmarks like 0, 1/2, and 1
lessons.key_concepts: Comparisons are valid only when the wholes are the same size; same denominator compares numerators; same numerator means the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction; benchmark to 1/2; use > , <, = with justification
lessons.key_vocabulary: compare, benchmark, common denominator, common numerator, greater than, less than
lessons.common_misconceptions: Whole-number bias: says 1/8 > 1/6 because 8 > 6; overcorrects and says a bigger denominator always means a smaller fraction even when numerators differ (3/8 vs 1/6); orders 2/7, 1/12, 5/9 by comparing denominators only
lessons.real_world_hook: Deciding which pizza deal gives more: 3/8 of a large or 1/3 of the same size

lessons.lesson_title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions with Unlike Denominators
lessons.learning_objective: Add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators by rewriting them as equivalent fractions with a common denominator
lessons.key_concepts: You can only add parts of the same size; a common denominator rewrites both fractions in same-size parts; add numerators, keep the denominator; regrouping when subtracting mixed numbers (borrow 1 whole as b/b)
lessons.key_vocabulary: common denominator, least common denominator, like fractions, regroup
lessons.common_misconceptions: Adds numerators and denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5; subtracts mixed numbers by subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger (3 1/4 - 1 3/4 = 2 2/4); finds a common denominator but forgets to change the numerator
lessons.real_world_hook: Combining 1/2 cup and 1/3 cup of flour in a recipe

lessons.learning_objective: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions and check answers for reasonableness with benchmark fractions
lessons.key_concepts: Identify the whole in each part of the problem; draw a bar model or number line; estimate with 0, 1/2, and 1 before calculating; check that the answer fits the estimate
lessons.prerequisites: Adding and subtracting fractions, benchmark fractions
lessons.key_vocabulary: estimate, benchmark, reasonable, bar model, total, difference
lessons.common_misconceptions: Accepts 2/5 as the answer to 1/2 + 1/3 even though it is less than 1/2 alone (no estimation check); uses a different whole for each fraction; picks the operation from keywords like 'left' without modeling
lessons.real_world_hook: Planning how much of a trail is left to hike after two rest stops

lessons.learning_objective: Multiply fractions and whole numbers by fractions using area models, and explain multiplication as scaling
lessons.key_concepts: a/b x c/d = (ac)/(bd); 2/3 of 3/4 means taking 2/3 of a 3/4 amount; area model with overlapping shading; multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes the product smaller, greater than 1 makes it larger
lessons.prerequisites: Fraction meaning, multiplication facts, area of rectangles
lessons.key_vocabulary: product, factor, scaling, area model, 'of' as multiplication
lessons.common_misconceptions: Believes 'multiplication always makes bigger', so says 1/2 x 8 > 8; finds a common denominator before multiplying and multiplies only the numerators (1/4 x 3/4 = 3/4); multiplies a mixed number by multiplying wholes and fractions separately (2 1/2 x 2 1/2 = 4 1/4)
lessons.real_world_hook: Making 2/3 of a recipe that calls for 3/4 cup of sugar

lessons.lesson_title: Dividing with Unit Fractions and Whole Numbers
lessons.learning_objective: Divide a unit fraction by a whole number and a whole number by a unit fraction, and interpret each with models
lessons.key_concepts: 4 divided by 1/3 asks how many 1/3s fit in 4 (answer 12); 1/3 divided by 4 splits 1/3 into 4 equal parts (answer 1/12); division by a number less than 1 gives a larger quotient
lessons.prerequisites: Fraction meaning, multiplication of fractions, division as equal groups
lessons.key_vocabulary: quotient, divisor, dividend, how many groups, size of each group
lessons.common_misconceptions: Believes 'division always makes smaller', so says 4 divided by 1/3 is 4/3; confuses 4 divided by 1/2 with 4 x 1/2 = 2; reverses the dividend and divisor
lessons.real_world_hook: How many 1/4-pound burgers you can make from 3 pounds of ground beef

lessons.learning_objective: Divide fractions by fractions and explain why multiplying by the reciprocal works using common denominators and 'how many groups' reasoning
lessons.key_concepts: a/b divided by c/d = a/b x d/c; with common denominators, 3/4 divided by 1/8 = 6/8 divided by 1/8 = 6; checking by multiplication (quotient x divisor = dividend); interpreting remainders as fractions of the divisor
lessons.prerequisites: Dividing with unit fractions, multiplying fractions, equivalent fractions
lessons.key_vocabulary: reciprocal, multiplicative inverse, divisor, invert and multiply, quotient
lessons.common_misconceptions: Flips the first fraction instead of the divisor (3/4 divided by 1/2 = 4/3 x 1/2); flips both fractions; divides numerators and denominators but then misreads the remainder (1 1/2 groups read as 1 R1)
lessons.real_world_hook: Cutting a 3/4-yard ribbon into 1/8-yard pieces for a craft project

lessons.lesson_title: Decimal Place Value and Fraction Connections
lessons.learning_objective: Read, write, and represent decimals to the thousandths using place value and relate them to fractions with denominators 10, 100, and 1000
lessons.key_concepts: Each place is 1/10 of the place to its left; 0.3 = 3/10, 0.03 = 3/100; 0.30 = 0.3 (trailing zeros do not change value); expanded form; multiplying or dividing by 10 shifts digits one place
lessons.prerequisites: Whole-number place value, fractions with denominators 10 and 100
lessons.key_vocabulary: decimal, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, decimal point, place value, expanded form
lessons.common_misconceptions: Reads 0.25 as 'zero point twenty-five' without knowing it means 25 hundredths; thinks 0.3 = 1/3; thinks multiplying by 10 means 'add a zero' so 0.5 x 10 = 0.50
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading race times to the hundredth of a second

lessons.learning_objective: Compare and order decimals to the thousandths using place value and number lines
lessons.key_concepts: Compare digits from the largest place value down; annex zeros to align (0.5 = 0.500); locate decimals on a number line between tenths
lessons.key_vocabulary: compare, order, greater than, less than, annex zeros, number line
lessons.common_misconceptions: 'Longer is larger': says 0.125 > 0.5 because 125 > 5; 'shorter is larger' overcorrection: says 0.4 > 0.45 because tenths are bigger than hundredths; compares the digits right after the decimal as whole numbers (0.12 > 0.9)
lessons.real_world_hook: Ranking gymnasts by scores like 9.45, 9.5, and 9.455

lessons.lesson_title: Adding, Subtracting, Multiplying, and Dividing Decimals
lessons.learning_objective: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using standard algorithms and estimate to check decimal point placement
lessons.key_concepts: Line up place values (decimal points) when adding or subtracting; product's decimal places equal the total in the factors; to divide by a decimal, multiply divisor and dividend by the same power of 10; estimate first (3.9 x 2.1 is about 8)
lessons.key_vocabulary: sum, difference, product, quotient, power of ten, estimate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Right-aligns the last digits instead of the decimal points, so 3.5 + 1.25 is computed like 35 + 125 and gives 1.60; lines up decimal points when multiplying and puts one decimal place in the answer (0.2 x 0.3 = 0.6); moves the decimal in only the divisor when dividing
lessons.real_world_hook: Splitting a $47.85 restaurant bill among 3 friends

lessons.learning_objective: Convert fractions to decimals using long division, identify terminating and repeating decimals, and convert simple decimals to fractions
lessons.key_concepts: a/b = a divided by b; 1/4 = 0.25, 1/3 = 0.333..., 1/8 = 0.125; a fraction in simplest form terminates only if the denominator's prime factors are 2s and 5s; bar notation for repeating digits
lessons.prerequisites: Fractions as division, long division, decimal place value
lessons.key_vocabulary: terminating decimal, repeating decimal, bar notation, long division, equivalent
lessons.common_misconceptions: Converts 3/5 to 3.5 or 0.35 by writing the digits next to each other; thinks 1/3 = 0.3 exactly; divides denominator by numerator (4/5 computed as 5 divided by 4 = 1.25)
lessons.real_world_hook: Turning batting averages and store discounts into decimals

lessons.learning_objective: Use ratio language and ratio tables to describe relationships between two quantities and generate equivalent ratios multiplicatively
lessons.key_concepts: A ratio a:b compares two quantities; part-to-part vs part-to-whole ratios; equivalent ratios come from multiplying both quantities by the same number; ratio tables and double number lines; order matters
lessons.prerequisites: Multiplication and division facts, equivalent fractions
lessons.key_vocabulary: ratio, part-to-part, part-to-whole, equivalent ratio, ratio table, double number line
lessons.common_misconceptions: Additive reasoning: thinks 2:3 is equivalent to 4:5 because 2 was added to each; reverses the order of the ratio; reads a part-to-part ratio 2:3 as the fraction 2/3 of the whole
lessons.real_world_hook: Mixing paint so a bigger batch stays the same shade

lessons.learning_objective: Find and use unit rates, including with fractions, to compare rates and solve problems
lessons.key_concepts: A rate compares quantities with different units; a unit rate is the amount per 1 unit; divide to find it; comparing unit prices; unit rates with fractions (1/2 mile in 1/4 hour is 2 miles per hour)
lessons.key_vocabulary: rate, unit rate, unit price, per, miles per hour
lessons.common_misconceptions: Divides in the wrong order and reports hours per mile when asked for miles per hour; decides the bigger package is always the better deal without computing unit prices; drops the units and cannot interpret the number
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing price per ounce between two sizes of cereal

lessons.learning_objective: Decide whether two quantities are proportional using tables, graphs, and equations, and identify the constant of proportionality in y = kx
lessons.key_concepts: Proportional means y/x is constant for every pair; the graph is a straight line through the origin; k is the unit rate; the point (1, k); non-examples like a fixed fee plus a rate
lessons.key_vocabulary: proportional relationship, constant of proportionality, origin, y = kx, unit rate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Calls any straight-line graph proportional even when it does not pass through the origin (a taxi fare with a starting fee); checks only one pair in a table; thinks k is the y-value of the first row
lessons.real_world_hook: Checking if a phone plan's cost is proportional to data used

lessons.learning_objective: Solve proportion problems with equivalent ratios, unit rates, and equations, apply them to scale drawings and similar figures, and recognize when proportions do not apply
lessons.key_concepts: Set up corresponding quantities in the same positions; cross-multiplication works because both sides are equal ratios; scale factor; lengths in similar figures share one scale factor; not all situations are proportional
lessons.key_vocabulary: proportion, cross-multiplication, scale factor, scale drawing, corresponding sides, similar figures
lessons.common_misconceptions: Cross-multiplies in non-proportional situations (if 1 person takes 3 hours to paint a room, 3 people take 9 hours); mismatches units when setting up a proportion; adds instead of multiplying with a scale factor to find a missing side
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a map scale to plan a road trip

lessons.learning_objective: Understand percent as a rate per 100 and convert between fractions, decimals, and percents
lessons.key_concepts: Percent means 'per hundred'; 35% = 35/100 = 0.35; benchmark percents (10%, 25%, 50%, 1%); percents over 100% and under 1%; using a 10-by-10 grid and a percent bar
lessons.key_vocabulary: percent, per hundred, benchmark percent, percent bar, hundredths
lessons.common_misconceptions: Converts 5% to 0.5 instead of 0.05; thinks percents can never be more than 100%; converts 0.4 to 4% by moving the decimal one place
lessons.real_world_hook: Understanding a phone battery at 7% versus 70%

lessons.lesson_title: Finding the Part, Whole, or Percent
lessons.learning_objective: Find a percent of a quantity, find the whole given a part and the percent, and find what percent one number is of another
lessons.key_concepts: Part = percent x whole; whole = part / percent; percent = part / whole x 100; double number lines and percent tables; identify which number is the whole
lessons.prerequisites: Percent as rate per 100, multiplying and dividing decimals, proportions
lessons.key_vocabulary: part, whole, percent of, what percent, base
lessons.common_misconceptions: Multiplies when asked to find the whole (if 30 is 20% of a number, answers 6); uses the part as the whole when asked 'what percent of 50 is 20'; forgets to divide by 100 and computes 20% of 50 as 1000
lessons.real_world_hook: Figuring out how many questions you need right to get 80% on a 45-question test

lessons.learning_objective: Calculate percent increase and decrease using change divided by the original amount, and apply growth factors like 1.15 and 0.85
lessons.key_concepts: Percent change = (new - original)/original x 100; increase by p% means multiply by (1 + p/100); decrease by p% means multiply by (1 - p/100); percent change vs percent of; percentage points vs percent
lessons.prerequisites: Finding the part, whole, or percent; multiplying decimals
lessons.key_vocabulary: percent increase, percent decrease, percent change, original amount, growth factor, multiplier
lessons.common_misconceptions: Divides the change by the new amount instead of the original; confuses 'percent of' with 'percent change' (says going from 20 to 25 is 125% change instead of 25%); treats a change from 10% to 15% as a 5% increase instead of 5 percentage points (a 50% increase)
lessons.real_world_hook: Deciding whether a sneaker price going from $80 to $100 is a 20% or 25% increase

lessons.lesson_title: Discounts, Tax, Tips, Markups, and Successive Percent Changes
lessons.learning_objective: Solve multi-step real-world percent problems involving discounts, sales tax, tips, markups, simple interest, and successive percent changes
lessons.key_concepts: Sale price = original x (1 - discount); total with tax = price x (1 + tax rate); simple interest I = Prt; successive changes multiply (up 10% then down 10% gives 0.99 of the original, not the original); reversing a percent change by dividing, not subtracting
lessons.prerequisites: Percent increase and decrease, decimal operations
lessons.key_vocabulary: discount, markup, sales tax, tip, simple interest, successive percent change, original price
lessons.common_misconceptions: Adds successive percents (20% off then 10% off = 30% off); finds the original price before a 25% discount by adding 25% back to the sale price; thinks up 50% then down 50% returns to the start
lessons.real_world_hook: Checking whether '20% off plus an extra 10% off' at the mall is really 30% off

lessons.lesson_title: Negative Numbers, Opposites, and Absolute Value
lessons.learning_objective: Represent negative numbers on a number line, identify opposites, order integers and rational numbers, and interpret absolute value as distance from zero
lessons.key_concepts: Negatives are to the left of zero; opposites are the same distance from zero on opposite sides; numbers increase to the right; |a| is the distance from 0 and is never negative; contexts like temperature, elevation, and debt
lessons.prerequisites: Number line placement, fractions and decimals on a number line
lessons.key_vocabulary: integer, negative number, opposite, absolute value, rational number, zero
lessons.common_misconceptions: Says -7 > -2 because 7 > 2; thinks absolute value means 'change the sign' so |-3| = -3 or |5| = -5; thinks -1/2 is between -1 and -2
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing winter temperatures of -8 and -3 degrees

lessons.learning_objective: Add integers and explain sums using the number line and zero pairs
lessons.key_concepts: Adding a positive moves right, adding a negative moves left; a number and its opposite make 0 (zero pair); same signs: add absolute values, keep sign; different signs: subtract absolute values, take the sign of the larger absolute value
lessons.key_vocabulary: sum, zero pair, additive inverse, number line, absolute value
lessons.common_misconceptions: Overgeneralizes 'two negatives make a positive' to addition: -3 + -5 = 8; ignores signs and adds absolute values (-7 + 4 = 11); gives the sign of the first number instead of the larger absolute value
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracking yards gained and lost in a football drive

lessons.learning_objective: Subtract integers by rewriting subtraction as adding the opposite and interpret differences as distances on a number line
lessons.key_concepts: a - b = a + (-b); subtracting a negative is adding a positive; a - b is the distance from b to a with direction; subtraction is not commutative
lessons.key_vocabulary: difference, additive inverse, add the opposite, distance, commutative
lessons.common_misconceptions: Treats subtraction as commutative (5 - 8 = 3); computes -4 - 6 as -2 by ignoring the negative; changes the sign of the first number instead of the second when adding the opposite
lessons.real_world_hook: Finding the temperature change from -6 degrees at night to 9 degrees at noon

lessons.learning_objective: Multiply and divide integers using sign rules justified by patterns and the distributive property
lessons.key_concepts: Positive x negative = negative; negative x negative = positive, justified by patterns (3 x -2 = -6, 2 x -2 = -4, ... -1 x -2 = 2); division follows the same sign rules; division by zero is undefined; -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q)
lessons.prerequisites: Adding integers, multiplication facts, distributive property
lessons.key_vocabulary: product, quotient, sign rules, undefined, distributive property
lessons.common_misconceptions: Applies multiplication sign rules to addition (-3 + -4 = +7); thinks -12 divided by -3 is -4; counts negatives wrong in a product of three negatives
lessons.real_world_hook: Calculating total change in a stock price that drops $3 each day for 5 days

lessons.lesson_title: Operations with Negative Fractions and Decimals
lessons.learning_objective: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers, including negative fractions and decimals, to solve real-world problems
lessons.key_concepts: Integer sign rules apply to all rational numbers; combine fraction procedures with sign rules; -3^2 = -9 but (-3)^2 = 9; checking reasonableness with estimation
lessons.prerequisites: Integer operations, fraction and decimal operations
lessons.key_vocabulary: rational number, negative fraction, exponent, base, grouping symbols
lessons.common_misconceptions: Computes -3^2 as 9 (squares the negative sign); adds numerators and denominators with signs (-1/2 + 1/3 = 0/5); loses the negative sign partway through a multi-step problem
lessons.real_world_hook: Balancing a bank account with withdrawals and deposits in dollars and cents

units.unit_title: Expressions, the Equals Sign, and One-Step Equations

lessons.lesson_title: The Equals Sign as a Balance
lessons.learning_objective: Interpret the equals sign as meaning both sides have the same value and use balance reasoning to find missing numbers
lessons.key_concepts: '=' is a relationship (same value on both sides), not a 'write the answer' command; true and false number sentences; balance models; doing the same thing to both sides keeps it balanced
lessons.key_vocabulary: equals sign, equation, balance, equivalent, true, false
lessons.common_misconceptions: Operational view of '=': answers 8 + 4 = __ + 5 with 12 instead of 7; writes run-on equations like 3 + 5 = 8 x 2 = 16; thinks an equation must have the answer on the right
lessons.real_world_hook: Balancing a scale to find the weight of a mystery package

lessons.learning_objective: Evaluate numerical expressions with whole-number exponents and grouping symbols using the conventional order of operations
lessons.key_concepts: Grouping symbols first, then exponents, then multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right; exponent means repeated multiplication (2^3 = 2 x 2 x 2); fraction bars act as grouping
lessons.key_vocabulary: order of operations, exponent, base, power, grouping symbols, evaluate
lessons.common_misconceptions: Reads PEMDAS as 'multiplication always before division' (12 / 3 x 2 = 2); computes 2^3 as 6; works strictly left to right (3 + 4 x 2 = 14)
lessons.real_world_hook: Figuring a total bill with a coupon and tax in a single expression

lessons.learning_objective: Use variables to represent unknown or changing quantities and write and evaluate expressions from verbal descriptions
lessons.key_concepts: A variable stands for a number, not an object or label; 'less than' reverses order (5 less than n is n - 5); terms, coefficients, and constants; evaluating by substitution with parentheses
lessons.prerequisites: Order of operations, the equals sign
lessons.key_vocabulary: variable, expression, term, coefficient, constant, evaluate, substitute
lessons.common_misconceptions: Reads letters as labels: writes 6S = P for 'there are 6 students for every professor'; translates '5 less than n' as 5 - n; evaluates 3x when x = 4 as 34
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a formula for the cost of a movie night with x friends

lessons.learning_objective: Generate equivalent expressions using the distributive property and combining like terms, including with negative coefficients
lessons.key_concepts: Distributive property a(b + c) = ab + ac; like terms have the same variable part; combine coefficients; factoring out a common factor; testing equivalence by substituting a value
lessons.prerequisites: Variables, integer operations, order of operations
lessons.key_vocabulary: equivalent expressions, distributive property, like terms, combine, factor, coefficient
lessons.common_misconceptions: Distributes only to the first term (3(x + 4) = 3x + 4); combines unlike terms (3x + 2 = 5x); drops the negative when distributing -2(x - 5) = -2x - 10
lessons.real_world_hook: Calculating the cost of 3 combo meals each with a burger and fries

lessons.learning_objective: Solve one-step equations of the forms x + p = q and px = q, including with fractions, decimals, and negatives, and check the solution
